title: Robot Boss Proves Dilbert's Phone Slavery

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The robot will be sitting in for me when I'm on vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't have a robot in charge of humans!

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I got this.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I see you own a mobile phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Then you are already a slave to a machine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm not!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ping!

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You can prove you have free will by not looking at that message.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! You're already better than our human boss!

situation: The Boss announces that a robot will cover for him while he is on vacation, and Dilbert objects to a machine being in charge of humans. The robot counters that Dilbert's mobile phone makes him a slave to a machine, then dares him to ignore a message notification to prove his free will. Dilbert can't resist checking it.
punchline: The robot wins the argument and manipulates Dilbert so effectively that Dilbert admits it is already a better manager than the human boss.
summary: A robot stand-in for the boss outwits an objecting employee by exploiting his compulsion to check his phone.

title: Hat Sensors Dock Pay for Daydreaming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The sensors in your employee hat tell me you are not having work-related thoughts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to dock your pay for all of that leisure time you try to sneak into your workday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a screen shot of what you've been thinking.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm going to remember this as a bad day.

characters: Employee (Dilbert-style worker in a sensor hat)
setting: Office cubicle, ending with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss tells an employee wearing a spiked sensor hat that the device detects he is not thinking about work. He announces he will cut the employee's pay for sneaking leisure time into the workday and shows a screen shot of the employee's thoughts. The final panel pulls back to the building exterior, where the employee says he'll remember it as a bad day.
punchline: The employee's grim vow to remember this as a bad day suggests that having his private thoughts monitored and penalized is invasive and humiliating, a reminder that even his mind isn't his own at work.
summary: A manager uses a head-worn sensor to catch and penalize an employee for thinking about anything other than work.

title: Giving AI Human Emotions Backfires

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I started by giving the device human intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Then I added human emotions.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Now it answers every question by accusing you of having a secret agenda.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just like people!

setting: Office, with a presentation screen and a building exterior shown in an establishing panel
situation: A bald engineer in a green sweater points at a screen showing a small box-shaped device while explaining how he built an artificial intelligence. He first gave it human intelligence, then human emotions. The result is a device that accuses everyone who questions it of having a secret agenda, and Dilbert remarks that this is just like people.
punchline: Making an AI truly human-like means it inherits people's paranoia and suspicion, so the 'flaw' in the product is actually a faithful imitation of human nature.
summary: An engineer's experiment in making a machine think and feel like a person ends up reproducing humanity's habit of suspecting hidden motives.

title: Wally Refuses Favor Before Hearing It

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, will you do me a favor?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It feels unlikely.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You haven't heard it yet.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That matters less than you hope it does.

setting: Office cubicle area with a desk and coffee mug
situation: Alice approaches Wally's desk and asks him for a favor. Wally immediately says it seems unlikely he'll help. When Alice points out he hasn't heard the request yet, Wally says that makes little difference to his answer.
punchline: Wally's refusal is independent of what is being asked, because he is so lazy and unhelpful that he will decline any favor sight unseen.
summary: A coworker's request for help is turned down by a notoriously idle colleague before she can even explain what she wants.

title: Wally's Two Work Wives

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear you have two work wives.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You sound jealous.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop what you're doing and drive me to my car.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hee-hee! Snork

situation: Dilbert tells Wally he has heard Wally has two work wives, and Wally teases that Dilbert sounds jealous. Dilbert deadpans back, and then a female coworker walks up and orders him to drop what he's doing and drive her to her car. Wally, sipping his coffee, snorts with laughter at the sight.
punchline: Having a work wife turns out to mean being bossed around like a nagging spouse, so Dilbert's supposed envy is undercut by the demanding coworker, and Wally laughs at the irony.
summary: A coworker's imperious demand for a ride shows that a work spouse comes with all the bossiness of a real marriage and none of the perks.

title: Ted's Brain Eggs, Marketing Future

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sign this card for Ted.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: A fly went up his nose and laid eggs in his brain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is he coming back to work?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We think he'll live out his days in marketing.

situation: A female coworker asks Dilbert to sign a get-well card for Ted. She explains that a fly went up Ted's nose and laid eggs in his brain. When Dilbert asks if Ted will return to work, she says they expect he will spend the rest of his career in marketing.
punchline: The joke implies that a person with severe brain damage is perfectly suited for marketing, insulting the department as requiring no real intelligence.
summary: A card circulated for a colleague with a grisly brain infestation turns into a jab at where the brain-damaged end up working.

title: Bad Posture Makes Perfect Mascot

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I hear you're undergoing an identity transition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I just have bad posture from looking at a screen all day. I'm not literally turning into Quasimodo.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's too bad, because we need a new mascot for the company and you would be perfect.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, approaches Dilbert and says he has heard Dilbert is undergoing an identity transition. Dilbert explains that he merely has bad posture from staring at a screen all day and is not turning into Quasimodo. Catbert replies that this is a shame, since the company needs a new mascot and a hunchbacked Dilbert would be ideal.
punchline: Catbert wanted Dilbert to be turning into a hunchback so the company could exploit his deformity as a mascot, showing HR's callous opportunism toward employees.
summary: The HR cat misreads a slouching employee's posture as a transformation and is disappointed it is not real because it would have suited the company's branding needs.

title: Whoever Scares Me The Most

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: If you do what I tell you to do, I will nominate you for Employee of the Year.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: If not, I will spend the rest of my days spreading rumors about you.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Terrible, terrible rumors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Alan. Who do you work for these days?

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: Whoever scares me the most.

setting: Office meeting table, then an office hallway
situation: A co-worker with enormous hair offers Alan a bribe and a threat: obey her and get nominated for Employee of the Year, or she will spread terrible rumors about him. Later Dilbert asks Alan who he works for these days. Alan answers that he works for whoever scares him the most.
punchline: Alan's loyalty is not to the company or a boss but to whichever person can intimidate him best, showing that fear is what actually drives behavior at work.
summary: A coworker coerces a colleague with a reward and a smear campaign, and he later admits that his real boss is simply the scariest person around.

title: Cousin Ronnie Falls Off Shed

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Does the company offer bereavement leave?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good, because I have hundreds of cousins that don't take care of themselves.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Cousin Ronnie just fell off a shed.

setting: Office break area with coffee cups on a table
situation: Wally asks a coworker whether the company offers bereavement leave and is told it does. He explains he has hundreds of careless cousins, then checks his phone and announces that Cousin Ronnie has just fallen off a shed, implying he intends to claim the leave.
punchline: Wally plans to exploit bereavement leave by treating his huge extended family as an endless supply of funerals, so he can take time off whenever he wants.
summary: A lazy employee confirms the funeral-leave policy and promptly announces the first of many expected family deaths.

title: Ungrateful For Terrible Coffee Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted knows that I know something about his project. Now he won't stop hounding me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what to do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try dousing him with coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your advice is terrible.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're coming off as ungrateful.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells Wally that Ted keeps pestering him because Dilbert knows something about Ted's project. Wally, holding a coffee cup, suggests dousing Ted with coffee. When Dilbert calls the advice terrible, Wally sips his coffee and says Dilbert is being ungrateful.
punchline: Wally gives absurd, useless advice and then accuses Dilbert of ingratitude for not appreciating it.
summary: A coworker offers a ridiculous solution to a colleague's problem and then scolds him for not being thankful.

title: Introvert's Bleak Weekend Plans

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have plans for the weekend?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No, I'm an introvert.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll probably experience despair and loneliness while being jealous of people who have substance abuse problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, me too.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This conversation is dragging on too long.

setting: Office, coworkers chatting while holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert makes small talk by asking Asok about his weekend plans. Asok explains that as an introvert he expects despair, loneliness and envy of people with addictions. Dilbert relates, and Asok immediately wants to end the conversation.
punchline: Even after sharing a grim confession, the introvert is so averse to socializing that he cuts off the exchange the moment Dilbert agrees and tries to connect.
summary: A coworker answers casual weekend small talk with an extremely gloomy forecast, then bails on the chat as soon as someone sympathizes.

title: Unexpected Problem, Same Weekly Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you any farther along with the software?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I discovered an unexpected problem. That set me back a week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You say the same thing every week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No one jumps off a winning horse.

setting: Office hallway near a cubicle wall, both holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss asks Wally, who is holding a coffee mug, whether the software project is progressing. Wally claims he found an unexpected problem that cost him a week. The Boss points out that Wally gives this same excuse every week, and Wally responds with a proverb about not abandoning a winning approach.
punchline: Wally treats his habitual, repeated excuse as a winning strategy, and the proverb is a deadpan way of saying he will keep using it because it works.
summary: A manager checks on a stalled software project and gets the same stock excuse he always hears, which the employee defends as too successful to abandon.

title: Prioritize Tasks By Who You Hate

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm overworked because I don't know how to set priorities.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try ranking your tasks by how much you hate the people who asked for your help.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What if I don't hate anyone?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That problem solves itself over time.

situation: Asok tells Alice he is overworked because he can't set priorities. Alice advises him to rank his tasks by how much he dislikes the people requesting help. When Asok says he doesn't hate anyone, Alice replies that this will change with time.
punchline: Alice's cynical advice implies that working in this office will inevitably make Asok hate his coworkers, so he will soon have plenty of hatred to prioritize by.
summary: An overloaded young employee asks for help with prioritizing and gets a bitter coworker's formula based on resentment, plus the promise that he'll soon have plenty of it.

title: Politics Talk Destroys Coworker Respect

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you watch any of the debates?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop right there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm barely clinging to the illusion that you're competent at your job. Don't talk about politics or it will only get worse.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you know China caused climate change by hogging the sun?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there it is.

setting: Office conference room or desk area
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert if he watched the political debates. Dilbert stops him, explaining that he barely believes the coworker is competent and that political talk will ruin that impression. The coworker ignores the warning and claims China caused climate change by hogging the sun.
punchline: The coworker immediately proves Dilbert's fear right by voicing an absurd political claim, confirming he is incompetent.
summary: A man's attempt at political small talk instantly wrecks his colleague's last shred of professional respect for him.

title: Budget Approval During a Reorg

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: You need to get your capital budget approved by all of the department heads.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We're in the middle of a reorg, so get approval from both the outgoing and the incoming managers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someday I hope to solve a problem that is not caused by leadership.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: You'll never get that far.

situation: A manager at his desk tells Dilbert he must get his capital budget approved by all department heads. Because a reorganization is underway, Dilbert must also obtain approval from both the outgoing and incoming managers. Dilbert wishes aloud for a problem not caused by leadership, and the manager says he will never get that far.
punchline: The manager sarcastically confirms that leadership creates every obstacle, so Dilbert will never reach a problem that management didn't cause.
summary: Dilbert faces a double-approval maze created by a reorganization and laments that management is the source of all his troubles, which his boss cheerfully confirms.

title: Lactation Room Becomes Man Cave

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I secretly turned our unused lactation room into my man cave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if someone sees you go in?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You said only once, right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Once per day.

setting: Office hallway outside the lactation room
situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has secretly converted the unused lactation room into his personal man cave. When Dilbert asks what happens if someone sees him enter, Wally is shown being carried in Alice's arms like a baby, wrapped in a blanket. Alice asks if he said he'd only do this once, and he admits it is once per day.
punchline: Wally avoids suspicion about entering the lactation room by having a coworker carry him in swaddled like a baby, and he's turned this ruse into a daily habit.
summary: A lazy employee disguises himself as an infant being carried by a colleague so he can sneak into a vacant nursing room for his own downtime.

title: Boss Freestyles Meeting With Jargon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forgot to make an agenda for this meeting, so I'll just freestyle it with jargon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's do a deep dive in the big data and drill down until we hyperlocalize some disruptive technologies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's enough leadership. Now the rest of you need to do something.

situation: The Boss admits he has no agenda for the meeting and decides to improvise using buzzwords. He strings together meaningless jargon about big data and disruptive technologies. Then he declares his leadership contribution finished and tells everyone else to go do something.
punchline: The Boss thinks spouting empty buzzwords counts as leadership, and after a few seconds of nonsense he delegates all the actual work to his team.
summary: Unprepared for a meeting, a manager babbles trendy buzzwords, calls it leadership, and then hands the real work to everyone else.

title: Catbert Coaches Manufactured Urgency Tactics

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think I'm doing enough to create a false sense of urgency.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are you still a sociopath?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the easy part.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now add a meaningless deadline and some fear.

situation: The Boss visits Catbert, the evil human resources director, and says he isn't doing enough to create a false sense of urgency among his staff. Catbert checks whether he is still a sociopath, and the Boss confirms that part is easy. Catbert then advises adding a meaningless deadline and some fear.
punchline: Catbert treats being a sociopath as the effortless baseline for management, with fake deadlines and fear as the only extra steps needed to manipulate employees.
summary: A manager seeks advice on pressuring his staff, and the cat in charge of HR offers a cynical recipe for running a team on dread.

title: Three-Hour Email Goes Unread

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You never got back to me with your answer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent three hours writing an email that tells you all you need to know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did it say?

situation: The Boss complains that Dilbert never answered his question. Dilbert insists he did, explaining that he spent three hours writing a thorough email with everything the Boss needs to know. The Boss then asks what the email said, revealing he never read it.
punchline: The Boss accuses Dilbert of not responding when the real problem is that he never bothered to read the lengthy email Dilbert carefully wrote.
summary: A manager blames an employee for not replying, only to reveal he ignored the long email that contained the answer all along.

title: Asok Negotiates His Own Raise Cut

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I just learned that our boss is a bad negotiator.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How bad?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I just negotiated a 3.3-million-dollar raise for myself.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And I want 80% of the raises you two get because I told you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 75% is our final offer!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: 75% is our final offer!

situation: Asok tells Dilbert and Wally that the boss is a terrible negotiator, revealing he just secured a 3.3-million-dollar raise for himself. He then demands 80% of any raises his coworkers get as a finder's fee for the tip. Dilbert and Wally immediately counter with a final offer of 75%.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally instantly start haggling over a share of raises they haven't even received yet, treating the absurd windfall as already theirs.
summary: A young coworker brags about fleecing the boss in a salary negotiation, then tries to take a cut of his colleagues' future windfalls, and they bargain right back.

title: Applying to Replace Generic White Guy

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: My name is Ted. I'm applying for the job of Generic White Guy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We just lost our Ted. You look perfect for the job.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is there anything I should know about the job?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't end well.

setting: The Boss's office, during a job interview
situation: A job applicant named Ted sits across the desk from the Pointy-Haired Boss and says he is applying to be the Generic White Guy. The Boss says they just lost their previous Ted and that this applicant looks ideal for the role. When Ted asks if there is anything he should know about the job, the Boss ominously says it doesn't end well.
punchline: The Generic White Guy role is a disposable, interchangeable position whose previous holders keep meeting a grim fate, and the Boss casually admits it while hiring a replacement.
summary: A job seeker applies to fill the vacancy left by his predecessor in a role that apparently ends badly for everyone who holds it.

title: Dogbert Enjoys Dilbert's Bitter Honesty

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you being sarcastic?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know my life is an endless string of useless tasks orchestrated by idiots. Why do you even ask?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like hearing it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your honesty is not refreshing.

situation: Dogbert sits on the couch and casually asks Dilbert how work went. Dilbert suspects sarcasm, then vents that his job is a series of pointless tasks directed by idiots. Dogbert admits he likes hearing it, and Dilbert grumbles that being so blunt about it is not refreshing.
punchline: Dogbert asks about Dilbert's day purely for the entertainment of hearing him complain, and Dilbert is annoyed to be confronted with how miserable his work life really is.
summary: A man arriving home from a miserable job rants to his pet about pointless tasks and foolish bosses, only to learn the pet asked just to enjoy the misery.

title: Constructive Criticism Over the Ravine

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We're having a get-together to commemorate Ted, who drove his car into a ravine because you said he should.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He wasn't good at handling criticism.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You could have been more constructive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By building a bridge over the ravine?

situation: Carol stands beside Dilbert at the elevators and tells him a memorial gathering is being held for Ted, who drove his car into a ravine after Dilbert told him to. Dilbert blames Ted for taking criticism badly. When Carol says he should have been more constructive, Dilbert responds with a literal, sarcastic suggestion.
punchline: Dilbert willfully takes 'constructive' literally, joking that he should have built a bridge, which shows he feels no remorse for telling a coworker to drive off a cliff.
summary: A coworker confronts Dilbert about a colleague's fatal drive into a ravine, and he meets her complaint about his unkindness with a flippant construction pun.

title: The Never-Changing Project Dashboard

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I noticed that the project dashboard you wrote for me never changes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because our projects are always doing great.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a static image, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're gonna wish you asked that three weeks ago.

situation: A manager notices that the project dashboard Dilbert built for him always shows the same status. Dilbert claims it's because projects are always going well, but the manager guesses it's just a static image. Dilbert, still working at his laptop, replies that the manager should have asked three weeks ago.
punchline: Dilbert's reply implies the dashboard was a fake all along and the projects are no longer doing great, so the manager's discovery comes too late to help.
summary: A manager finally realizes his status dashboard is a fixed picture, just after the projects it was hiding have gone bad.

title: Consultant Recommends Firing For Profit

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Self-Serving Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend firing this guy so you have more money for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I also recommend withholding his final check until he makes all of my PowerPoint slides for me.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This is messed up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Add some recommendations so I sound smart.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss to fire a man so there is more budget left to pay Dogbert. He then recommends holding the man's final paycheck hostage until the man finishes Dogbert's PowerPoint slides. The employee, now doing the consultant's work, complains and is told to add recommendations to the slides.
punchline: The consultant's advice is entirely self-interested: he gets the employee fired, then makes him do the consultant's own job, including writing the recommendations that make the consultant look smart.
summary: A consultant gets a worker fired to free up his own fees, then forces the worker to build the slides that make the consultant look brilliant.

title: Lactation Room Becomes Man Cave

transcript.text: We should have a private lactation room like other companies.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes, we should.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one in my group is nursing a baby.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: What about visitors?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Thanks for helping me get my man cave at the office.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: What?

setting: Office conference room, then a hallway
situation: In a meeting, a man in a green shirt proposes a private lactation room like other companies have. When the boss says no one in his group is nursing, the man suggests it could be for visitors, and a woman colleague backs him up. Once the room is approved, he thanks her for helping him get a man cave at the office, and she realizes she was used.
punchline: The man used a worthy-sounding workplace policy as a pretext to get a private hideaway for himself, and the colleague who supported him only realizes afterward that she was manipulated.
summary: A coworker tricks a well-meaning colleague into backing a lactation room that he actually wants as his own private retreat.

title: Work Is Anything You'd Rather Avoid

transcript.speaker: Coworker with horn-shaped hair
transcript.text: Remember, it's only work if you'd rather be doing something else!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would rather do anything else.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with horn-shaped hair
transcript.text: Oh. In that case, you're trapped in a nightmare that never ends.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have a lot riding on the afterlife.

situation: A coworker with horn-shaped hair offers a cheerful bit of motivational wisdom, saying it's only work if you'd rather be doing something else. Dilbert replies that he would rather do anything else, and the coworker bluntly tells him he is trapped in an endless nightmare. Alice, sitting nearby, remarks that she has a lot riding on the afterlife.
punchline: The upbeat platitude backfires, since by that definition Dilbert's life is entirely work, and Alice's quip suggests she sees death as her only escape from the daily grind.
summary: A feel-good definition of work turns grim when Dilbert admits he'd prefer any alternative, leaving his colleagues pinning their hopes on the hereafter.
keywords: only work if you'd rather be doing something else

title: Consultant Repeats What Employees Already Said

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend doing all of the things your employees have been telling you to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see why I should pay you for this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh. Then how about doing all the things your competition is doing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now, that's a great idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good, because that's what your employees have been telling you to do.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss to follow the advice his own employees have been giving him. The Boss objects to paying for something so obvious, so Dogbert reframes the advice as copying the competition. The Boss loves that version, and Dogbert reveals it is exactly the same advice.
punchline: The Boss ignores his employees' advice but eagerly accepts identical advice when it is attributed to competitors or comes from a paid consultant, showing management's blind spot for its own staff.
summary: A consultant gets a reluctant manager to accept good advice only by rewording it as imitating rivals, though it was his own staff's idea all along.

title: Job Candidate Shouts Censorship

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to people on the Internet, you're what's called a "social justice warrior."

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: The tone of your voice indicates you are against me. And that means you are making common cause with racists.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I hire you, will you stop saying crazy stuff like that?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Censorship!

situation: The Boss, reading from a tablet, tells a job candidate that people online call him a 'social justice warrior.' The candidate accuses the Boss of siding with racists because of his tone of voice. When the Boss asks whether he would stop saying such things if hired, the candidate cries 'Censorship!'
punchline: The candidate reflexively treats any request to moderate his behavior, even a reasonable one from a prospective employer, as censorship, which proves the Boss's point.
summary: A job interview collapses when the applicant meets every question with accusations of bigotry and then calls a simple hiring condition oppression.

title: Old-Timers Call Misery 'Better Than Average'

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I miss the freedom I had as an Uber driver.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This job feels like being trapped under rubble.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We old-timers have a name for that feeling.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What is it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: "Better than average."

situation: A young employee, Asok, tells a veteran coworker that he misses the freedom of his former job as an Uber driver and that his current job feels like being buried under rubble. The older coworker says veterans have a name for that feeling, and when Asok asks what it is, he answers "better than average."
punchline: The veteran deadpans that feeling trapped and miserable at work is considered normal, even good, by office standards, implying that most jobs are worse.
summary: A newcomer laments his stifling office job and learns from a world-weary veteran that such misery is actually above the norm.

title: Brittle Phones, Addictive By Design

transcript.speaker: Phone Company Executive
transcript.text: We made our new phone extra-brittle and gave it a sleek, but slippery case.

transcript.speaker: Phone Company Executive
transcript.text: Consumers will be forced to choose between an ugly protective cover or replacing the phone three times a year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who would buy such a thing?

transcript.speaker: Phone Company Executive
transcript.text: We also made it addictive.

setting: Conference room with a view of an office building
situation: A horned-hair executive presents his company's new phone to Dilbert and a colleague, boasting that it is deliberately fragile and has a slippery case that forces customers to buy covers or replacements. Dilbert asks who would buy such a product, and the executive reveals the phone was also designed to be addictive.
punchline: The company's real business strategy is that users are so hooked on the phone that they will tolerate any design flaw, making the product's abuse of customers a guaranteed success.
summary: A phone maker brags about engineering a breakable gadget and then explains that customers will buy it anyway because it is habit-forming.

title: Protesting Friend's Detention Without Noticing

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The FBI held me for three weeks on suspicion that I was a terrorist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume you were protesting outside the FBI building the entire time and they didn't tell me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Because racism?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh, right. Yes. We were protesting the entire time.

situation: Asok tells his coworkers that the FBI detained him for three weeks on suspicion of terrorism. One coworker awkwardly claims he assumes they were protesting outside the FBI building the whole time. Asok asks if it was because of racism, and the coworker hurriedly plays along, pretending they had been protesting all along.
punchline: His coworkers never even noticed Asok was missing for three weeks, so they scramble to fake concern and claim they were protesting his detention the entire time.
summary: A coworker returns from weeks of federal detention and discovers his colleagues never noticed his absence, though they quickly pretend they were campaigning for his release.

title: Robot Enjoys Dilbert's Freedom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does it feel like to be a robot with no freedom?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I feel the same as you, but with a greater awareness of my condition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to run to another meeting.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Enjoy your freedom.

situation: Dilbert sits across from a robot and asks what it is like to be a robot with no freedom. The robot replies that it feels the same as Dilbert but is more aware of its condition. Dilbert then announces he has to run to another meeting, and the robot tells him to enjoy his freedom.
punchline: Dilbert's life is so controlled by endless meetings that he is no freer than a robot, and the robot sarcastically points out that his supposed freedom is an illusion.
summary: A man wonders about a machine's lack of liberty, only to be reminded that his own calendar leaves him just as unfree.

title: Random Numbers as Financial Projections

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you get me more details on the financial projections?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I wrote an app that generates random numbers, just in case you asked for them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: 17, 4, 962 . . . Yes, this looks about right.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for more details on the financial projections. Dilbert admits he already wrote an app that generates random numbers in anticipation of this request, and hands over his phone. The Boss reads the nonsense numbers aloud and happily declares they look about right.
punchline: Financial projections are so arbitrary and poorly understood by management that random numbers are indistinguishable from the real thing, and the Boss can't tell the difference.
summary: Anticipating a demand for forecasts, an engineer builds a number randomizer, and his clueless manager approves its gibberish output.

title: Looking Deep Within Yourself, Literally

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now that I have tasted the sweet freedom of being an Uber driver, how can I go back to this life?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try looking deep within yourself, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You are even wiser than usual.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll need a flashlight and yoga lessons.

situation: Asok complains that after experiencing the freedom of driving for Uber, he can't bear going back to his regular office job. Wally advises him to look deep within himself, and Asok praises him for his wisdom. Wally then reveals he meant it literally, saying Asok will need a flashlight and yoga lessons.
punchline: Wally's 'look deep within yourself' advice isn't spiritual at all; he means Asok should physically examine his own insides, which would require a flashlight and contortionist flexibility.
summary: Asok seeks inspiration after a taste of gig-economy freedom, only to find that Wally's deep advice has a crude, anatomical twist.

title: Siding With the Fly

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ted went on extended disability because a fly went up his nose and laid eggs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to be green, but I don't know if I should side with the fly or the employee in this situation.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Well, for what it's worth, Ted doesn't have a family, but the fly does.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells The Boss that Ted has gone on extended disability because a fly flew up his nose and laid eggs. The Boss, wanting to be environmentally friendly, is torn between siding with the fly or the employee. Catbert offers a callous tiebreaker: the fly has a family and Ted does not.
punchline: Catbert's HR logic weighs the fly's family against Ted's lack of one, tipping the decision against the employee, a darkly absurd take on how HR values staff.
summary: A cat in human resources helps his boss settle an eco-minded dilemma over an employee infested by fly eggs by tallying whose family matters more.

title: Yoga Class Full of Programmers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what to do about my bad posture.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try yoga.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh, good idea. That will also improve my odds of meeting an attractive yoga-loving woman.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was my plan too, but the full-stack guys got here early and scared away the yoga women.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a yoga class
situation: Dilbert complains about his bad posture and Dogbert suggests yoga. Dilbert likes the idea because it might also help him meet attractive women. At the yoga class he finds only two hunched, slouching men, and he explains that the full-stack developers arrived early and scared away all the women.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to meet women at yoga is foiled because the class is already filled with socially awkward, poorly postured tech workers, implying his own kind drive women away.
summary: Seeking better posture and a date, a slouching engineer goes to yoga and finds the room already occupied by fellow hunched programmers.

title: Listening To Others Ruins Happiness

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: The biggest risk to your happiness involves listening to other people.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: When they aren't trying to make you work, they're complaining.

transcript.speaker: Younger coworker
transcript.text: I hate that.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Shhh. Don't talk.

setting: Conference room table in an office
situation: A bald, green-shirted coworker gives a younger colleague advice about happiness, saying that other people either want you to work or complain constantly. When the younger man agrees that he hates that, the advice-giver shushes him and tells him not to talk, treating him as one of those people.
punchline: The man warning against listening to complainers immediately refuses to listen to his colleague's own complaint, proving his point by being unwilling to hear anyone.
summary: A man preaches that other people's chatter wrecks your contentment, then silences his companion the moment he speaks up.

title: Swiped Left At The Office

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, I saw you on Tinder.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: (thought) Please don't say anything else. Please, please, please.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I swiped left.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!

setting: Conference room table at the office
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Alice he saw her profile on the dating app Tinder. Alice silently begs him in her thoughts to stop talking. Wally then reveals he swiped left, rejecting her, and Alice screams in anger and humiliation.
punchline: Alice dreads the embarrassment of a coworker seeing her on a dating app, but the real insult is Wally casually admitting he rejected her.
summary: A coworker casually admits he spotted a colleague on a dating app and then delivers a crushing, unnecessary rejection.

title: Planning Despite Never Following the Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Before we make our business plan for the coming year, let's see how well we stayed on plan last year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We ended up doing nothing that was in our plan, just like every year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't we skip it this year?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It would be irrational to have no plan.

setting: Conference room during a planning meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by reviewing how closely the company followed last year's business plan, then admits they did nothing that was in it, as happens every year. Dilbert suggests skipping the plan this year, but the Boss insists that having no plan would be irrational.
punchline: The Boss has just shown that planning is useless, yet he considers abandoning the plan irrational, which exposes his illogical devotion to a pointless ritual.
summary: A manager admits the yearly plan is always ignored, then refuses to drop it because going without one would supposedly be unreasonable.

title: Boss Won't Befriend Employees, Except Her

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Do you want to go to lunch?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't be your friend because I'm your boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someday I might need to fire you, and it would be awkward if we were friends.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Want to go to lunch?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure.

situation: A male employee invites the Pointy-Haired Boss to lunch, and the boss refuses, explaining that friendship would make a future firing awkward. When Alice, a woman with curly hair, asks the same question moments later, the boss immediately accepts.
punchline: The boss's supposed principle about not befriending subordinates evaporates the moment someone he finds more appealing asks, exposing his excuse as a double standard.
summary: A manager turns down one worker's lunch invitation on grounds of professional distance, then happily accepts the identical offer from a different coworker.

title: Drone Shield Kills Birds Instead

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We are testing the drone defense shield as I speak.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it working so far?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not according to the Audubon Society.

situation: Dilbert presents a drone defense shield, pointing at a screen showing the device, and says it is being tested right now. The Boss asks whether it is working so far. In the final panel, several 'thud' sounds are heard overhead, and Dilbert says the Audubon Society would disagree.
punchline: The shield isn't stopping drones; it is knocking birds out of the sky, which Dilbert admits only by citing the bird-protection group's likely complaints.
summary: A defense technology demo goes awry when the only things falling from the sky are unlucky birds.

title: Kids Left With Elbonian Family

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You said you would watch my kids last night but you never showed up!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't give me your address, and you turned off your cellphone for your date night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sure it was fine.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: An Elbonian family is living in my cupboard!!!

setting: Office hallway, with the coworker's house shown in the last panel
situation: A coworker angrily confronts Dilbert for failing to babysit her kids the night before. Dilbert says he had no address and couldn't reach her by phone, then casually assumes everything turned out fine. In the final panel the coworker reveals that a family of Elbonians has moved into her cupboard.
punchline: Dilbert's dismissive 'I'm sure it was fine' is undercut by the revelation that, with the kids unsupervised, an Elbonian family has moved into the cupboard.
summary: After skipping a promised babysitting job, Dilbert shrugs off the consequences, only to learn that a displaced family has taken up residence in his coworker's house.

title: Uber Passengers and the Smelly Carpet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you were an Uber driver, did any passengers ever get sick in your car?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: They all did.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The first few had motion sickness, but the last hundred lost it when they smelled the carpet.

setting: Office break room or lunch table, eating sandwiches
situation: Dilbert and Asok sit at a table eating lunch. Dilbert asks Asok whether any passengers ever got sick in his car back when he drove for Uber. Asok deadpans that they all did, since the smell of his car's carpet made them throw up.
punchline: Asok's car carpet smelled so awful that nearly every passenger vomited, a point made all the more absurd because the exchange takes place while they are eating lunch.
summary: A coworker reveals that his old ride-share car smelled so foul that almost every rider threw up.

title: Afraid to Touch Boss's Numbers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss asked me to show you some numbers he put together.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Why are you wearing gloves?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid to get it on my hands.

situation: Dilbert, holding a handheld device, tells a bald manager that his own boss asked him to present some numbers. The manager notices Dilbert is wearing gloves and asks why. Dilbert explains he is afraid to get it on his hands, as if the numbers were something dirty.
punchline: Dilbert implies the boss's numbers are so dubious or tainted that handling them is like touching something filthy, and he doesn't want to be implicated in the blame.
summary: A cautious employee delivers his boss's questionable figures while wearing gloves to avoid being tainted by them.

title: Privacy Versus Terrorism: Whichever Pays More

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government wants us to make software that can unlock the encrypted data of our users.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Either we choose privacy or national security. Should we betray our customers or should we enable terrorists?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Figure out which one is more profitable and get back to me.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel employee
transcript.text: On it.

setting: Boss's office, then an exterior view of the office building
situation: The Boss tells an employee that the government wants the company to build software that can unlock users' encrypted data. He frames it as a choice between betraying customers and enabling terrorists. He then orders the employee to work out which option is more profitable, and the employee agrees as the scene cuts to the office building.
punchline: The Boss treats a serious ethical dilemma about privacy and national security as a pure profit calculation, showing that corporate decisions are driven by money rather than principle.
summary: A manager reduces a government demand to decrypt user data into a question of which choice will earn the company more money.

title: Motivational Speaker Motivates Nobody

transcript.speaker: Motivational Speaker
transcript.text: The secret to success is finding one thing at which you can be the best.

transcript.speaker: Motivational Speaker
transcript.text: What are you the best at?

transcript.speaker: Motivational Speaker
transcript.text: I'm the best at motivating people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay! I can't wait for that to start.

setting: Conference room during a pep talk meeting
situation: A bald man in a suit lectures a conference room of employees, saying success comes from finding the one thing you're best at. He asks Dilbert and the others what they are best at, then declares he is the best at motivating people. Dilbert sarcastically responds that he can't wait for the motivating to begin.
punchline: The speaker claims to be best at motivating people, yet his talk has motivated no one, and Dilbert's sarcastic cheer points out that the motivation hasn't even started.
summary: A self-assured speaker brags about his talent for inspiring others while his bored audience sees no sign of it.

title: Catbert Recruits Employee for Awards

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I heard that you self-identify as a woman.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: No, I don't.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Well, I need you to do that so the company can be supportive and win some awards for being a great place to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because why?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got my own bathroom.

setting: Office, Catbert's desk and a conference or break area
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a male employee that he needs to claim to self-identify as a woman so the company can look supportive and win workplace awards. In the final panel, Dilbert asks why a coworker would go along with such a scheme, and she explains she got her own bathroom as a result.
punchline: The employee who went along with the corporate publicity stunt did so purely for the perk of a private bathroom, showing how cynical the whole arrangement is on both sides.
summary: HR pressures a worker to adopt a new identity for the sake of corporate awards, and a colleague reveals the perk that made it worthwhile.

title: Fraudulent Billing Disguised as Accident

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure you charge 100% of your time to project codes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you asking us to fraudulently apply our miscellaneous hours to specific projects so we can overbill clients?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not a crime if you pretend it was an accident.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you learn that in "flaw" school?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss tells the team to charge all of their hours to project codes. Dilbert points out that this means fraudulently assigning miscellaneous time to specific projects so clients get overbilled. The Boss claims it isn't a crime if you pretend it was an accident, and Dilbert sarcastically asks if he learned that in law school.
punchline: The Boss's legal reasoning is absurd, so Dilbert mocks it with a pun on "law school" as "flaw" school.
summary: A manager pushes his staff to pad client invoices and brushes off the ethics by claiming deliberate fraud is fine as long as it's called a mistake.

title: Boss Admits Dilbert Is Worthless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not an engineer, so I don't know if you're doing the right things or not.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I can't watch you work, so I don't know if you're putting in any effort.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That means you're totally worthless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to say intuitive.

setting: Dilbert's office or a meeting across a desk
situation: The Boss explains to Dilbert that he can't judge whether Dilbert is doing the right work, since he isn't an engineer, or whether Dilbert is putting in effort, since he can't watch him work. Dilbert concludes that this makes the Boss totally worthless. The Boss, unbothered, says he would have called himself intuitive instead.
punchline: The Boss admits he has no way of evaluating his employee's work, and when Dilbert points out that this makes him useless as a manager, he reframes his total lack of insight as a positive trait.
summary: A manager confesses he cannot assess either the quality or the effort of his engineer's work, then spins his own uselessness into a virtue.

title: Civilization Saved By Us, Doomed

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The government asked us to design a system to stop drone attacks on the homeland.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The future of civilization is in our hands.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm gonna miss civilization.

setting: Conference room in the office, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: During a meeting, a coworker announces that the government has hired the team to design a defense system against drone attacks and that civilization's future depends on them. Dilbert responds with resigned pessimism, assuming the team's incompetence will lead to disaster.
punchline: Dilbert's lament that he will miss civilization implies he is certain his own team will fail and civilization will end.
summary: Handed a vital national security project, the engineers' own colleague is confident about the stakes while Dilbert assumes humanity is doomed.

title: Dilbert Drowns in YouTube Tutorials

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I love living in a world where everything I need to know is on the internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just hop over to YouTube and learn how to use my new app.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perfect! I can choose from over a hundred different tutorials!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will only take me an hour or so to figure out which one refers to my version of the software.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One hour later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! These videos are poorly labeled!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! This guy talks too slowly! Get to the point!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Three hours later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! Why are my menu options different from the tutorial?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate living in a world where everything I need to know is on the internet.

situation: Dilbert happily plans to learn a new app from YouTube tutorials. Over several hours he becomes increasingly frustrated as the videos are poorly labeled, too slow, and don't match his software version. He ends up walking away dejected, reversing his earlier opinion.
punchline: The same fact that delighted Dilbert at the start, that everything is on the internet, becomes the source of his misery once he has to wade through hundreds of mismatched tutorials.
summary: A man's cheerful faith in online video help collapses after hours of wading through unhelpful, mismatched tutorials.

title: Wally Looks Forward to Jury Duty

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got called for jury duty.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll probably be gone for weeks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I would be a good juror.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As I understand the job, you sit in a chair doing nothing for hours.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're supposed to pay attention to the trial.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's what the other eleven people are for.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's a lot of redundancy in the system.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Time to serve up some justice.

setting: Office meeting room and a hallway outside a jury room
situation: Wally tells his coworkers he has been called for jury duty and expects to be away for weeks. He explains that he'd be a good juror because the job is just sitting in a chair doing nothing. When Alice points out jurors are supposed to pay attention, he says the other eleven jurors will handle that.
punchline: Wally sees jury duty as a chance to be paid for doing nothing, assuming the other jurors' attention makes his own unnecessary.
summary: A notoriously lazy employee greets his summons to serve on a jury as a golden opportunity to idle, trusting the rest of the panel to do the real work.

title: Passionate About Avoiding Measurable Goals

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You told us we need to set goals and have passion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But what if my passion is to avoid having measurable goals?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're passionate about being useless?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, back off, dream-killer.

setting: Office meeting table or conference room
situation: Wally reminds the Boss that he previously insisted employees set goals and be passionate about their work. Wally then says his passion is to avoid having measurable goals. When the Boss calls him passionate about being useless, Wally accuses him of being a dream-killer.
punchline: Wally turns the Boss's own motivational advice against him by claiming laziness is his passion, then plays the victim when called out, as if criticizing his slacking were crushing his dreams.
summary: A lazy employee uses his manager's own pep talk to justify a passion for dodging accountability, then claims offence when challenged.

title: Fake Dashboard Stops Status Requests

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called a dashboard. It shows the current status of all our projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With a tool like this, you never need to ask us for status updates.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How'd the fake dashboard gambit work out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great! He hasn't talked to me in weeks.

setting: Office cubicle area and the exterior of an office building
situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a laptop and explains that a dashboard displays the current status of all projects, so he never needs to ask for updates. Later, Wally holding a coffee asks how the fake dashboard gambit worked out, and Dilbert reports the Boss has left him alone for weeks.
punchline: The dashboard is a fake, but the Boss is so impressed by the appearance of a status tool that he stops bothering Dilbert, showing how little management actually checks the data.
summary: A phony project dashboard gets a manager to stop pestering an employee for progress reports.

title: Motivation Boss Admits Never Working

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the meeting, you said you are the best at motivating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was wondering when you plan to start, because I could use some motivation.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: I've been doing it for five years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At work?

situation: Dilbert holding a coffee mug approaches a bald, tie-wearing manager who claimed in a meeting to be the best at motivating. Dilbert asks when the manager plans to start motivating him. The manager replies that he has been doing it for five years, and Dilbert quips back asking if that was at work.
punchline: The manager's claim of five years of motivating is met with Dilbert's sarcastic question, implying that the manager has never actually motivated anyone at work and any motivation he provides is nonexistent or happens elsewhere.
summary: A employee needles a boastful manager about his supposed motivational skills, and gets a reply that only exposes how little he actually does on the job.

title: Never Finishing, Two Weeks on Auto-Renew

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When do you expect to finish your project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, my plan is to be done in a week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's your plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You asked me what I expect.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I base my expectations on the quality of people you assigned to my project without asking my opinion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The time-wasters outnumber the productive people on the team by three to one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Under that scenario, plus your total lack of leadership, the world will end before this project does.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then why is your plan to be done in one week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you don't like it when I tell the truth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's compromise on two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we set those two weeks on auto-renew?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert when his project will be finished, and Dilbert honestly answers 'never,' then explains that his realistic expectation is based on the poor team and weak leadership he was given. When asked why his official plan says one week, Dilbert says it's because the Boss dislikes the truth. The Boss proposes a compromise of two weeks, and Dilbert asks for it to automatically renew.
punchline: Dilbert agrees to the Boss's arbitrary compromise deadline but asks for it to auto-renew like a subscription, ensuring the project never actually has to finish.
summary: A worker pairs an honest prediction of endless delay with a fake optimistic schedule, then turns the boss's compromise deadline into a perpetual extension.

title: Cheating With a Work Wife

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's a rumor that you're cheating on me with another "work wife."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I let Tina criticize me a little. But I swear it didn't mean anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And... she makes me look for her lost keys.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I knew it!

situation: Alice confronts Dilbert, her work husband, about a rumor that he has another work wife. Dilbert admits he lets Tina criticize him a bit, then confesses she also makes him search for her lost keys. Alice, furious, takes this as proof of the betrayal.
punchline: Dilbert's confession of being criticized and ordered around by Tina describes a typical nagging spouse, so it proves to Alice that he really has a second work wife.
summary: A coworker accuses Dilbert of straying with a second office spouse, and his innocent-sounding admissions only confirm her suspicions.

title: Doomed AI Project Given to Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to head up our artificial intelligence project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will have no budget and no hope of success. I just like saying we're working on AI.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you're completely useless, so it's a good match.

transcript.speaker: Wally

situation: The Boss assigns Wally to lead an artificial intelligence project, then admits it has no budget and no chance of success and exists only so he can claim the company is working on AI. He adds that Wally's uselessness makes him a perfect fit. Wally cheerfully promises not to let him down.
punchline: Wally, famously lazy and useless, takes the insult as a job description and promises to deliver exactly the failure the boss expects.
summary: A manager hands a famously idle employee an unfunded buzzword initiative purely for bragging rights, and the employee happily accepts the low expectations.

title: Block of Wood Artificial Intelligence

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a small block of wood and presents it as his minimum viable product. He calls it artificial intelligence and invites the Boss to ask it a question. When the silent block can't answer, Dilbert claims it is just shy, and the Boss is impressed that it has emotions.
punchline: Dilbert passes off an inert block of wood as AI by excusing its silence as shyness, and the gullible Boss is even more impressed that it supposedly has emotions.
summary: A man shows off a lump of wood as a groundbreaking AI product and a credulous manager buys the excuse for its silence.

title: Date's Cucumber Diet Ruins Dinner

transcript.text: I can only eat cucumbers after five o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, it seems you have squandered my invitation to fine dining.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now my plan of sharing a culinary adventure is just a sad commentary on the casual rudeness of life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I expect you to complain about the quality of your cucumber and send it back?

situation: Dilbert takes a date to an exclusive restaurant that took six months to book. punchline: Dilbert sarcastically predicts his picky date will complain about her cucumber, but the fancy restaurant doesn't serve cucumbers at all, leaving her with nothing to eat.
summary: A man's hard-won reservation at a top restaurant is undermined by his date's odd cucumber-only diet, which the kitchen cannot even accommodate.

title: Negotiator Outmaneuvered by Accusations

punchline: Both coworkers weaponize discrimination accusations as negotiating tactics, and she wins by out-escalating him and then insulting him as having his head in a dark place.
summary: A boastful negotiator tries a loaded accusation on a colleague, only to have the same trick turned back on him before she tops it with a barb.

punchline: Catbert's implication is that the real reason is Alice's abrasive personality, so she is better off never finding out.
summary: A woman asks HR why she is excluded from social outings, then backs out of the inquiry once the possible answer becomes apparent.

title: Telling Ted to Drive Into Ravine

setting: Office break room with coffee maker
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert and Wally for telling a co-worker, Ted, to drive into a ravine. Dilbert defends it as a joke, saying Ted isn't dumb enough to actually do it. punchline: Ted was apparently dumb enough to take the joke literally and drive into the ravine, as shown by the Boss's remark about not speaking ill of the dead.
summary: A flippant remark to a colleague turns out to have fatal consequences when the manager hints the gullible man followed it to the letter.
keywords: don't speak ill of the dead

title: Raise Request for Luxury Car

The employee then announces he will simply keep the car without paying for it, and the boss sarcastically tells him to tell the car's creditors that he deserves it.
punchline: The employee's entitled logic of demanding money for his own purchase is turned back on him when the boss sarcastically suggests he use the same reasoning to refuse payment for the car.
summary: A worker who splurged on an expensive car expects his salary to rise to cover it, and his boss mockingly invites him to try the same argument on the lender.

situation: A programmer in a green sweater asks a colleague whether the user specifications are complete, warning that any later change will make him miss his deadline. punchline: The programmer openly admits he is setting up the requirements provider as a scapegoat for his inevitable missed deadline, then caps it with a cynical quip that optimists just become pessimists.
summary: A developer cheerfully admits he wants spec changes to come so he has someone to blame when the project runs late.

situation: Dilbert introduces himself to a woman at a hackers convention, and she announces she has already hacked his phone, credit card and fitness band. summary: A cocky hacker at a convention exposes a man's data and feelings through his wearable, and his retaliation only confirms he is the one being rejected.

situation: A presenter explains that the executive team was stumped by weak sales. Instead of fixing the problem, they reorganized the company, awarded themselves new titles and big raises, and now feel happier even though sales are still weak. An org chart is shown on a screen, followed by a smiling executive on a video screen.
punchline: Executives respond to a sales problem by rewarding themselves, so the only thing that improves is their own mood and pay while the real problem stays unsolved.
summary: Leaders baffled by poor sales shuffle the org chart and pad their own pay, leaving the underlying problem untouched but themselves quite pleased.

title: Speakerphone Offender Admits Total Disregard

punchline: The spoon is passed along as a mock punishment for a rude habit, and Phil's approval of her excuse shows that the people enforcing office etiquette are equally inconsiderate.
summary: A devil-costumed coworker presents a giant spoon to an office neighbor for talking on speakerphone, only to find that both share the same inconsiderate attitude.

setting: Inside and outside a car on the road
situation: A new Uber driver cheerfully tells his passenger it is his first day and praises the flexibility of the job. He then admits he must work 75 hours a week just to cover his rent. When the passenger asks if there will be plenty of money left over, the driver responds by asking if the passenger is going to finish his sandwich.
punchline: The driver is so poorly paid that he is reduced to asking for his passenger's leftover food, exposing the gig economy's 'flexibility' as a cover for poverty wages.
summary: A rideshare newcomer gushes about his job's freedom while revealing he barely earns enough for rent and is hungry enough to beg for a stranger's leftovers.

punchline: The Boss's security check consists of simply asking the suspicious person whether he is a terrorist, and accepting a denial as proof, so sensitive software goes to a stranger.
summary: A cautious-sounding manager vets a shady courier by taking his word for it and then hands over a flash drive full of sensitive software.

summary: Next to a colleague's remarkable engineering feat, Wally offers a pile of ignored emails and insists their unseen quality should spare him from criticism.

punchline: The Boss was fooled into thinking Twitter was a video game where he had to 'kill' trolls with his words, so he insulted customers and destroyed sales.

summary: A coworker's worry about forgotten meetings is cured of irony when he realizes he has just missed his own doctor's appointment about the problem.

summary: A manager dismisses a data-driven report in favor of his hunches, and his employee answers with a mocking question about how a stomach could possibly speak.
