title: Bad Leadership Radicalizes Asok

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: We've been tracking an accused terrorist named Asok.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: We believe he was radicalized here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What did you do to him?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leadership?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yup. That's the top cause.

situation: A government agent shows a photo of Asok to The Boss and Alice, explaining that Asok is an accused terrorist who was radicalized at this company. Alice asks what they did to him, and The Boss guesses that it was leadership. The agent confirms that poor leadership is the top cause of radicalization.
punchline: The agent confirms that bad management, exemplified by The Boss, is the leading cause of turning employees into extremists.
summary: Investigators tracking a suspected extremist trace his radicalization back to the clueless management at his own workplace.

title: Wally's Agile Class Turns Acrobatic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll ask Wally to write this software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I haven't seen him since he took that agile programming class.

situation: Dilbert walks along thinking he will ask Wally to write some software. In the next panel Wally is seen flipping over a cubicle wall, and in the last panel he hangs from the top of a partition while Dilbert thinks he hasn't seen Wally since the agile programming class.
punchline: Wally apparently took 'agile' literally and treated the programming class as gymnastics training, which conveniently makes him impossible to pin down for actual coding work.
summary: A coworker's plan to delegate coding falls apart when the colleague has taken the word 'agile' as an invitation to vault over cubicle walls.

title: Vendor Says Software Needs Different Electricity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I bought new software for our network.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who helped you on the technical side?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The vendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He said our current software uses the wrong kind of electricity.

situation: The Boss announces he has bought new network software. Dilbert asks who advised him on the technical side, and the Boss says it was the vendor. He then repeats the vendor's absurd claim that the existing software runs on the wrong kind of electricity.
punchline: The Boss blindly trusts a salesperson's nonsensical technical claim, showing he can't tell a self-serving sales pitch from real technical advice.
summary: A gullible manager buys new software because the salesman told him the old programs ran on the wrong sort of power.

title: Misleading Summary or Incomprehensible Analysis

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want the detailed analysis you won't understand...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or the executive summary that is dangerously misleading?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want an executive summary that is not misleading.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll count on you not knowing the difference.

situation: Dilbert offers his boss two reports: a detailed analysis the boss won't be able to understand, or an executive summary that is dangerously misleading. The boss asks for a summary that is not misleading, and Dilbert replies that he is counting on the boss being unable to tell the difference.
punchline: Dilbert will hand over a misleading summary anyway, relying on the boss's ignorance to get away with it.
summary: An employee gives his manager a choice between a report he can't grasp and a summary that deceives him, then admits he'll simply bank on the manager never noticing the difference.

title: Retirement Plan: Die at Desk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw an article that says most people don't have any kind of retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I plan to live an unhealthy lifestyle and pass away in my cubicle, preferably on a Monday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a terrible plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Better than average, according to you.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert mentions an article saying most people have no retirement plan. Wally cheerfully announces his own plan: live unhealthily and die in his cubicle, ideally on a Monday. Dilbert calls it terrible, and Wally points out that by Dilbert's own statistic it still beats most people's non-existent plans.
punchline: Wally turns Dilbert's statistic against him: since most people have no plan at all, even a morbid plan to die at his desk counts as above average.
summary: Wally's grim scheme to expire at work turns out to be superior to the nonexistent plans of most people.

title: Too Many File Sharing Options

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you send me the file?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want it by email, Dropbox, Google Drive, iCloud Drive, AirDrop, or Creative Cloud?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Surprise me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The surprise will be if you find it.

setting: Office meeting table with cubicle partitions
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to send him a file. Dilbert responds by listing a long series of file-sharing services he could use, and when the coworker tells him to just pick one, Dilbert says the surprise will be if the coworker ever locates the file.
punchline: With so many competing file-sharing services, Dilbert could send the file to any of them, and the recipient will probably never find where it ended up.
summary: Faced with a request for a file, Dilbert rattles off half a dozen sharing platforms and then warns that choosing at random means the recipient will struggle to track it down.

title: Blaming the Boss for Delays

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is three weeks behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the exact amount of time I was waiting for you to answer my questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to manage me better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, you're fired.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: The Boss, holding a tablet, tells Dilbert his project is three weeks late. Dilbert replies that the delay matches exactly how long he waited for the Boss to answer his questions. The Boss says Dilbert should manage him better, and Dilbert turns it around by firing him.
punchline: Dilbert takes the Boss's absurd demand to 'manage up' literally and answers with the ultimate managerial act, firing his own boss.
summary: A manager blames an employee for a late project, but the employee turns the tables when told to manage his boss better.

title: Never Ask Him How He Is

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for meeting me on short notice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How are you?

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: Well, actually, someone stole my identity and ruined my credit score.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: I couldn't refinance my loan and lost my house.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: So I ate myself into poor health.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: I stopped shaving for a month and ended up on the terrorist watch-list.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: My boss hates me and is trying to make me quit by giving me bad assignments.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: My car broke down and I haven't been hugged in a year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, let's get started.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: That's all the time I had.

situation: Dilbert opens a meeting with a polite 'How are you?' and the bearded coworker answers literally, reciting a long chain of personal misfortunes including identity theft, losing his house, poor health, and loneliness. Dilbert sits through all of it, then says to get started, only to learn the coworker has used up the entire meeting time.
punchline: Asking 'How are you?' as a mere pleasantry backfires when the coworker answers honestly and burns the whole meeting on his woes.
summary: A routine greeting unleashes a torrent of one man's bad luck that swallows the entire meeting slot.

title: Spittle Gives Away Office Romance

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How's your office romance with Loud Howard coming along?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: How did you hear about us?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He's loud and you're always covered with his spittle.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I was hoping it looked like perspiration.

setting: Office desk, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Carol asks Tina how her secret office romance with Loud Howard is going. Tina is surprised and wonders how Carol found out. Carol explains that Howard is loud and Tina is always covered in his spittle, and Tina admits she hoped it looked like sweat.
punchline: Tina's attempt to keep the romance secret is blown by the obvious evidence of Loud Howard's spitting, which she had hoped would pass for perspiration.
summary: A coworker spots a hidden workplace relationship because one partner's constant loud talking leaves telltale moisture on the other.

title: Ransomware Smartwatch Excuse for Laziness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People say the complexity of modern life is a bad thing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But for useless people such as me, it creates endless opportunities.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why aren't you done yet?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My smartwatch was infected with ransomware.

setting: Office hallway and the boss's office
situation: Wally chats with Dilbert in the hallway, holding his coffee mug, and explains that modern life's complexity is a gift to useless people like him. He then sits in front of his boss, who asks why his work isn't finished. Wally blames a ransomware infection on his smartwatch.
punchline: Wally demonstrates his point by using absurdly modern technology problems as a fresh, hard-to-challenge excuse for doing no work.
summary: A habitually idle employee explains how today's tangled technology gives him ever-new reasons to avoid working, then promptly deploys one on his manager.

title: Sweater of Ice Packs Compromise

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's freezing in here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm hot. Put on a sweater.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why am I the one who has to change? You should wear a sweater made of ice packs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's time to admit I'm a bad negotiator.

situation: Alice complains the office is freezing while Dilbert, who is sweating, tells her to put on a sweater. She retorts that he should be the one to adapt and sarcastically suggests a sweater made of ice packs. In the last panel Dilbert is wearing exactly that, covered in ice packs, and concedes he is a poor negotiator.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic suggestion was taken as a real compromise, and Dilbert ended up wearing the ice pack sweater, proving he loses every negotiation.
summary: A thermostat dispute ends with one coworker bundled in frozen gel packs after losing the argument to a sarcastic remark.

title: Wally Gaming the Referral Bonus

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stop! Why are you here?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I have an interview for a job as an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My name is Wally. Tell Human Resources I referred you and I'll get a $1,000 bonus.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed that all of our new hires were referred by the same person?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sounds like we found our Employee of the Year!

setting: Office hallway and Human Resources office
situation: Wally stops a stranger in the hallway and learns he is there to interview for an engineering job. Wally hands him a card and tells him to say Wally referred him so Wally can collect a $1,000 referral bonus. Later, a man in a suit points out that every new hire was referred by the same person, and Catbert cheerfully says that makes him Employee of the Year.
punchline: Wally exploits the employee referral bonus by claiming credit for strangers, and the company rewards the scheme instead of seeing it as a scam.
summary: A lazy engineer cashes in on strangers heading to job interviews, and the company's own HR cat applauds the racket.

title: Spreadsheet Approval Needs a Hug

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I approve this project based on your boss' spreadsheet calculations.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: His calculations must be accurate because an engineer handed them to me.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Is that all you need?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a hug, but I don't want to catch whatever caused all of this.

situation: A bald executive with a tablet approves a project because of spreadsheet calculations from Dilbert's boss. He decides the numbers must be accurate simply because an engineer passed them to him. Dilbert, who is that engineer, asks for a hug but fears catching whatever condition caused such flawed reasoning.
punchline: Dilbert treats the executive's baseless faith in the spreadsheet as a contagious illness, saying he would like a hug but doesn't want to catch whatever caused it.
summary: A manager trusts questionable figures merely because an engineer delivered them, leaving that engineer in need of comfort but wary of catching the stupidity.

title: Identity Thief Makes Smart Investment

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: An identity thief stole my identity and opened a brokerage account.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did they know he was an impostor? Did he make a smart investment?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That isn't funny.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did the impostor have a sense of humor?

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker complains that an identity thief stole his identity and opened a brokerage account. Dilbert and Wally respond with jokes, implying the impostor must have been detectable because he invested wisely, and then asking whether the impostor had a sense of humor. The coworker, who is the victim, says it isn't funny.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally mock the victim by joking that the thief's smart investing would have revealed he was an impostor, and that the impostor was probably funnier than the real person.
summary: A man reports his stolen identity and gets teased by his two colleagues, who suggest the fraudster was a better investor and a better comedian than he is.

title: Referral Bonus For Gullible Acquaintances

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any friends with technical skills who you can recommend to work here?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't have any friends, but if I did, why would I be so mean to them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You get a $1,000 bonus for referring a friend.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How much for a gullible acquaintance?

situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he knows any technically skilled friends he could recommend for a job at the company. Wally says he has no friends and wouldn't subject them to working there anyway. When the Boss mentions a $1,000 referral bonus, Wally asks what the payout is for a gullible acquaintance instead.
punchline: Wally implies the company is such a bad place to work that he would only refer someone naive enough to be tricked into it, and he is happy to sell out a sucker for cash.
summary: Wally wouldn't inflict his workplace on a friend, but a cash incentive makes him willing to hand over someone easily fooled.

title: Boss's Praise Feels Like Stalking

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you're doing a great job and the company values you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your insincere management babble is making me uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's motivation you're feeling.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm getting more of a stalker vibe.

situation: The Boss stands beside Alice's desk holding a coffee mug and delivers a generic compliment about her job performance. Alice, still typing at her computer, tells him his insincere management talk makes her uncomfortable. He insists she is feeling motivated, and she replies that it feels more like being stalked.
punchline: Alice deflates the Boss's attempt at motivational praise by saying his hovering, scripted flattery comes across as creepy stalker behavior rather than inspiration.
summary: A manager hovers over an employee with canned praise, and she points out it feels more creepy than encouraging.

title: People Are the Biggest Risk

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk with your plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's people. They're terrible once you get to know them.

transcript.speaker: Voice from offscreen
transcript.text: Then don't get to know them.

transcript.speaker: Voice from offscreen
transcript.text: I tried that with you and it didn't work.

setting: Office, with a final panel showing the outside of the office building
situation: The Boss, absorbed in a handheld device, asks Dilbert about the biggest risk in his plan. Dilbert answers that people are the risk, because they turn out to be terrible once you know them. Two voices over an exterior shot of the building reply with advice and then a pointed retort aimed at Dilbert.
punchline: The suggestion to avoid getting to know people is undercut by the retort that Dilbert already tried that with the speaker and it failed, implying that Dilbert is himself one of the terrible people.
summary: Asked to name the main hazard of his project, Dilbert blames the humans involved, and the building itself seems to fire back that he is no exception.

title: Robot Boss Will Work You to Death

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The good news is that none of you will lose your jobs to robots.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But a robot will take MY job next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll retire with an enormous severance package and live out my days in splendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meanwhile, the robot that takes my job will be working all of you to death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Robots are natural leaders because they don't care about your feelings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will experience mental and physical misery on a scale the world hasn't seen since slavery was legal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But hey, it's better than losing your job to a robot. Am I right?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Apparently, nothing makes them happy.

situation: The Boss addresses his staff and announces that none of them will lose their jobs to robots, but that a robot will replace him next week. He will retire with a huge severance package while the robot boss works everyone to extreme misery. He then asks the unhappy employees if that isn't better than being replaced, and Catbert remarks on their lack of joy.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully presents a horrific future of robot-driven overwork as good news, oblivious to the fact that his employees are miserable while he cashes out.
summary: A manager gleefully explains that a robot successor will drive the staff to misery while he enjoys a lavish retirement payout.

title: Negotiating Class Teaches Nothing, Network Threatened

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The employees who took your class on negotiating are complaining that they learned nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I heard those same employees scheming to vandalize your network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that's all I can think about! How did you do that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gotta go!

situation: The Boss complains to Dogbert, a consultant, that employees who took his negotiating class say they learned nothing. Dogbert responds by mentioning a rumored plot to vandalize the company network, which instantly consumes the Boss's attention. Dogbert then leaves while the Boss is left wondering how it was done.
punchline: Dogbert deflects the complaint about his useless training class by planting a scarier worry in the Boss's mind, distracting him completely, and then walks away having proved he can manipulate better than his class could teach.
summary: A consultant dodges criticism of his worthless training by dropping an alarming rumor that completely hijacks his client's attention.

title: Goal Is Quitting; Boss's Goal Backfires

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is it important to have goals?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes! You need goals to succeed.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Good, because my goal is to become an Uber driver.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What is your goal?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reducing employee turnover.

situation: An employee asks the Boss whether having goals is important, and the Boss enthusiastically says yes. The employee announces his own goal is to become an Uber driver and quits on the spot. He then asks the Boss for his goal, which turns out to be reducing employee turnover.
punchline: The Boss's cheerful advice about goal-setting immediately causes an employee to quit, directly undermining the Boss's own goal of reducing turnover.
summary: Motivational advice about setting goals prompts a worker to resign, ironically defeating the manager's own objective of keeping staff.

title: Alice's Paradox Beats Zeno's Paradox

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why didn't you tell me about this sooner?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a fool's game because Zeno's Paradox says there will always be a time sooner than the one I pick.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice's Paradox says that no matter how many criticisms you explain away, there are always plenty more.

setting: Office, with a later scene in Dilbert's home or office
situation: Dilbert confronts Alice, who is looking at her phone, and asks why she didn't tell him about something sooner. Alice dismisses the complaint by invoking Zeno's Paradox, claiming there is always an earlier time she could have spoken. Dilbert, with Dogbert beside him, counters with a paradox of his own naming Alice, saying that however many criticisms she explains away, more remain.
punchline: Alice uses a pseudo-philosophical paradox to dodge blame for not speaking up sooner, so Dilbert invents a paradox in her name to point out that her excuses will never fully cancel out the criticisms against her.
summary: A coworker waves off a complaint with a pompous philosophical excuse, and the complainer responds by coining a paradox that turns her own trick back on her.

title: Endless Loop of Vague Deadlines

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Can you get that done by Friday?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I'll get back to you on that.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: When will you get back to me?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Soon.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How soon?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I can do this all day.

situation: A woman asks a bald, bespectacled coworker whether he can finish a task by Friday. He dodges with 'I'll get back to you,' then gives only 'soon' when pressed for a timeline. When she asks how soon, he sips his coffee and declares he can keep stalling all day.
punchline: The coworker treats evading a commitment as a contest he is happy to win, showing he would rather endlessly dodge a deadline than actually answer.
summary: A worker keeps deflecting a simple deadline question with ever vaguer replies until he cheerfully admits he could stall forever.
keywords: i can do this all day

title: Dilbert Dumps Alice for Tina

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, I am breaking up with you as my work wife.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina complains less and she sends me on fewer errands, so I choose her.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: What's your game?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm running a bait-and-switch on him.

situation: Dilbert tells Alice he is ending their 'work wife' relationship and replacing her with Tina, because Tina complains less and gives him fewer errands. Tina then suspiciously asks Alice what her game is, and Alice reveals she is running a bait-and-switch on Dilbert.
punchline: Alice's apparent loss is actually a scheme: by letting Dilbert switch to Tina, she is passing off the burden of being his work spouse and its errands onto someone else.
summary: A coworker coldly trades up to a less demanding office companion, only to learn the discarded one has engineered the swap to her own advantage.

title: Low Expectations Prevent Disappointment, Mostly

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why is Alice always so angry?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a function of her unrealistic expectations.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm never disappointed because I expect people to be ignorant, self-absorbed, and useless.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Present company excluded?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And there it is.

situation: Asok asks Wally why Alice is always angry. Wally explains that her expectations of people are unrealistic, while he is never disappointed because he expects everyone to be ignorant, self-absorbed and useless. When Asok hopefully asks whether that includes present company, Wally sips his coffee and says that is exactly the kind of thing he expected.
punchline: Asok's self-centered question proves Wally's cynical point about people being self-absorbed, so Wally's low expectations are confirmed once again.
summary: A coworker who never gets let down because he assumes the worst of everyone has his theory confirmed the moment he is asked if he includes the person he is talking to.

title: Agile Programmers Dodge Falling Ceilings

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You should move the agile programmers to building six because it has poor earthquake protection.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: They can jump out of the way if stuff starts falling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Can I have one of their cubicles near a window?

setting: Office, a meeting table or break area
situation: A bald coworker with a coffee mug advises the Boss to relocate the agile programmers to a building with poor earthquake protection. His reasoning is that agile people can dodge falling debris. The Boss accepts this, and the coworker then asks for one of their window cubicles.
punchline: The coworker pretends to value agility as a safety feature but is really scheming to grab the desirable window cubicles that will be vacated by moving the agile team to the dangerous building.
summary: A sly colleague sells the boss on putting nimble programmers in a quake-prone building, with a selfish motive that surfaces in the last panel.

title: Dogbert's Think-Past-the-Sale Trick

transcript.text: Do you want to prepare and serve my favorite food to me now or in one minute?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you always use that manipulative trick of making me think past the sale?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because it works.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One minute! Not a second sooner!

situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert whether he wants to serve Dogbert's favorite food now or in one minute, a choice that assumes Dilbert has already agreed to do it. Dilbert calls this out as a manipulative sales trick and asks why Dogbert always uses it. Dogbert says it works, and Dilbert immediately falls for it again by insisting on the one-minute option.
punchline: Dilbert correctly names the manipulation tactic but still falls for it, proving Dogbert's point that it works.
summary: Dogbert offers Dilbert a choice of timing that skips over whether he'll serve the food at all, and Dilbert protests the trick while still complying.

title: Boss's One-Size-Fits-All Management System

transcript.text: I'm bored.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's some more work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm overwhelmed with work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's some more work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Managing was hard until I figured out a system.

setting: Office, at the Boss's desk and in a hallway near a filing cabinet
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he is bored, and the Boss hands him more work. Alice then says she is overwhelmed with work, and the Boss hands her more work too. The Boss then explains to Catbert that managing got easy once he found a system.
punchline: The Boss's 'system' is to respond to every employee complaint, whether too little work or too much, by giving them more work, which shows his lazy and thoughtless approach to management.
summary: Whether an employee has too little work or too much, the boss's answer is always the same, and he proudly calls it a management system.

title: Registering Lustful Feelings With Legal

transcript.text: Rumor has it that you are dating a co-worker named Loud Howard.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, confronts a black-haired employee about a rumor that she is dating a co-worker named Loud Howard. He informs her that company policy requires registering her romantic feelings with the legal department. In the last panel a balding lawyer in glasses has her covered in paperwork and is about to staple it to her.

summary: HR treats an employee's office crush as a legal matter and has her buried in forms that are then literally fastened onto her.

transcript.text: Is the software almost done?

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.text: Not the final release — more like a beta MVP.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe more of an alpha.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you even started?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The mental stuff is almost done.

Wally keeps lowering expectations, describing it as a beta MVP and then an alpha, while the second panel shows only an office building. When the Boss asks if he has even started, Wally admits that only the 'mental stuff' is nearly finished.
punchline: Wally's progress claims shrink from a release candidate to an alpha until it's clear he has done no actual work, just thinking about it.
summary: Wally dodges a progress check by retreating through ever-lower software maturity labels until he confesses he has only been planning in his head.

title: Chatbot Replies Sound Like Wally

transcript.text: I got approval to work from home.

transcript.text: My chatbot will answer all of my emails and text messages.
