transcript.text: Chatbot answers would be useless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope so. Otherwise it won't sound like me.

situation: Wally, carrying a bag, tells Dilbert he has been approved to work from home. He explains that a chatbot will handle all of his emails and text messages. Dilbert points out that chatbot answers would be useless, and Wally cheerfully agrees, hoping they are.
punchline: Wally wants his chatbot's replies to be useless because that is exactly how his own communications sound, so a useless bot would be a perfect imitation of him.
summary: A notoriously unhelpful coworker plans to hand his correspondence to a bot and welcomes the news that its output will be worthless, since that makes it a faithful impersonation.

title: Dress Code Violation Earns Napping Day

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is inappropriate office attire!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go home and work remotely for the rest of the day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd it work out?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Phase one was a total success. Phase two involves napping.

situation: The Boss scolds Wally, who is holding a coffee and wearing a short green top that exposes his midriff, for inappropriate office attire. He orders Wally to go home and work remotely for the rest of the day. Wally then tells Dilbert that the outfit was a deliberate plan and that the next step is to nap.
punchline: Wally deliberately dressed inappropriately so the boss would send him home, giving him a free afternoon of napping instead of working.
summary: Wally gets sent home for his outfit, which turns out to have been a calculated scheme to earn himself a nap.

title: Quality Assurance Guy Won't Do His Job

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alan, from Quality Assurance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it true that the only thing you have been doing is assuring people we have quality?

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: I don't like to tell people how to do their jobs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Telling people how to do their jobs is literally your job.

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: In that case, stop doing all of this.

situation: The Boss confronts Alan from Quality Assurance, asking whether all he does is reassure people that the company has quality. Alan says he dislikes telling people how to do their jobs, and the Boss points out that this is exactly what his job entails. Alan flips this around and tells the Boss to stop doing all of this.
punchline: Alan turns the Boss's own logic against him by telling him to stop what he is doing, since telling people how to do their jobs is also what the Boss does.
summary: A quality assurance employee dodges his own responsibilities by claiming to hate giving instructions, then deflects his boss's rebuke right back at him.

title: Coworker Tries To Dump Kids

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Uh-oh. My babysitter canceled for tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too bad.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, I have an idea. Do you like kids?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will not watch your kids tonight.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was going to ask you to adopt them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Absolutely not. The best I can do is watch them tonight.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: A coworker complains that her babysitter canceled and Dilbert coldly brushes her off. She asks whether he likes kids, and when he refuses to babysit, she says she was actually going to ask him to adopt them. Dilbert panics and agrees to babysit instead, having been manipulated.
punchline: By floating an absurdly extreme request (adoption), the coworker makes the babysitting favor she wanted seem like a reasonable compromise, and Dilbert falls for the negotiation trick.
summary: A colleague gets a reluctant coworker to take her children for the evening by first suggesting he adopt them.

title: Simplify the Slide for Smart People

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You need to simplify that slide.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you understand it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why do you think smart people will be confused?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't tell if that was an insult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask a smart person.

setting: Office cubicle, with a final panel showing the office building exterior
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert to simplify his presentation slide, so Dilbert asks whether the coworker understood it. When the coworker says yes, Dilbert asks why he thinks smart people would be confused. The coworker is left unsure whether he was just insulted.
punchline: Dilbert's logic implies the coworker is not smart, and when the coworker can't tell if it was an insult, Dilbert suggests asking a smart person, which confirms the insult.
summary: A request to dumb down a presentation slide turns into a clever put-down that the coworker is too slow to catch.

title: Marketing Gets the Two Good Results

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My tests show we underperform our competition on nine out of eleven dimensions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give the two good ones to marketing. We can't be more honest than that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm almost certain we can.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, we really can't.

setting: Conference room table in an office
situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a tablet with test results indicating the company's product loses to the competition on nine of eleven measures. The Boss tells him to hand only the two favorable results to marketing, claiming that is as honest as they can be. Dilbert suggests they could be more honest, and the Boss flatly denies it while sipping his coffee.
punchline: The Boss treats cherry-picking the only two flattering results as the upper limit of honesty, when a fully truthful disclosure would obviously be more honest.
summary: A manager decides that passing along just the two flattering test results is the most candor a company could possibly muster.

title: Time Slows Down for Dense People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to Einstein, time flows more slowly in meetings than it does in empty space.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because people are dense.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is that true?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For you it is.

situation: Dilbert walks with Wally and Alice and claims that Einstein said time flows more slowly in meetings than in empty space. He explains it is because people are dense. In the meeting room, Wally asks if that is true, and Alice replies that it is, at least for him.
punchline: Alice turns the physics joke about density into an insult, implying Wally himself is dense and so slows down the meeting.
summary: A pseudo-scientific quip about meetings dragging on gets turned into a personal jab when a coworker is called dense.

title: Rat Grows Unwanted Human Ear

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Scientists grew a human ear on the back of a rat.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: When asked for a comment, the rat said, "Hey, get this ear off my back. I didn't agree to this."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The lead scientist on the project said, "Great. Now you made it all weird."

setting: Dilbert's desk, reading a news story on a tablet while drinking a beverage
situation: Dilbert sits at a desk sipping a drink and reading a news story on a tablet. The story reports that scientists grew a human ear on the back of a rat, then quotes the rat and the lead scientist in a mock interview. In the last panel he taps the screen with a click as he reads the scientist's reply.
punchline: The rat objects to being used in the experiment without consent, and the scientist's reaction is to complain that the rat's protest made things awkward, showing how little regard researchers have for their test subjects.
summary: A news item about a rat sprouting a human ear turns into a joke when the unwilling rodent complains and the scientist is merely irritated at the awkwardness.

title: Competitors Have Better Management, Or Lied

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are our competitors beating us on the benchmark speed tests?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do they have better engineers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, they have better management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Their management probably got them the budget they needed to do the job right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm guessing they were helpful, instead of being useless, blamecasting time-wasters.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear you can do a lot when you have good management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll probably try to get a job with a competitor. They sound great.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is also possible they lied about their benchmark test results.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should have said that first!

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why competitors are beating the company on benchmark speed tests. Dilbert replies that the competitors have better management, and he elaborates by insulting the Boss's own management style. When the Boss says he'll try to get a job with a competitor, Dilbert adds that they may have lied about their results.
punchline: The Boss ignores the pointed criticism of his own management and only reacts to the possibility that the competitors cheated, since he would rather believe they cheated than that he is the problem.
summary: After being told his rivals win because of superior leadership, a manager only perks up when offered the excuse that those rivals might have cheated.

title: Phone Beats Talking to Humans

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everything went wrong for me this week.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have problems. . . all kinds of problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For the zillionth time in a row, my phone is more fun than talking to a human.

situation: A coworker sits next to Dilbert and tries to vent about his terrible week. Dilbert stays hunched over his phone the whole time, ignoring him. In the last panel Dilbert finally speaks, admitting that his phone is more entertaining than the conversation.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly admits that his phone is consistently more fun than talking to a person, showing how little he cares about his coworker's problems.
summary: A man pours out his troubles to a colleague who is glued to his smartphone and finally explains that the device beats human company.

title: Million-Dollar Negotiation Expert, Five Minutes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an expert on negotiating to teach us a few things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He only costs a million dollars, and for that we get five minutes of his time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's get started.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're out of time, unless you want to renegotiate.

situation: The Boss announces he has hired a negotiating expert to teach the team, then reveals the expert costs a million dollars for only five minutes of his time. When the Boss says to get started, Dogbert, the consultant, says the five minutes are already used up unless the Boss wants to renegotiate.
punchline: The Boss was so badly outnegotiated on the consultant's fee that the time he paid for ran out before the lesson began, and a renegotiation would only be another demonstration of the expert's skill at his expense.
summary: A manager overpays dearly for a short negotiation lesson, only to be fleeced again by the instructor he hired.

title: Accused Coworker Radicalized by Accusations

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hear you're a terrorist sympathizer.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What? No! I'm not even close.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't want to hate you! Please stop radicalizing me!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sweating, agitated. He looks suspicious to me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Who are you talking to???!

situation: Alice accuses Asok of being a terrorist sympathizer, which he denies. As the accusation continues he becomes visibly upset and begs her to stop radicalizing him. Alice then phones someone to report that he is sweating and agitated and looks suspicious, which makes him even more frantic.
punchline: Alice's baseless accusation makes Asok so upset that his distress appears to confirm her suspicions, so she reports him, creating a self-fulfilling cycle of suspicion.
summary: A groundless accusation of extremism rattles a coworker so badly that his nervous reaction gets him reported as suspicious.

title: Dilbert Becomes Hunched Company Mascot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Management has selected Dilbert to be our new company mascot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His bad posture speaks volumes about his hard work and long hours.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pat pat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you ever dream you would be so successful?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is exactly how I dreamed it.

situation: The Boss announces that management has chosen Dilbert as the new company mascot, citing his slouched posture as proof of his dedication. He pats Dilbert on the back, which hurts, and then asks whether Dilbert ever imagined being so successful. Dilbert answers flatly.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic reply shows that this miserable, back-aching 'honor' is the opposite of the success he hoped for, and that management praises exhaustion as if it were achievement.
summary: A manager rewards an employee's bad back with a mascot role and congratulates him on a career outcome he clearly finds dismal.

title: Dilbert Over-Analyzes a Dinner Invitation

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you want to go to dinner and a movie with me on Friday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That plan is poorly conceived.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The best time to watch a movie is also the best time to eat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And what are the odds we want to see the same movie?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're a picky eater, so it would be a nightmare to decide where we both want to eat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One of us would have to compromise, and I assume it would be me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm offended by your offer to suboptimize my Friday experience.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you have a better option?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope. See you Friday.

setting: Office break area near the coffee machine
situation: A female coworker invites Dilbert to dinner and a movie on Friday. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, systematically picks apart her plan, listing logistical flaws and claiming he would be the one to compromise. After declaring himself offended, he admits he has no better option and agrees to go.
punchline: Dilbert critiques and insults the invitation in exhaustive detail, only to accept it because he has nothing better to do on Friday.
summary: A coworker's simple date invitation gets dissected like a flawed project plan before Dilbert reluctantly says yes.

title: Dilbert's Hesitation Reveals Too Much

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I saw you talking to my boss. Did he say anything about my project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your hesitant response tells me you know something and he asked you not to tell me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is something terrible going to happen to me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

setting: Office cubicle, with an exterior view of the office building in the last panel
situation: A coworker in a green shirt approaches Dilbert at his desk and asks whether Dilbert's conversation with the coworker's boss involved his project. Dilbert only says 'Um,' and the coworker deduces that Dilbert is hiding something. Dilbert's continued stammering makes the coworker fear something terrible is coming.
punchline: Dilbert's inability to say anything but 'um' confirms the coworker's fears, showing that failing to keep a secret convincingly is itself a way of revealing it.
summary: A worried colleague reads bad news into Dilbert's nervous stammering and concludes that his project, and maybe his job, is doomed.

title: Billionaire Ted's Start-Up Collapse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too bad your overhauled unicorn start-up failed, Ted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Last week you were a billionaire, and today you're doing a two-hour commute to work in a box.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: What can I do to make this stop?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Earn a billion dollars.

situation: Dilbert gloats to Ted that his hyped unicorn start-up has failed, reminding him he went from billionaire to enduring a long commute to a cubicle. Ted desperately asks what he can do to reverse his fortunes, and Dilbert gives an unhelpfully obvious answer.
punchline: Dilbert's advice to Ted is to simply earn a billion dollars, which is exactly the thing Ted can't just do on demand, making the answer sarcastic and useless.
summary: After a formerly wealthy colleague's flashy company implodes, he begs for a way out of his misery and is told to just get rich again.

title: Mordac Invents His Own Job

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Step away from that open source code!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Because I am Mordac, the Preventer of all efficient solutions in the information technology realm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That isn't an actual job.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I was hoping it was. I lost the file with my job description.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: That was five years ago. I've been winging it since then.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: My parents taught me that I could be anything I wanted to be.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: And I wanted to be this.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: So don't use that code!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not even when you turn around?

situation: Mordac storms up to Dilbert and orders him to stop using open source code, declaring himself the Preventer of all efficient IT solutions. When Dilbert says that isn't a real job, Mordac admits he lost his job description five years ago and has been making up his role ever since. He insists his parents taught him he could be anything, and he chose this.
punchline: Mordac's obstructive role may be entirely self-invented, and Dilbert's last question suggests he can simply keep using the code whenever Mordac isn't watching.
summary: A self-appointed IT gatekeeper confesses he has been improvising his obstructive role since misplacing his job description years ago.

title: Uber Driver Begs for Job Back

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm here to beg for my job back. Driving for Uber was less glamorous than I'd hoped.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My mental health and my bladder have been stretched to their limits.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we could discuss this over a tiled floor area.

situation: A former employee who left to drive for Uber comes to his old boss's desk and asks for his job back, admitting the gig work was worse than he expected. He says it strained both his mental health and his bladder. The boss responds by suggesting they talk over a tiled floor area.
punchline: The boss's oddly worded 'tiled floor area' is a euphemism for a bathroom, a sarcastic reply to the employee's bladder complaint that suggests he is just as unsympathetic as the gig economy.
summary: A worn-out ex-employee who tried ridesharing pleads for his old position back and gets a cheeky bathroom-themed reply from his boss.

title: Man Cave in the Lactation Room

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone turned our lactation room into a personal man cave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That guy sounds awesome.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The janitor found a recliner, a TV, and a coffee maker in there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I asked myself who would put a coffee maker in a lactation room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I drink mine black.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that someone converted the company lactation room into a private man cave. The janitor discovered a recliner, a TV and a coffee maker inside. The Boss reasons that only someone who drinks coffee with milk would put a coffee maker there, and Dilbert replies that he drinks his black, cheekily proving he is innocent and hinting at his own guilt.
punchline: The Boss's flawed deduction that the culprit must be a coffee-with-milk drinker is answered by Dilbert's deadpan 'I drink mine black,' which both clears him in the Boss's logic and quietly confirms he is the guy who set up the man cave.
summary: A manager hunts for whoever set up a secret lounge in the nursing room, and his own absurd detective reasoning lets the culprit slip away with a dry remark.

title: Soul Lost at Performance Review

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I hate my job, but I'm looking forward to my afterlife.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you hearing good things about decomposing?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My soul will live forever.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good luck. I lost mine at my first performance review.

situation: Three coworkers stand holding coffee mugs. One says he hates his job but is looking forward to the afterlife. Dilbert jokes about decomposing, and the character on the left insists his soul will live forever, prompting Wally to say he lost his soul at his first performance review.
punchline: Wally's cynical quip implies that corporate performance reviews are so soul-crushing that they strip employees of their souls, so there is nothing left to live on in the afterlife.
summary: Colleagues chat over coffee about death and the hereafter until one claims the workplace already destroyed his spirit long ago.

title: Boss Dodges Telling Ted About Cancellation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't talk to Ted until I have time to tell him I cut his project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When will that be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know. My European vacation starts tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Do you have ten seconds to talk?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Check back in fifteen days.

situation: The Boss holding a coffee cup tells Dilbert not to talk to Ted until the Boss has had time to tell him his project was cancelled. When Dilbert asks when that will be, the Boss says he doesn't know because he leaves on a European vacation tomorrow. Ted then approaches Dilbert at his desk asking for a few seconds, and Dilbert stalls him for fifteen days.
punchline: Dilbert is stuck covering for the Boss's cowardice, stonewalling Ted for the length of the Boss's vacation rather than anyone delivering the bad news.
summary: A manager leaves it to a subordinate to keep a coworker in the dark about a cancelled project while he heads off on holiday.

title: Dilbert Gives Terrible Parenting Advice

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My teenager wants to pierce his ear. Should I let him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. It's only a tiny hole and it heals.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next day

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now he wants a small tattoo.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, if it doesn't show...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next week

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now he wants to grow a human ear on his back, the way scientists did with that rat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As long as he can cover it with a shirt when he gets a job, I see no problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to let him live his own life.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One week later

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He joined ISIS.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I forgot to mention that I'm not good at giving advice.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert whether to let his teenage son pierce his ear, and Dilbert breezily approves. Over the following days and weeks the son's requests escalate to a tattoo and a human ear grown on his back, and Dilbert keeps approving as long as it can be covered up. A week later the teen has joined ISIS, and Dilbert admits he is bad at advice.
punchline: Dilbert's permissive, appearance-focused advice escalates absurdly until the son joins a terrorist group, and he only then admits he's unqualified to advise anyone.
summary: A dad keeps asking for guidance as his son's requests grow wilder, and each easygoing reply from his coworker leads to an increasingly disastrous outcome.
keywords: let him live his own life

title: Where My Time Really Went

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You asked for a breakdown of what I did this month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wasted 25% of my time in useless meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent 33% of my time listening to co-workers complain about other co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I used 11% to resend files I already sent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 14% went to dealing with a rumor you started by accident.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 16% went toward working on the wrong things because you communicate poorly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did you do with the 1% that was left?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just experienced it.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for a breakdown of how he spent his month. Dilbert lists percentages of his time lost to useless meetings, co-worker complaints, resending files, a rumor the Boss started and the Boss's poor communication. When the Boss asks about the leftover 1%, Dilbert says it was this conversation.
punchline: The only time Dilbert spent on actual work was the brief moment of answering the Boss's question, implying the entire month was consumed by workplace dysfunction, much of it caused by the Boss.
summary: An employee itemizes his month in percentages, revealing that nearly every hour vanished into office waste and the manager's own failings.

title: Why Would I Work Here

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I want all of you to be creative, self-empowered, and accountable.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I could do any of that stuff, why would I work here?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just find the whole thing confusing.

situation: The bald boss addresses his team at a meeting and demands that they be creative, self-empowered, and accountable. Wally, holding his coffee mug, responds that if he possessed any of those qualities he wouldn't be working at this company, then adds that the whole idea confuses him. Dilbert and the boss sit by listening.
punchline: Wally frankly points out that anyone with real creativity and accountability would have left for a better employer, so the boss's demand contradicts the kind of employees the company actually attracts.
summary: A manager lists the virtues he wants from staff, and a coffee-sipping employee wryly notes that anyone with those virtues would have gone elsewhere.

title: Voting Between Two Lying Budgeters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't decide if I want to vote for the liar with the budget plan that doesn't add up or...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...the other liar with a budget plan that doesn't add up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you tried using your ignorance to figure out which one is lying the least?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh, that could work.

setting: Office desk, with an exterior shot of a building in the middle panel
situation: The Boss complains to Dogbert that he cannot choose between two political candidates who both have budget plans that don't add up. Dogbert sarcastically suggests he use his own ignorance to judge which candidate lies least, and the Boss takes the idea seriously.
punchline: Dogbert's suggestion to rely on ignorance to detect lies is a insult, but the Boss is too clueless to notice and thinks it's a great idea.
summary: Faced with two equally dishonest candidates, a baffled voter is advised to trust his own cluelessness to pick one.

title: Hush Money After Raise Boast

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did you both negotiate huge raises with our boss the way I did?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently, you're the only good negotiator in the department.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Are you being racist?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will give you $1,000 to never say that about me again.

situation: Asok brags to Dilbert and Wally that he negotiated a huge raise from their boss and asks if they did the same. Dilbert remarks that Asok must be the only good negotiator in the department, and Asok responds by asking if that comment is racist. Dilbert, rattled by the accusation, offers Asok $1,000 to never say it again.
punchline: Dilbert's offhand remark gets him accused of racism, and he immediately offers Asok a cash payment to silence him, ironically making Asok an even better negotiator.
summary: After a coworker boasts about his big raise and gets a dry remark in return, he plays the discrimination card and ends up with a payout for his silence.

title: Accusing Dilbert Outside the Restroom

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think you know something about my project and your boss told you to keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha! You just confirmed it by avoiding eye contact!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could get your own stall.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why? What do you have to hide?

setting: Office hallway and men's restroom door
situation: A coworker follows Dilbert down the hall, accusing him of knowing something about his project that the boss ordered him to keep secret. He claims Dilbert's avoidance of eye contact proves it. When Dilbert tries to enter the restroom, the coworker follows him in, and Dilbert asks for some privacy.
punchline: The paranoid coworker is so fixated on his suspicion that he follows Dilbert into the restroom and treats Dilbert's request for privacy as further evidence of guilt.
summary: A suspicious colleague trails Dilbert all the way to the bathroom, reading every reaction as proof of a hidden secret.

title: Window Cubicle Superiority Complex

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you think you're better than me just because you have a cubicle with a window?

transcript.speaker: Man with window cubicle
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Man with window cubicle
transcript.text: Continuous exposure to new stimuli makes my brain create useful pathways and connections.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I did not see that coming.

transcript.speaker: Man with window cubicle
transcript.text: I pity the windowless.

situation: A coworker confronts a colleague, asking whether he thinks he is better than her just because his cubicle has a window. He bluntly says yes and backs it up with a pseudo-scientific claim about how new stimuli improve his brain. She is taken aback, and he finishes by saying he pities people without windows.
punchline: Instead of being modest about a trivial office perk, the man openly claims real cognitive and social superiority because of his window, and condescendingly pities everyone else.
summary: A man brazenly admits that his window-side desk makes him smarter than his coworkers and then looks down on them for it.

title: Depressed Block of Wood Computer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it true that you invented a device with human intelligence and human emotions?

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: I'd give you a demo, but the device is depressed and wants to be left alone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like a block of wood.

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: I'm only trying to copy the human mind. There's no reason to over-engineer it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can respect that.

situation: Dilbert visits an inventor who claims to have built a device with human intelligence and emotions. The inventor refuses a demo because the device is depressed, and the device on the desk is just a block of wood. Dilbert picks it up and accepts the inventor's reasoning.
punchline: The inventor's 'artificial human mind' is an inert block of wood that is conveniently too depressed to perform, implying that a faithful copy of the human mind needs no complexity and that humans are mostly gloomy and unproductive.
summary: A supposed breakthrough in emotional artificial intelligence turns out to be a moody lump of timber that won't come out and play.

title: Quality Assurance Guy Only Reassures

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Alan, from the Quality Assurance department.

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: Don't be worried about quality. I assure you we have plenty of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's all you do?

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: Hey, I don't tell you how to do your job.

situation: Alan from Quality Assurance walks up to Dilbert at his desk and introduces himself. He simply assures Dilbert that there is plenty of quality, without testing or checking anything. When Dilbert asks if that is all he does, Alan gets defensive and says he doesn't tell Dilbert how to do his job.
punchline: The Quality Assurance employee interprets 'assurance' literally, merely telling people quality is fine instead of verifying it, and deflects criticism by claiming his job is none of Dilbert's business.
summary: A quality department rep turns out to do nothing but verbally promise that everything is fine, then bristles when questioned.

title: Thermostat Power Corrupts Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My new cubicle is the nearest one to the office thermostat.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That makes me the de facto ruler of the indoor climate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't let the power corrupt you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll start by freezing all the skinny women who laughed at me!

setting: Office cubicle and the exterior of an office building
situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert that his new cubicle is closest to the office thermostat, making him the unofficial ruler of the building's temperature. Dilbert warns him not to let the power corrupt him. Wally immediately announces he will use it to freeze the skinny women who once laughed at him.
punchline: Wally's first act of petty power is to take revenge by making the office cold for the thin women, who are typically the ones who complain about being cold, showing he is instantly corrupted.
summary: A man who gains control of the office thermostat by sitting near it promptly plans to use it for petty revenge on his former tormentors.

title: The Endless Kitten Video Search

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see the viral video of the kitten riding a zebra?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know where this is heading and I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're going to spend the next ten minutes looking for that video on your phone while we wait.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It will only take a second.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And so it begins.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Here it is. No, wait. Dang. Wrong one. Okay, here it is. Oops, no, wrong one.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ten minutes later

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't see it because you keep moving.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I would let you hold it, but I don't want your germs on my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are a lot of unsatisfying parts to this interaction.

transcript.speaker: Green-shirted coworker
transcript.text: Now my coffee is cold.

setting: Office hallway or break area, coworkers standing holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker asks if Dilbert has seen a viral kitten-on-a-zebra video, and Dilbert correctly predicts the coworker will waste ten minutes hunting for it on his phone. The coworker keeps pulling up the wrong videos, then waves the phone around so no one can see it. He refuses to let Dilbert hold the phone because of germs.
punchline: After wasting ten minutes and never actually showing the video, the coworker insults Dilbert by refusing to hand over the phone, leaving everyone with cold coffee and nothing to show for it.
summary: A colleague's promise of a quick funny clip turns into a long, fruitless phone fumble that ends with an insult and cold coffee.

title: Boss Offloads His Own Evaluations

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't bring me problems. Bring me solutions!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would make you more useless than you already are.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also need you to fill out your own performance evaluations.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to stop bringing him problems and bring solutions instead. Dilbert points out that if he solved everything himself, the Boss would become even more useless. The Boss ignores the insult and dumps another task on Dilbert: writing his own performance evaluation.
punchline: The Boss proves Dilbert's point by shifting even his own managerial duties onto Dilbert, showing how little he actually contributes.
summary: A manager demands ready-made answers from his employee, then casually hands over the work of reviewing that same employee.

title: Alice Accuses Dilbert of Sexism

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You give Wally your full attention when he talks, but not me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You hang on every word the man says, but if I try to talk, you act distracted in five seconds.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally gets more eye contact too. You don't even look at me half the time I'm talking.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Deep down, in your DNA, you know you are a sexist because you don't take me seriously when I speak to you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There is no other explanation, so don't insult me by trying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I give both of you the same amount of attention, but you spread it over more words.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hate both of you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I play that wrong?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yup.

situation: Alice complains that Dilbert pays full attention to Wally but ignores her, and she accuses him of being sexist at a DNA level. She preemptively dismisses any explanation he might offer. Dilbert replies that he gives both of them equal attention but she talks too much, and she storms off angrily.
punchline: Dilbert's honest explanation is that Alice simply uses more words, which he delivers as an insult to both her and Wally, proving he handled the accusation badly.
summary: A colleague's charge of sexism gets answered with the blunt claim that she is just wordier than the other guy, which goes over poorly.

title: Long Email Too Dangerous to Summarize

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time to read your long email. Tell me what it said.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote a long email because a summary would be dangerously misleading.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be the judge of that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How?!!!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has no time to read Dilbert's long email and asks for a verbal summary. Dilbert replies that a summary would be dangerously misleading, so the email had to be long. The Boss insists he will decide that himself, leaving Dilbert incredulous about how he could possibly judge without reading it.
punchline: The Boss wants to judge whether a summary is misleading without having read the original, which is logically impossible.
summary: A manager who refuses to read a lengthy message demands to personally evaluate whether a condensed version would be accurate.

title: Dilbert's Unimpressed Date Marvels Only Briefly

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Do you ever marvel at the miracle of consciousness?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People are just fish plus time.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Does ANYTHING amaze you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is my longest date ever! 49 minutes!

setting: Outdoor path with grass, on a walk
situation: Dilbert walks with a woman on a date. She asks whether he ever marvels at the miracle of consciousness, and he flatly says no and reduces people to 'fish plus time.' When she asks if anything amazes him, he checks his watch and says the only amazing thing is that this is his longest date ever at 49 minutes.
punchline: Dilbert is so cynical and dateless that the only thing that amazes him is that his dismissive attitude hasn't driven her away yet, since his dates normally end in under 49 minutes.
summary: A cynical engineer shrugs off philosophical wonder on a walk, then admits the only astonishing thing is how long this date has lasted.

title: Wally Replaced Himself With Chatbot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally's emails make no sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He replaced himself with a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He designed the chatbot to be useless so you'd think it was him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And he thought this would fool me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's been gone for four months.

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that Wally's emails are nonsensical. Dilbert explains that Wally replaced himself with a deliberately useless chatbot so it would pass for him. The Boss scoffs that Wally thought he could be fooled, and Dilbert reveals Wally has actually been gone for four months.
punchline: Wally's plan worked perfectly, because the boss hasn't noticed he has been absent for four months, so the boss is the one who was fooled.
summary: A manager puzzles over a coworker's garbled emails without realizing that an absent employee's automated stand-in has been fooling him for months.

title: Forgery Punished For Project Success

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You stand accused of forging an expense approval from the head of marketing.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your malfeasance caused the project to finish on time and under budget.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Next time, just give up and lose hope like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will do.

setting: Catbert's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: Catbert, acting as the HR disciplinarian, accuses Dilbert of forging an expense approval from the head of marketing. He then reveals that the forgery let the project finish on time and under budget. Catbert's reprimand is to tell Dilbert to give up and lose hope like everyone else next time, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: The company punishes an employee for getting results by breaking the rules, and the 'correct' behavior it demands is resignation and hopelessness, implying the bureaucracy makes success impossible through proper channels.
summary: An HR cat reprimands an engineer for cutting through approval red tape to deliver a project successfully, and instructs him to adopt the apathy that everyone else has.

title: Faster Delivery Means Lower Quality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will you have that done?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Two weeks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you do it faster?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I need to do is lower the quality.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me what your minimum acceptable quality level is and I'll tell you when you can have it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want it in one week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can do that at 50% of planned quality.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does it feel as if I'm not really managing anything here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could go manage someone else now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if I'm doing my job now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it your job to prevent me from working?

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and office; one panel shows an office building exterior
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long a task will take and then asks him to do it faster. Dilbert explains that speed requires lower quality, so the Boss tries to haggle over a minimum acceptable quality level and ends up demanding delivery in a week. The Boss then realizes he isn't really managing anything, and Dilbert suggests he go bother someone else.
punchline: Dilbert points out that the Boss's only contribution is interfering with the work, so the Boss's real job seems to be preventing Dilbert from getting anything done.
summary: A manager pushing his engineer for faster delivery learns that speed is bought with lower quality, and ends up questioning whether he adds any value at all.

title: Catbert's Self-Authored Policy Refusal

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you give me Carol's home address? I agreed to watch her kids and she turned off her phone for her date night.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It is against company policy for me to use my good judgment to save children.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure it says that?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yes. I wrote it myself.

situation: Dilbert asks Catbert, the HR director, for Carol's home address because he agreed to babysit her kids and she has turned off her phone on a date night. Catbert refuses, claiming company policy forbids using good judgment to save children. When Dilbert doubts the policy exists, Catbert admits he wrote it himself.
punchline: Catbert hides behind a heartless policy that he personally invented, showing how HR uses rules as a flimsy excuse to be unhelpful and cruel.
summary: A babysitter in a bind is denied basic help by an HR cat who cites a rule he made up on his own.

title: Boss Delegates Ridiculous Presentation Anyway

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO wants me to make a fifty-slide presentation for him that will motivate the employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! Now you know how we feel when you ask us to do ridiculous things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, I don't have time, so I need you to do it for me.

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that the CEO has demanded a fifty-slide motivational presentation. Dilbert laughs and points out that the Boss is now experiencing what employees feel when given ridiculous requests. The Boss, unmoved, simply hands the task off to Dilbert because he is too busy.
punchline: Rather than gaining any empathy from being given an absurd assignment, the Boss immediately passes it down to Dilbert, proving he learned nothing.
summary: A manager handed an absurd task from above shrugs off his employee's gloating and dumps the work on him.

title: Zeno's Paradox Project Delay Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.text: It means every step we take gets us halfway closer to launch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you keep up that pace?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm hoping it will look that way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is Zeno's Paradox a real thing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next week

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Halfway closer than last week!

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: The boss asks about the software project, and Wally claims they are in the 'Zeno's Paradox phase,' meaning each step only gets them halfway closer to launch. The boss, not understanding the term, asks if the pace can be kept up and whether the paradox is real, and Dilbert ominously says he will find out. A week later Wally gives the same non-answer, claiming to be halfway closer than before.
punchline: Wally uses Zeno's Paradox to excuse never finishing the project, since by his logic the launch can never actually be reached, and the clueless boss accepts it as progress.
summary: A lazy employee dresses up endless project delays with a philosophy puzzle about never quite arriving, and his baffled manager buys it.

title: Blah Blah Software Security Handoff

situation: Dilbert hands a flash drive containing anti-encryption software to a man in an orange shirt with spiky hair. He warns that if it falls into the wrong hands it could eliminate all privacy on Earth, then asks whether the man understands. The man's reply shows he heard only meaningless jargon.
punchline: The person being trusted with a world-altering piece of surveillance technology tunes out the warning and treats it all as incomprehensible 'blah, blah, software', so the safeguarding is hopeless.
summary: A developer entrusts a dangerous privacy-destroying tool to a recipient who clearly isn't listening to the risks.

title: Dilbert's High-Five Etiquette Problem

transcript.text: Those situations look the same to me.

transcript.text: What's my problem?

transcript.text: But in this specific case, the problem is your total lack of masculinity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: High-five?

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building in one panel
situation: Dilbert confides to Alice that he never knows when to high-five versus when to yell 'woo-hoo', suspecting he lacks a male instinct for it. He asks what his problem is, and Alice says there are many, but here it's his total lack of masculinity. Dilbert responds by offering her a high-five anyway.
punchline: Dilbert's obliviousness is so complete that, right after being told he lacks masculinity, he cheerfully offers a high-five, proving her point.
summary: A socially clueless engineer asks a coworker why he can't read high-five cues and, after hearing a blunt diagnosis, answers her insult with the very gesture he was confused about.

title: Long Emails Mean Disorganized Minds

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert for ignoring his email. Dilbert explains he skips long emails because he believes they signal a disorganized mind, and that he avoids such people. The coworker points out that he is standing right there, and Dilbert admits his avoidance strategy isn't foolproof.
punchline: Dilbert's strategy of avoiding people who write long emails fails the moment one of them tracks him down in person, and he concedes this only by noting it doesn't work every time.
summary: A man who refuses to read lengthy messages gets cornered face to face by the sender of one he ignored.

title: Dilbert's Longest Date: Silence Wins

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that his latest date lasted 53 minutes. Dogbert, noting it's a personal record, asks whether the woman was physically trapped, such as under rubble. Dilbert reveals his secret was staying silent for the first 49 minutes.
punchline: Dilbert's dates only last longer when he doesn't speak, implying that his conversation is what drives women away.
summary: A man celebrates a personal-best date duration and credits his success to keeping his mouth shut for nearly the entire evening.

title: Thermostat War Amuses Robot Overlord

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm too cold to think!

situation: Dilbert and Asok argue over the office thermostat, each insisting on a different temperature needed for his brain to function. A robot looks on and asks what it's like to rule the planet while being so fragile about temperature. Dilbert wonders if it was a joke while Asok, shivering, says he's too cold to think.
punchline: Humans claim to dominate the Earth yet can't function across a two-degree temperature difference, which a robot finds absurd, and Asok proves the point by being too cold to even process the insult.
summary: A pair of coworkers squabbling over thermostat settings are mocked by a robot for being the planet's rulers despite their delicate temperature requirements.

title: Identity Thief Complains About Reputation

transcript.text: Ha! Take that!

transcript.text: You always said that would pay off someday.

situation: The Boss reads an email from the person who stole his identity. The thief complains that the Boss's racist internet comments are damaging the thief's reputation. The Boss gleefully pumps his fist in triumph, and Alice dryly remarks that he always claimed his behavior would eventually pay off.
punchline: The Boss treats it as a victory that his offensive online behavior is so bad that even an identity thief is embarrassed, and Alice sarcastically points out that he has finally found a payoff for it.
summary: A man whose identity was stolen celebrates when the thief begs him to stop posting offensive comments that are tarnishing the thief's good name.

title: End of the Pay-It-Forward Line

setting: Office conference room table, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: Asok asks Wally, who is holding his coffee mug, about his philosophy of life. Wally says he tries to make the world a better place, then explains that he is the end of the line for any pay-it-forward chain, so nobody after him has to do anything.
punchline: Wally claims that stopping kindness from spreading any further counts as a public service, since his laziness spares everyone else the effort.
summary: A lazy coworker recasts his refusal to pass along favors as a generous contribution to society.

title: Software Never Done With Changes

situation: The boss asks a programmer whether the software is finished. The programmer points out that the boss keeps adding feature requests, so it can never be done, and says it will be done one week after the final changes. When the boss is cornered with his own 'change is good' philosophy, he flees the meeting.
punchline: The programmer turns the boss's love of constant change against him, framing endless feature requests as a choice between being a stagnant bureaucrat or a dynamic leader, so the boss has no good answer and leaves.
summary: A programmer neatly traps his manager into admitting that his own stream of new requests is the reason the project never finishes.

title: Meetings Double Perceived Lifespan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Researchers discovered a way to double the perceived length of a human's life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's something called "meetings."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can we start now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought we were already an hour into it.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Dilbert and a coworker sit at a meeting table, Dilbert looking at his phone. Dilbert announces that researchers found a way to double the perceived length of life, then reveals it is meetings. The coworker asks if the meeting can start, and Dilbert says he thought they were already an hour in.
punchline: Meetings are so tedious that time seems to crawl, so Dilbert thinks the meeting has been going for an hour when it hasn't even started.
summary: A bored employee jokes that dreary meetings stretch out a person's sense of time, then proves it by mistaking a not-yet-begun meeting for one that has dragged on for an hour.

title: Dogbert Sells Clothes to Ghosts

transcript.text: I'm starting a new business selling clothes to ghosts.

transcript.text: My garments are made of the finest ectoplasm.

transcript.text: Ghosts don't have money.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They don't need money. I'm using a life insurance business model.

transcript.text: If you pay me until you die, I will keep your ghost well-dressed for eternity.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I also offer reincarnation services.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Leave all of your stuff to me when you die and I'll give it back to you when I find the baby that got your soul.

transcript.text: You'll be in trouble if your customers realize you're running a scam.

situation: Dogbert announces a business selling clothes to ghosts, and Dilbert points out that ghosts have no money. Dogbert explains it works like life insurance: customers pay while alive for a service delivered after death. He adds a reincarnation service in which he keeps their belongings until he locates their reborn soul, and Dilbert warns him about being exposed as a scam.
punchline: Dogbert's afterlife scam is safe because the only customers who could discover he's cheating would be dead, and dead people complaining would be a far bigger problem than fraud.
summary: Dogbert pitches an afterlife con that borrows its payment structure from life insurance and counts on the victims never being able to complain.

title: Past Failures Don't Doom Ideas

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ideas like yours have been tried in the past and always failed!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever been on an airplane? Those didn't work on the first few tries either.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then we have the entire history of science.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop. You're embarrassing yourself.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A coworker in an orange shirt with dark hair tufts dismisses Dilbert's idea by saying similar ideas have always failed in the past. Dilbert counters that airplanes and all of science failed at first before succeeding. The coworker tells Dilbert to stop because he is embarrassing himself.
punchline: The coworker accuses Dilbert of embarrassing himself when it is actually the coworker's weak 'it failed before' argument that was thoroughly debunked, showing he cannot admit being wrong.
summary: A colleague rejects an idea because similar ones flopped before, and Dilbert's examples of aviation and science only get him told he is the one looking foolish.

title: Boss Has an Eye for Design

transcript.text: I have an eye for design.

situation: The Boss stands behind Dilbert at his desk and asks him to change a link button's colour from burnt orange to blue. Dilbert explains that the change would reduce clicks and reflects bad design. The Boss insists he has an eye for design, and Dilbert replies with a nonsensical boast of his own.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the Boss's claim of design talent by matching it with an absurd, equally baseless claim of having an elbow for music.
summary: A manager second-guesses a button colour, and when told it would hurt clicks, he boasts of his design sense and gets a sarcastic body-part boast in return.

title: Entrepreneur Comparisons Make Staff Miserable

punchline: Encouraging employees to emulate entrepreneurs makes them compare themselves to billionaires, so they feel like failures instead of feeling fine next to their cubicle neighbors.
summary: Urging staff to think like entrepreneurs only leads them to measure themselves against billionaires and feel terrible.

punchline: Right after he complains about workplace safety, the employee suffers another bizarre mishap, and Catbert's deadpan comment that the fly looked pregnant implies he is now carrying a growing swarm up his nose.
summary: A worker with an eye injury from a ping-pong ball protests about safety hazards, only to have an insect fly into his nostril while a nonchalant Catbert comments on its condition.

situation: The Boss questions an employee about allegedly threatening to kill a coworker named Dick. The employee explains that Dick accused him of being a terrorist. punchline: The employee's furious reaction to being falsely accused of terrorism, a rant about blowing up the building, makes him look exactly like what he's denying, and the Boss is understandably alarmed.
summary: A man wrongly branded a terrorist by a coworker reacts with an explosive rant that only deepens his manager's suspicions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I meant until my next meeting.

situation: A coworker at her desk reads out a gloomy horoscope to the Boss, spouting astrological gibberish about the moon and feng shui. The Boss asks how long he has, and she says he will be dead by noon. He reveals he was only asking how much time he had before his next meeting.
punchline: The Boss treats a dire death prediction as a mere scheduling concern, showing he cares more about his meeting calendar than his own life.
summary: A worker delivers an ominous made-up horoscope, but her boss is only worried about how much time he has before his next meeting.

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: The Boss criticizes Wally for accomplishing nothing all month. Wally says he's been waiting for others to respond, and the Boss insists it's Wally's job to push those people to do their work. When Wally reluctantly agrees to follow up, the Boss says he'll simply wait for Wally to report back.
punchline: The Boss lectures Wally about waiting on others, then immediately does exactly the same thing by passively waiting for Wally to get back to him.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for idly waiting on colleagues, then adopts the very same idle waiting himself.

title: Dogbert's Cardboard Particle Accelerator Scam

transcript.text: When scientists fail to confirm my discoveries, I will say they need better accelerators.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is eating chips on the couch, that he is building a particle accelerator in the basement. When Dilbert says it sounds expensive, Dogbert explains he will make it from cardboard and simply claim to discover a new particle every week. If other scientists cannot reproduce his results, he will blame their inferior equipment.
punchline: Dogbert plans to fake scientific discoveries with a cardboard machine and deflect any failure to replicate by insisting everyone else's accelerators are inadequate.
summary: A scheming dog plans to fabricate weekly physics breakthroughs with a homemade prop and blame his critics' gear when they can't verify them.

punchline: Dogbert dismisses ethical objections to rigging peer review by branding any critic as anti-science, turning a corrupt practice into a loyalty test.
summary: A scheming dog buys his way through scientific peer review and shames anyone who objects by calling them hostile to science.

punchline: After being mocked by a manager who gave no real requirements, the programmer replies with a deadpan threat that he may not survive until tomorrow.
summary: A manager blames a programmer for lacking specs he never provided and then trivializes her work, earning a chilling reply.

title: Making the World Better, For Some

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Is that what you had in mind by "making the world a better place"?

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The boss announces in a meeting that the company's goal is to make the world a better place. Dilbert points out the contradiction with their goal of destroying competitors, then lays out how the plan means job losses, monopoly pricing, enriched shareholders, tax avoidance and meaningless lives for employees. The boss admits he didn't mean better for everyone.
punchline: The boss's mission statement about improving the world only ever meant improving it for a select few, exposing corporate idealism as a cover for greed.
summary: A meeting about a lofty corporate mission turns sour when an employee spells out its ruthless real-world consequences and the boss shrugs it off.
keywords: make the world a better place

title: Ignoring Twitter Complaints Tanks Stock

transcript.text: Sounds like a seasonal thing.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the company is receiving many product complaints on Twitter. The Boss dismisses the customers as trolls and orders Dilbert to make them go away. Soon after, a bald executive demands to know why the company's stock has dropped to zero, and the Boss shrugs it off as seasonal.
punchline: The Boss's dismissal of customer complaints as trolling leads to a total stock collapse, which he absurdly blames on seasonality rather than his own negligence.
summary: A manager brushes off social media customer complaints as harassment, then explains away his company's worthless stock as a mere seasonal fluctuation.

title: Fifty Slides of Pure Excitement

punchline: The Boss misses the point entirely, believing that a fifty-slide presentation will fix the problem of being boring when a slide deck is exactly what makes him boring.
summary: A clueless manager asks why nobody listens to his pep talks and responds to blunt advice by planning an enormous slideshow.

summary: A personified internet commenter twists a simple hypothetical into a hostile accusation and then blames his target for the dispute.

The coworker says Dilbert must find the root cause of his poor posture before he can fix it. Dilbert guesses bad ergonomics, but the coworker answers that the cause is work itself.
punchline: The coworker deadpans that the real root cause of Dilbert's slouching is work itself, not his desk setup, implying that the job is what is crushing him.
summary: A stooped employee seeks advice on standing tall and learns that his job is what keeps bending him down.

The employee casually admits he skipped it because he was tired and it looked hard, then assumes someone else will do the difficult work for him. punchline: Dilbert blames the employee's upbringing for his shameless entitlement, implying his parents never taught him to do hard work himself.
summary: A coworker blithely admits he dodged his task because it seemed difficult and expects others to cover for him, prompting a pointed remark about how he was raised.

situation: A female coworker with a black bob haircut announces that, in her role as Dilbert's 'work wife', she has constructive criticism for him. She tells him he would be more attractive if he were taller, then admits she doesn't actually know how constructive criticism differs from ordinary criticism. Dilbert sits silently through the exchange.
punchline: The coworker's 'constructive' feedback is just a plain insult about something Dilbert cannot change, and she only realizes afterward that she can't tell the two kinds of criticism apart.
summary: A coworker offers feedback to her office companion that turns out to be a simple insult, then belatedly admits she can't tell helpful advice from rudeness.

title: Billing Clients for Thinking Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a client is objecting to being billed for the time Dilbert spent thinking about their project. Dilbert responds that thinking is the core of an engineer's job, and the Boss suggests he could meet with someone while he thinks so the time looks more legitimate. Dilbert sarcastically asks how that is working for the Boss right now.
punchline: The Boss's idea that thinking only counts as billable work if it happens in a meeting is itself evidence that meetings don't produce thought, and Dilbert's sarcastic reply points out the Boss is clearly not thinking during this one.
summary: A manager balks at charging clients for an engineer's contemplation and proposes pairing it with a meeting, which the engineer mocks by implying the manager isn't doing much thinking himself.

summary: A manager vows to make finances understandable, buries his staff in jargon, sneaks in gibberish, and discovers nobody was paying attention.

setting: Office, a casual conversation between two coworkers, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert if he has any vacations planned. Dilbert says no, explaining that he hasn't botched his career so badly that he needs to escape from it. When the coworker replies that he does take vacations, Dilbert fires back that he's heard the coworker needs a lot of them.
punchline: Dilbert insults the coworker twice, first by implying that taking vacations means your career is a failure you want to flee, then by claiming the coworker must be doing especially badly because he needs so many.
summary: Dilbert turns a friendly question about holiday plans into a jab at anyone who relies on time off to escape a failing career.

situation: A bald employee in a green shirt holding a coffee asks the Pointy-Haired Boss, who is looking at his phone, for permission to work smarter instead of harder. transcript.text: Later
