situation: Wally hands a coworker a pair of virtual reality goggles and pitches them as a way to upgrade how he experiences the world. Later, the goggle-wearing coworker stands holding a coffee mug and points at a plant while the boss compliments Wally on how hard he is working. The boss is actually talking to the wrong person: the one wearing the goggles, not Wally.
punchline: The goggles leave their wearer so disconnected from reality that he cannot tell Wally has handed them off and walked away, and the boss ends up praising the wrong person for working hard.
summary: A coworker gets talked into wearing VR goggles all day and is soon too out of touch to notice that the praise for hard work is aimed at the wrong person.

title: Carol Refuses to Rebook Flight

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, move my flight one hour earlier Friday.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you have any idea how hard that would be?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I know it sounds easy, but it won't be. Not at this late date. Not with all your pickiness.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: When I fail, you will think I didn't look hard enough for a new flight.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I can't prove a negative, so I will forever suffer your disdain.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My career is ruined.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never mind! Forget it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is it so hard to ask you to do anything?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been telling people you're stupid, but I'm open to other theories.

situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol to move his Friday flight one hour earlier. Carol escalates a simple request into a catastrophe, claiming it will be impossible and that he will blame her and ruin her career. The Boss gives up and, exasperated, muses that he has been calling her stupid but would consider other explanations.
punchline: The Boss is so baffled by Carol's dramatic obstruction that he admits he's been calling her stupid but is willing to consider other explanations, though the implication is that he has none.
summary: A simple travel change request spirals into an assistant's melodramatic prediction of doom, leaving her boss ready to blame her competence.

title: Work Husband Wanted, Criticism Qualifies

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm in the market for a "work husband." Do you have a "work wife" yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not sure. Alice criticizes me a lot. Does that count?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's all I wanted to do, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but don't let Alice find out.

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut and a purple top approaches Dilbert and says she wants a 'work husband', asking if he has a 'work wife' yet. Dilbert says the closest thing is Alice, who criticizes him constantly. She replies that criticism is all she wanted to do too, so Dilbert agrees to the arrangement but asks her to keep it from Alice.
punchline: The 'work spouse' relationship is reduced to one person nagging and criticizing the other, and Dilbert is more afraid of Alice discovering the arrangement than bothered by the criticism itself.
summary: A coworker looking for an office 'spouse' finds Dilbert's existing pattern of being scolded by Alice is exactly the dynamic she wants, so they strike a secret deal.

title: Bereavement Leave for Cousin Ronnie

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need to take some bereavement time, with pay, because my cousin Ronnie died.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Cousins don't count unless you married one.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We were domestic partners. What's the policy on that, you bigot?

situation: An employee asks Catbert, the HR director, for paid bereavement leave because his cousin Ronnie died. Catbert refuses, saying cousins only qualify if you married one. The employee then claims he and Ronnie were domestic partners and accuses Catbert of bigotry.
punchline: The employee gets around the restrictive policy by lying that his cousin was his domestic partner and uses an accusation of bigotry to pressure HR into granting the leave.
summary: A worker who is denied funeral leave for a dead relative reinvents the relationship to fit the rules and shames the HR chief into reconsidering.

title: Boss Forgets He Assigned Duplicate Tasks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great update, Ted. Now let's hear what Dilbert did this week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I unnecessarily duplicated Ted's work because you forgot you asked both of us to do the same task.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And how about Alice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're three for three.

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: In a team meeting, the boss praises Ted's update and then asks Dilbert what he accomplished. Dilbert explains that he wasted the week duplicating Ted's work because the boss forgot he had assigned the same task to both of them. The boss then asks about Alice, and she says she did the same thing too.
punchline: The boss has assigned the identical task to all three employees without remembering it, so the whole team has wasted a week on redundant work.
summary: A manager's forgetfulness leads him to give the same assignment to three people, and the status meeting reveals the wasted effort.

title: Efficiency Disguised as Laziness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've noticed you don't work as much as your co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's an illusion caused by the combination of my efficiency and my modesty.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... you're getting your work done?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stop poisoning our culture with your distrust.

situation: A manager tells Wally he has noticed Wally works less than his colleagues. Wally claims it only looks that way because he is efficient and modest. When the manager asks whether the work is actually getting done, Wally turns the tables and accuses him of harming the company culture by distrusting employees.
punchline: Wally dodges any proof of productivity by recasting a reasonable question as an attack on workplace culture, so the manager ends up on the defensive.
summary: Confronted about doing less than his peers, a slacker deflects scrutiny by blaming his boss for being untrusting.

title: Performance Review Shifts Blame Onto Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure we get all of the cost savings that our vendor promised with our new software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those savings are not real. The vendor lied to you because you know nothing about technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If only I had some way to turn my mistake into his mistake.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's called a performance review.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to make sure the company captures the cost savings a vendor promised for new software. Dilbert replies that the savings are fake and that the vendor lied to the Boss because he knows nothing about technology. The Boss muses about how to turn his own mistake into Dilbert's, and Catbert, the evil HR director, points out that a performance review will do it.
punchline: Instead of accepting responsibility for being fooled by the vendor, the Boss gets Catbert to suggest the performance review as a tool for pinning his mistake on the employee who pointed it out.
summary: A manager who was duped by a software vendor decides to punish the employee who exposed the truth, and HR happily supplies the method.

title: Government Listening Hears Schedule Status

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government asked me for an update on your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll talk into your phone. They listen to you all day long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is unsettling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything is on schedule.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the government has asked for a project update. Since the government supposedly listens to Dilbert's phone all day, the Boss decides to speak the status request into Dilbert's phone. Dilbert is unnerved and answers into the phone that everything is on schedule.
punchline: Dilbert, spooked by the idea of being surveilled, hurriedly gives the project update to the government's ears, turning mass phone surveillance into a convenient status-reporting channel.
summary: A manager lets government eavesdroppers on an employee's phone do his project reporting for him.

title: Lunch Hour Training Replaces You With Robot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Schedule your training during your lunch hours so it doesn't impact your projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But... my lunch hour is the only freedom I experience in a typical day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The rest of my time is either scheduled to the minute or driven by whatever crisis is happening.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't take my lunch hour and reduce me to nothing but a prisoner in a digital chain gang.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm barely clinging to my illusion of free will as it is. This could push me over the edge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you take away my one hour of freedom in the day, I might as well be a robot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Relax. This is temporary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For how long?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until I can replace you with a robot.

setting: Conference room / meeting at the office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to do his required training during his lunch hours so it won't interfere with his projects. Dilbert passionately protests that lunch is his only free time and that losing it would make him no better than a robot. The Boss calmly reassures him the arrangement is only temporary, then reveals it will last until he can replace Dilbert with an actual robot.
punchline: The Boss's 'reassurance' that the loss of Dilbert's lunch hour is temporary is undercut by the revelation that it only ends when Dilbert is replaced by a robot, confirming the threat of automation.
summary: A manager tries to soothe an employee's objections to losing his midday break by promising it will end once a machine takes over his job.

title: Ruling Out Your Own Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't believe how stupid this person is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you rule out the hypothesis that you're too dumb to understand his point?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Take your time. I can wait.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: For starters, he dis-agrees with me.

setting: Office hallway, with both characters looking at handheld devices
situation: A coworker staring at a phone complains about how stupid someone is, apparently reading a online post or comment. Dilbert asks how he can rule out that he is simply too dumb to understand the other person's point. The coworker's only answer is that the person disagrees with him.
punchline: The coworker treats disagreement with himself as proof of the other person's stupidity, which is circular reasoning that rules out nothing.
summary: A man scornful of a stranger's online opinion is challenged to prove he isn't the one who is missing the point, and his only evidence is that they disagree.

title: Raise Denied By Imaginary Comparisons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because your performance was only average.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you calculate an average for my performance?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one has ever been in my exact situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I compared you to other employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You compared me to strangers doing entirely different things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I compared you to imaginary people doing your exact job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called managing, and I'm very good at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know you're good at it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because imaginary people do this job worse than I do.

setting: Conference room during a performance review
situation: The Boss refuses Dilbert a raise because his performance was merely average. When Dilbert questions how an average could be calculated for a unique role, the Boss reveals he compared Dilbert to imaginary people doing the exact same job. He then justifies his own competence by claiming imaginary people manage worse than he does.
punchline: The Boss's performance benchmarks are entirely fictional, and he validates his own skill with the same made-up comparison, making his reasoning perfectly circular and self-serving.
summary: A manager justifies denying a raise by measuring an employee against invented colleagues, then praises himself using the same invented yardstick.

title: Doctor Says He Heals Fast

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My doctor says he's never seen anyone heal as quickly as me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you suppose that means?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Obviously it means I am genetically gifted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that the only explanation?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, maybe ten percent of it is because of good medical care.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you think of any other reason at all?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doctors tell idiots their bodies are magic because it makes them feel special.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He would have gotten there.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't have that kind of time.

setting: Office break area or hallway, with coffee cups in hand
situation: A coworker with a bandaged arm brags that his doctor has never seen anyone heal so fast and insists it proves he is genetically gifted. Dilbert keeps asking leading questions, hoping the coworker will consider other explanations. When the coworker can't, Dilbert bluntly delivers the real reason, and Alice remarks she can't wait around for him to work it out himself.
punchline: Dilbert says doctors flatter fools by telling them their bodies are magic, and Alice notes the coworker would never have worked it out on his own in a reasonable time.
summary: A boastful colleague credits his rapid recovery to superior genes until Dilbert bluntly explains that doctors simply flatter gullible patients.

title: Job Candidate Admits Family Lies

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: If you hire me, I will dedicate 100% of my energy to making this company succeed!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would your family think if they heard that?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: They'd understand. They're all huge liars, too.

situation: A job candidate sits across the desk from Dilbert, who is conducting the interview, and promises to give 100% of his energy to the company. Dilbert asks what the candidate's family would think of such a pledge. The candidate calmly replies that they would understand because they are all liars too.
punchline: The candidate admits that his interview promise is a lie and that dishonesty runs in his whole family, so everyone would see through the claim.
summary: An applicant's grand vow of total devotion is undercut when he cheerfully confesses that lying is a family trait.

title: How Hard Could Electric Cars Be

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Welcome to the first meeting of our project to design an electric car.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've never tried to build an electric car, but how hard could it be?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's very hard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't feel that way. My part is mostly talk.

setting: Conference room during a project kickoff meeting
situation: The Boss opens the first meeting of a project to design an electric car and cheerfully assumes the work can't be that difficult, despite the company having no experience. Dilbert, an engineer, states that it is very hard. The Boss dismisses this because his own role in the project is mostly talking.
punchline: The Boss judges the difficulty of the project by how easy his own part feels, which only involves talking, ignoring the hard engineering work done by everyone else.
summary: A manager launching a car-building project brushes off an engineer's warning because his own contribution is just chatter.

title: Boss Refuses to Understand Communication Class

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I take a class to improve my communication skills?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you talking about?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want to take a class that teaches me how to communicate better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand what you're asking me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am asking permission to take a class to help me communicate better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see your lips moving but I can't figure out what you're asking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! There's no way to get there from here!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm glad I took that management class on how to not listen. It already paid off.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to attend a class on improving communication skills. The boss claims not to understand the request no matter how many times and ways Dilbert rephrases it, until Dilbert collapses in frustration. The boss then reveals he took a management class on how not to listen, which is clearly working.
punchline: The boss feigns incomprehension to deny a training request and credits a management class on 'how to not listen' for his success, implying managers are trained to avoid engaging with employees.
summary: A manager stonewalls an employee's request for training by pretending he cannot comprehend it, then credits his own training in ignoring people.

title: Worn-Out Socks Legacy Worry

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you ever worry about your legacy?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I worry about someone finding out my socks are so worn out that all I have left are the ankle parts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, that's enough about you.

situation: The Boss asks Asok, seated across from him, whether he worries about his legacy. Asok answers with an embarrassing confession about his socks being worn down to just the ankle parts. The Boss, now looking at his phone, cuts him off and ends the conversation.
punchline: The Boss asks a deep question but has no real interest in the answer, dismissing Asok's oversharing as soon as it stops being about himself.
summary: A manager poses a weighty question to a coworker, then brushes off the awkward, mundane reply to turn back to his own business.

title: Blaming Each Other Over Missing File

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I never got the file you said you would send.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what file type you want.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why didn't you ask?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why didn't you check your email and see that I did?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why didn't you text me to say you emailed me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you drive into a ravine?

situation: A coworker complains to Dilbert that he never received a file Dilbert promised to send. Dilbert says he didn't know what file type to use, and the two trade escalating 'why didn't you' accusations about asking, checking email and sending text notifications. Dilbert ends the exchange by telling the coworker to drive into a ravine.
punchline: A petty blame-shifting argument over a missing file escalates until Dilbert abandons logic and wishes death on his coworker.
summary: Two cubicle neighbors bounce blame back and forth over a lost attachment until one snaps with a dark insult.

title: Vote Like You Decide Work

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't decide who to vote for in this election.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Make your voting decisions the same way you make your work decisions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Common sense and gut instinct?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We just call it "wrong."

setting: Office desk or conference table, with both people looking at their phones
situation: A coworker with horn-shaped tufts of hair says he cannot decide who to vote for in an election. Alice advises him to decide the way he makes work decisions, and he assumes she means common sense and gut instinct. Alice deadpans that at work they simply call that approach wrong.
punchline: Alice implies that workplace decisions are so poor that relying on common sense and gut instinct is considered the wrong way to decide, which makes it a terrible model for choosing a candidate.
summary: Asked how to pick an election candidate, Alice recommends the coworker's usual workplace decision method, then reveals that method is considered a mistake.

title: Babysitter Warned About Ungovernable Kids

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is there anything I need to know before I babysit your kids tonight?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They won't do anything you ask, and they don't respond to threats or consequences.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So... what am I supposed to do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try finding some idiot to babysit for you.

situation: A coworker in a purple coat offers to babysit Dilbert's kids and asks if there is anything she should know. Dilbert explains the kids ignore every instruction and are immune to threats and consequences. When she asks what she should do, he suggests she hand the job off to some other fool.
punchline: Dilbert's only advice for handling his uncontrollable kids is to trick someone else into taking over, which reveals the babysitter has just become the idiot he is describing.
summary: A willing babysitter learns that the children cannot be controlled by any means and is told to pass the job to a sucker.

title: Chatbot Replies Indistinguishable From Boss

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There's a rumor that you use a chatbot to reply to email with useless nonsense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't prove that because I've ALWAYS answered my email with useless nonsense.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That was disturbingly well-played.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's all about creating the base case.

situation: Catbert, the red HR cat, confronts a bald, bespectacled manager sitting at his desk with a coffee cup. He accuses the manager of using a chatbot to answer email with useless nonsense. The manager replies that nobody can prove it, because his own email replies have always been useless nonsense.
punchline: The manager has pre-emptively made his human email replies so worthless that a chatbot's replies can't be distinguished from them, making the accusation unprovable.
summary: A manager's long history of worthless email answers gives him perfect cover for automating them with a chatbot.

title: Fun Jobs Wouldn't Pay You

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I want a job I can enjoy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want to work for free?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No, I just want to get paid for doing things I want to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perhaps you misunderstand the true nature of "work."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The reason your employer pays you is because work is unpleasant by its very nature.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If the job were fun, the company would charge you a fee for letting you do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to climb into the dumpster and find out what's making it smell so bad.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: At least I'm doing something useful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, it's more of a curiosity situation.

setting: Office break area with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker says he wants a job he can enjoy, and Dilbert lectures him that work is inherently unpleasant, which is why employers pay people to do it. Dilbert argues that a fun job would make the company charge employees a fee instead. Then the Boss orders Asok to climb into the dumpster to find the source of a bad smell.
punchline: Asok's attempt to find purpose in the dumpster task is deflated when it's pointed out that the job is just satisfying idle curiosity, confirming that work really is unpleasant and not even necessarily useful.
summary: A lesson that pay exists because work is miserable is proven right when a junior employee gets sent to rummage through a stinking dumpster for no real reason.

title: Robot Attends Meetings For Wally

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Wally asked me to scan his brain and download his thoughts so I can attend meetings on his behalf.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But all you are is a soulless container of knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: That's all Wally is too.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stop trying to alter my worldview.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Well, look who doesn't like being programmed.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A robot sits at a meeting table between Dilbert and a coworker and explains that Wally had it scan his brain so it can attend meetings for him. The coworker insults the robot as a soulless container of knowledge, and the robot replies that Wally is exactly the same. When the coworker complains about the robot altering his worldview, the robot turns it around, noting he dislikes being programmed.
punchline: The robot is a perfect stand-in for Wally because Wally is also a soulless container of knowledge, and the coworker's resistance to changing his views shows that he, too, is just a programmed machine.
summary: A brain-scanned robot sent to meetings in Wally's place turns every insult about its lack of a soul back onto the humans around it.

title: Cramming Everything Onto One Slide

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took me hours to figure out how to fit everything you wanted into one slide.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's great. Now add in some stuff about the budget, our risks, and all of our competition.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And keep it all on one slide.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever listened to the noise coming from your mouth?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he spent hours squeezing all of the requested content onto a single presentation slide. The Boss responds by piling on new requirements about budget, risks and competitors, while insisting it all stay on one slide. Dilbert finally snaps and asks if the Boss ever listens to what he is saying.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the Boss's demands are self-contradictory nonsense, since he keeps adding content while refusing to allow more space.
summary: After painstakingly squeezing a presentation onto one slide, an employee is told to cram in even more material without adding a slide.

title: Window Cubicle Broadens Worldview

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I love travelling because it broadens my understanding of the world.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I know what you mean. I just got a cubicle near the window and now I see the world as an alleyway between me and the parking garage.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's not what the alley people say.

setting: Office break area, with coffee cups in hand
situation: Alice says she loves travelling because it broadens her understanding of the world. Wally, who recently got a cubicle near a window, claims he now sees the world as an alleyway between himself and the parking garage. Alice calls this dumb, and Wally replies that the alley people would disagree.
punchline: Wally's tiny window view of an alley is his idea of broadened horizons, and he absurdly defends it by citing the opinion of the alley people.
summary: A coworker's boast about worldly travel is met with another's pathetic claim that his new window seat gives him his own limited view of the world.

title: Engineer Out-Argues His FBI Interrogator

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: FBI secret facility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am a nonviolent Hindu. You use violence as a tool, and your religion is centered around one of Islam's prophets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... technically, you're closer to being a radical Islamic terrorist than I am.

transcript.speaker: FBI Agent
transcript.text: I hate engineers.

situation: Dilbert is tied up in a chair and being interrogated by an FBI agent who suspects him of terrorism. Dilbert calmly argues that he is a nonviolent Hindu while the agent, who uses violence and follows a religion built around an Islamic prophet, is the one who better fits the terrorist profile. The agent has no rebuttal.
punchline: Dilbert's engineer-style cold logic turns the profiling argument back on his interrogator, who can only respond with irritation at engineers for being right.
summary: A bound prisoner uses airtight logic to show that his interrogator matches the terrorist profile better than he does, leaving the agent annoyed at engineers.

title: Boss Demands Replies to Late-Night Texts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why didn't you answer my text last night?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have no social life, and you aren't dead, so there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I own you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoever said honesty is refreshing never heard any.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert for not responding to a text message sent the night before. When Dilbert hesitates, the Boss argues that since Dilbert has no social life and isn't dead, he has no excuse for being unreachable. The Boss then declares that he owns Dilbert, and Dilbert responds with a sarcastic remark about honesty.
punchline: The Boss's blunt, insulting honesty about owning his employee's free time makes Dilbert sarcastically observe that honesty is not actually refreshing.
summary: A manager scolds his employee for ignoring an after-hours message and bluntly insults his personal life, prompting a wry comment about candor.

title: One Button, Eleven Functions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I simplified the user interface as you suggested.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You wanted one button to do eleven different functions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It wasn't easy, but I think you'll be pleased.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you want to turn up the volume. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You hold the button for exactly five seconds. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then double-tap, and double-tap again. Then hold for exactly six seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then press it all the way down, then halfway up, then 27% back down. And hold for nine seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could admit that you don't know anything about interface design.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never!

setting: Office, at a desk with a device that has a single button
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has simplified a device's user interface as the Boss demanded, reducing it to a single button that performs eleven functions. He demonstrates the absurdly complicated sequence of holds, taps and partial presses needed just to turn up the volume. He then offers the Boss an alternative: admit he knows nothing about interface design.
punchline: The Boss would rather endure an unusable, ridiculous interface than ever admit his design instruction was wrong.
summary: An engineer meets a clueless manager's demand for a one-button gadget with a maddening press-and-hold ritual, and the manager's pride keeps him from backing down.

summary: Asked to name the main barrier to a project's success, an employee points straight at his manager, who only wants the answer left vague on paper.

summary: A coworker's morbid goal of dying triumphantly meets Dilbert's plan for digital immortality, and the simulation hypothesis casts doubt on which of them has already finished.

punchline: Dilbert's attempt to be clever about her long checklist counts against him, as his comment adds yet another requirement to her list.
summary: A man's quip about a woman's exhaustive dating checklist only manages to lengthen it.

summary: A slow network turns out to be caused by most employees streaming questionable clips, and the boss's only complaint is that he wanted to do the same.

summary: A lonely, broke young coworker asks for advice and gets a deadpan reply that he is only a hybrid car away from becoming a rideshare driver.

punchline: An inert block of wood is passed off as artificial intelligence, and the engineer's deadpan claim that it is moody and silent gets turned into a joke about wives, which the engineer flips into an insult against the wood.
summary: An inventor's lump of lumber earns a Nobel nomination for mimicking human smarts, and a joke about its sulky silence backfires on the boss.

summary: Wally dodges a request for help by claiming a lofty title, then reveals that the job consists of sipping coffee while doing nothing.

setting: Office break room or conference table
situation: Dogbert sits across a table from Dilbert, both with coffee mugs, and observes that Dilbert's daily work has done nothing to improve the world. Dilbert doesn't argue; he calmly stands up to leave, saying he's late for doing nothing useful. Dogbert dismissively replies that he's already forgetting Dilbert's name.
punchline: Dilbert cheerfully admits his job is useless, and Dogbert responds by treating him as instantly forgettable, underlining how insignificant his work is.
summary: A sarcastic dog chides an engineer for showing up to work without ever fixing the world, and the engineer shrugs off the critique as he heads back to meaningless tasks.

title: Wife Called Me About Curling Iron

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you two hours late for work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your wife didn't want to bother you, so she called me and asked if I would go to your house and see if she left her curling iron plugged in.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you believe me, or do you want to risk being the first person she calls next time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well played.

situation: The Boss confronts Wally, who holds a coffee cup, about arriving two hours late. Wally invents a story that the Boss's wife asked him to check her curling iron at the Boss's house. He then pressures the Boss to accept it by suggesting that doubting him would make the Boss the first person she calls next time.
punchline: Wally turns his lame excuse into a trap: challenging it would imply the boss's wife prefers calling a coworker over her husband, so the boss grudgingly accepts it.
summary: A late employee dodges blame by fabricating a story that implicates his boss's wife and daring the boss to question it.

title: Forging Approval During a Reorg

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to get approval from the head of marketing, but the reorg makes it impossible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The outgoing director says I need to ask the incoming director, but that person hasn't been named.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bring me solutions, not problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Forgery it is.

setting: Office, in front of the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert explains to his boss that he cannot get a required approval because a reorganization has left the head of marketing role in limbo. The outgoing director sends him to the incoming director, who hasn't been named yet. When the boss tells him to bring solutions rather than problems, Dilbert picks up a pen and decides to forge the approval.
punchline: Management's demand for solutions instead of problems, applied to an impossible bureaucratic situation, leaves forging the approval as the only solution available.
summary: Stuck in a leadership vacuum and scolded for raising problems, an employee takes the boss's advice literally and opts for fraud.

title: Wrong Answers Are Fine If Wanted

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: What are the odds that you made this complicated spreadsheet without any critical errors?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does it matter, as long as it gives me the answer I want?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It should.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But ask yourself if it does.

situation: An employee holding a phone to her ear asks the boss how likely it is that the complicated spreadsheet he made is free of critical errors. He replies that accuracy is irrelevant as long as the result gives him the answer he wants. She says it should matter, and he tells her to ask herself whether it actually does.
punchline: The boss openly admits he values a spreadsheet for producing the conclusion he wants rather than for being correct, and implies that in practice nobody really cares about accuracy.
summary: A manager shrugs off doubts about his error-prone spreadsheet because it delivers the result he was hoping for.

title: Electric Cars: Impressive Until Discovered Wrong

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're getting into the electric car business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because it sounds impressive and it will take years for anyone to figure out we did it wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll have new jobs by then.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just turn my job into a criminal conspiracy?

situation: The Boss announces the company is entering the electric car business. When Dilbert asks why, the Boss explains it merely sounds impressive and that it will take years for anyone to discover the company botched it. He adds that they will have new jobs by then, prompting Dilbert to complain that his job has just become a criminal conspiracy.
punchline: The Boss's plan to launch an impressive-sounding venture and be gone before the failure is discovered amounts to knowingly planning a fraud, and Dilbert is now an unwilling accomplice.
summary: A manager reveals a new product line is chosen purely for show, with the failure expected to surface only after everyone has moved on.

title: Disliking People You Get to Know

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: People are complaining that you're antisocial.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only dislike the people I get to know.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Then why do you get to know them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It happens by accident when they talk.

situation: Catbert, the Evil Director of Human Resources, tells Dilbert that coworkers are complaining he is antisocial. Dilbert explains that he only dislikes people he gets to know, and Catbert asks why he gets to know them at all. Dilbert replies that it happens by accident when they talk.
punchline: Dilbert treats conversation as an unavoidable hazard that leads to getting to know people, which is what makes him dislike them, so he is antisocial in self-defense.
summary: Called out by HR for avoiding coworkers, an introverted engineer says the problem is that other people keep speaking and revealing themselves.

title: Social Justice Warrior Dinner Invitation Rejected

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I'm a social justice warrior. That means I'm on your side. Do you want to go to dinner with me?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No, thanks. I'm into men.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I am a man.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Don't make me turn around and prove you wrong.

situation: A male coworker in a yellow shirt announces he is a social justice warrior and therefore on a female coworker's side, then asks her to dinner. She declines, saying she is into men, implying he doesn't count. He protests that he is a man, and she retorts without turning around that he shouldn't make her prove him wrong.
punchline: The woman flatly insults his masculinity, implying he is not man enough to attract her, which deflates his attempt to use his social justice credentials as a pickup line.
summary: A coworker tries to leverage his activist identity to land a date, only to be shot down with a jab at his manliness.

title: Checking Pulse for Boredom Death

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop checking the time when I talk to you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wasn't checking the time. I was checking my pulse to see if I'm dying from boredom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope this is a coincidence.

situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for glancing at his watch during a conversation. Dilbert replies that he was actually checking his pulse to see whether he was dying of boredom. In the last panel Dilbert has apparently keeled over, with only his feet visible above the desk, while the Boss nervously hopes it's a coincidence.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically claims to be checking whether the Boss's talking is killing him from boredom, and then he seemingly actually dies, leaving the Boss worried he caused it.
summary: A manager's irritation at being rudely timed turns to alarm when his bored employee seems to collapse and die on the spot.

title: Two Ways To Avoid Listening

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There are two good ways to avoid listening to others.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: 1) Do all of the talking yourself, and 2) be too busy to listen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds sim-plistic.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm late for a meeting.

situation: Wally walks down the hall holding a coffee cup and lecturing Dilbert on how to avoid listening to people. He lists two methods: dominate the conversation, or be too busy to listen. When Dilbert objects that this sounds simplistic, Wally ignores him, cuts the conversation off, and waves goodbye.
punchline: Wally demonstrates the second technique on the spot by dismissing Dilbert's feedback with a claim of being late for a meeting, proving he really doesn't listen.
summary: A coworker explains how to tune out other people, then proves his point by brushing off the first person who tries to answer him.

title: Invented Device Is Just Like People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard you invented a device with human intelligence and human emotions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I ask it a question?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: It's in a bad mood. It's not talking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! It's just like people!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: You'd better leave before you make it cry.

setting: Small office or lab with a desk
situation: The Boss visits an engineer who supposedly invented a device with human intelligence and emotions. The engineer says the device is in a bad mood and refuses to talk, and the Boss is impressed by how lifelike it is. The engineer then warns him to leave before he makes it cry, sipping coffee while the device never actually appears or does anything.
punchline: The engineer has no real invention and cleverly passes off non-responsiveness as human-like moodiness, and the gullible Boss accepts it as proof of success.
summary: A boss is easily convinced that a silent, invisible gadget has genuine human emotions because its sulking matches how people behave.

title: Dogbertium Exists Without Questions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My particle accelerator has discovered a new fundamental particle that I call "Dogbertium."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Its properties are awesomeness and mystery.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One of the mysteries is that it only exists when people don't ask too many questions.

setting: A lecture hall stage with a podium and curtains, facing an audience
situation: Dogbert, speaking at a podium, announces that his particle accelerator has discovered a new fundamental particle named after himself. He describes its properties as awesomeness and mystery, then adds that it only exists when the audience doesn't ask too many questions.
punchline: The particle's convenient 'property' is that it vanishes under scrutiny, which is a transparent way of shielding a bogus scientific claim from any questioning.
summary: A scientific announcement is quietly rigged so that the discovery can only be believed by an audience that never probes it.

title: Facebook Politics Ruins Coworker Opinions

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I saw your political opinion on Facebook and now I think you're an awful person.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What did you think about me before?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't think about you before.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds like I got promoted.

situation: Alice tells Wally that after seeing his political opinion on Facebook she now thinks he is an awful person. Wally calmly asks what she thought of him before, and Alice admits she never thought about him at all. Wally sips his coffee and concludes that having her think badly of him is an improvement.
punchline: Wally is so thoroughly ignored at work that being judged as an awful person counts as a promotion in attention.
summary: A coworker's disapproval of a social media post turns out to be the first time anyone has bothered to form an opinion of the office slacker.

title: Phone Time Beats Small Talk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The weather will be good this weekend.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stop right there.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your proposed topic of conversation is far below the level of entertainment I can get from my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how conversations work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're interrupting my phone time.

situation: Dilbert tries to make small talk about the weekend weather with a coworker who is absorbed in her smartphone. She curtly shuts him down, saying her phone is more entertaining than his topic. Dilbert admits he does not understand how conversations work, and Dogbert, also on a phone, complains that Dilbert is interrupting his phone time.
punchline: Everyone is so absorbed in their phones that ordinary conversation is treated as an annoying interruption, and even the dog resents being disturbed.
summary: A coworker dismisses Dilbert's weather chat as inferior to her phone, and even Dogbert is too busy scrolling to talk.

title: Smart People On Both Sides

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed that there are smart people on both sides of every political issue?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe it only seems that way to you because you're not one of the smart ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I seem smart?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't realize you were trying.

setting: Conference room meeting table, then the office break area
situation: Dilbert remarks to a coworker at a meeting table that there are smart people on both sides of every political issue. The coworker retorts that it only seems that way because Dilbert isn't one of the smart ones. Dilbert then asks Wally if he seems smart, and Wally says he didn't realize Dilbert was trying.
punchline: Dilbert gets insulted twice in a row, first by the coworker and then by Wally, whose reply implies Dilbert doesn't come across as smart and isn't even making an effort.
summary: A mild political observation from Dilbert earns him one put-down about his intelligence, and then a second, even blunter one from Wally.

title: Just A Guy In A Box

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to think the work I'm doing here will change the world.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your project didn't get funded because Carol forgot to put a meeting on my calendar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is, however, a non-zero chance that I'm just a guy sitting in a box.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer in his cubicle, imagining his work will change the world. A cheerful coworker with a coffee cup strolls up and casually tells him his project was denied funding because Carol forgot to schedule a meeting. Dilbert then reflects that he may just be a guy sitting in a box.
punchline: His grand belief in the importance of his work is crushed by the trivial administrative slip that killed his project, leaving him to conclude his job may be meaningless.
summary: A hopeful engineer learns that a scheduling oversight sank his project and starts doubting that his cubicle work matters at all.

title: Elbonian Religion: Three Strikes Policy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you Elbonians have a religion?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Of course we do! We're not savages!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We believe in killing anyone who offends us three times in a row.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Harsh.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: That's two.

setting: Workplace or visit with an Elbonian, Dilbert holding a coffee cup
situation: Dilbert asks an Elbonian whether his people have a religion. The Elbonian indignantly says yes, then explains that his faith demands killing anyone who offends him three times in a row. Dilbert calls this harsh, and the Elbonian replies that this was the second offense.
punchline: The Elbonian counts Dilbert's casual criticism as his second offense, implying Dilbert is one remark away from being killed.
summary: A casual question about faith turns into a deadly countdown when an Elbonian tallies his visitor's reactions as insults.

title: Counselor's Advice Just Adds Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have too much work, and it's stressing me out.

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: I've been reading about this sort of situation.

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Try writing down all the things that make you feel grateful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be more work!

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: For your anger issues, try keeping a journal of all the times you lose your temper.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That would be more work!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has anyone ever taken your advice?

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Do you know the guy in marketing with the eye patch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He followed your advice?

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Half of it.

situation: Dilbert complains to a counselor that he has too much work and is stressed. Each coping suggestion, like keeping a gratitude list, gets rejected as more work, and the counselor's anger-journal idea gets the same reaction from an angry person (shown shouting from a building). When Dilbert asks if anyone has ever taken the counselor's advice, the counselor cites the marketing guy with the eye patch.
punchline: The counselor's advice is so bad that the one person who took it only followed half and ended up with an eye patch, implying he lost his temper violently.
summary: A therapist's homework-style stress remedies keep burdening an overworked patient, and the only success story involves a coworker's mysterious eye injury.

title: Thermostat Trade for Boss Lookout

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My cubicle is near the thermostat and your desk has the best view of our boss's office.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll see that you get the temperature you want if you warn me whenever our boss is on the move.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you give me 76 degrees?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa! That'll cost you extra, Lucifer.

situation: Wally proposes a trade to a coworker with a bob haircut: he controls the thermostat near his cubicle, and she has a good view of the boss's office. He offers her the temperature she wants in exchange for warnings whenever the boss is approaching. When she asks for a balmy 76 degrees, Wally says that costs extra and calls her Lucifer.
punchline: Wally treats a mild 76 degrees as a hellish, premium request, charging extra and calling her Lucifer, which shows how petty office bartering and thermostat wars can get.
summary: A lazy employee barters control of the office thermostat for early warnings about the boss, then hikes the price when his partner asks for a warm temperature.

title: Boss Tricked by Virtual Reality Goggles

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I convinced our boss to wear virtual reality goggles all day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good job, Wally! I've never seen you work so many hours!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Reality is nice, but I find it limiting.

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has convinced the boss to wear virtual reality goggles all day. The goggled boss then praises Wally for working more hours than ever, while Wally stands nearby doing nothing. Wally ends by saying he prefers the boss's fake reality to the real one.
punchline: Wally exploits the boss's VR goggles to make him believe in a hardworking Wally who doesn't exist, and he declares reality limiting because the illusion lets him slack off without consequence.
summary: A lazy employee gets his manager hooked on a headset so the manager happily imagines a productive workforce that isn't there.

title: Mom Monitors Fitbit With Drone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: This is your mom. I've been monitoring your Fitbit and...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Whatever you're doing, cut it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: It was disturbing on many levels.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Mom drone" behind you.

setting: Dilbert's home, via phone call from his mom's house
situation: Dilbert's mom phones him to say she has been watching his Fitbit data and tells him to stop whatever activity she saw. She adds that it was disturbing on many levels. Dogbert then points out that a "mom drone" is hovering right behind Dilbert, implying she is spying on him in person too.
punchline: Dilbert's mom is not only monitoring his fitness tracker data but also sending a drone to spy on him directly, making the surveillance even more invasive and embarrassing.
summary: A mother's phone scolding over her son's wearable fitness data takes an extra creepy turn when a surveillance drone is spotted hovering behind him.

title: Quasimodo Posture or Attitude Problem

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This job is turning me into Quasimodo.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it mostly a posture thing, or do you have some of Quasi's attitude as well?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's wrong with my posture?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I could ask you what's wrong with his attitude.

situation: Dilbert, hunched over, complains that his job is turning him into Quasimodo. A coworker asks whether the problem is just his posture or whether he has the hunchback's attitude too. When Dilbert defensively asks what's wrong with his posture, she retorts that she could ask the same about Quasimodo's attitude.
punchline: Dilbert protests the posture criticism but lets the insult to his attitude slide, so the coworker's reply implies his attitude really is bad, since she turns the question around and gets no defence of it.
summary: A slouching worker blames his job for making him a hunchback, and a colleague pointedly asks whether his sour disposition has changed as well.

title: Selling Buy-In for Cash

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need everyone's buy-in on my project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can have my buy-in for $25.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ted only charged me $15.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It isn't my fault that Ted is a bad negotiator.

situation: Dilbert holds up a paper and tells a seated coworker he needs everyone's buy-in on his project. The coworker offers to sell her buy-in for $25. In the final panel, with an office building shown, she says Ted only charged $15 and that it isn't her fault Ted is a bad negotiator.
punchline: The coworker treats project support as a commodity for sale, and she shamelessly blames the earlier price, which Ted charged, on Ted's bad negotiating skills while pushing her own price up.
summary: A colleague turns a request for project support into a paid transaction and then shrugs off the lower rate someone else charged.

title: Breathe Smarter, Not Harder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm happy to announce that we launched our company's spaceship to Mars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We only had enough in the budget to give them oxygen for three-quarters of the trip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I told them to breathe smarter, not harder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called leadership.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: The Boss announces to a meeting that the company has launched a spaceship to Mars. He reveals that the budget only covered oxygen for three-quarters of the trip, and that his solution was to tell the astronauts to breathe smarter, not harder. He proudly calls this leadership while Dilbert and the other attendees sit listening.
punchline: The Boss thinks a clichéd motivational slogan can replace the missing oxygen he failed to budget for, endangering the astronauts while praising himself as a leader.
summary: A manager brags about sending a spaceship to Mars with too little air, offering the crew a catchy slogan instead of oxygen.

title: Out-Suffering Wallet Complaints at Work

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I hate to complain, but it hurts when I sit on my wallet for too long.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I risked an honor killing to pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: This is why I hate to complain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know a hundred ways to eat a spider.

situation: A bald coworker mentions a minor discomfort from sitting on his wallet. Asok immediately tops it with a far more extreme hardship, and Dilbert follows with an absurd boast about eating spiders. The coworker gestures at them in exasperation, noting this is exactly why he avoids complaining.
punchline: Any small complaint gets one-upped by someone with a wildly more dramatic story, so complaining is never worth the trouble.
summary: A mild gripe about a sore backside is steamrolled by colleagues who trade increasingly grim and bizarre hardships.

title: Doctor's Note Forbids Any Criticism

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I have a note from my doctor.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It says I'm too sensitive to handle criticism.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't understand all the medical details.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It has something to do with the mind-body connection.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: One minor criticism from you and my lungs will collapse.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If that happens, you'll need to pinch my nose, create a seal with your mouth, and reinflate them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This doctor's note looks like your handwriting.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ow! My lung!

situation: A bald employee in a green shirt hands his boss a doctor's note claiming he is too sensitive to be criticized, because any criticism could collapse his lungs. He even explains how the boss should perform mouth-to-mouth to reinflate them. The boss points out that the note appears to be in the employee's own handwriting, and the employee responds by clutching his chest and feigning lung pain.
punchline: The employee's forged medical excuse is exposed as fake, and he doubles down by faking a collapsed lung rather than admit it.
summary: A worker tries to shield himself from feedback with a dubious medical note, then fakes a symptom when his boss spots the forgery.

title: Worst Employees Sent to Mars

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the Mars spaceship project going?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Good. I picked our worst employees to be on the first flight, just in case it explodes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good thinking.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We have two ways to win and no way to lose.

situation: The Boss asks a horned-hair manager how the Mars spaceship project is progressing. The manager explains that the first flight will carry the company's worst employees in case the ship explodes. The Boss praises the idea, and the manager boasts that the plan cannot lose.
punchline: Management treats its least valued staff as expendable test subjects, so a deadly failure counts as a win because it gets rid of them.
summary: A manager proudly staffs a risky first space mission with the weakest workers so that either success or a fatal explosion benefits the company.

title: Everyone Blames Everyone, Including Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our salespeople are blaming marketing for the low demand.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing is blaming engineering for making a product no one wants.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I blamed our customers for misleading us about their needs.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now I don't feel so bad about our price-gouging.

setting: Office break area with coffee cups, plus an exterior shot of a corporate building
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Asok that sales is blaming marketing for weak demand. An establishing shot of the building explains that marketing in turn blames engineering for building an unwanted product. The Boss then announces he has blamed the customers for misleading the company, which lets Asok feel justified about overcharging them.
punchline: Once every department has passed the blame along, the company ends up blaming its own customers, which conveniently excuses price-gouging them.
summary: After a chain of departments each pin a failed product on another, management settles on faulting the buyers themselves.

title: Rotating Lies For The CEO

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our CEO stopped by to see how long before we finish the new software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whose turn is it to lie to him?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I blamed Elbonian hackers last week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're using all the good ones!

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that the CEO dropped by to ask when the new software will be finished. Dilbert asks whose turn it is to lie to the CEO, and the coworker says he already blamed Elbonian hackers last week. Dilbert protests that he is using up all the good excuses.
punchline: The team treats lying to the CEO about project delays as a routine chore with a rotating schedule, and Dilbert complains that his coworker is exhausting the supply of believable excuses.
summary: Two employees casually take turns inventing fake reasons for a late software project, and one is accused of burning through the best excuses.

title: Reality Show About Phone Charging

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm creating a reality TV show about ten people locked in a room with one electrical outlet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The central tension will revolve around their daily struggle to charge their phones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is violence allowed?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, but my producers get a big bonus if it happens anyway.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside path
situation: Dilbert walks outside with Dogbert, who pitches a reality TV show about ten people locked in a room with a single electrical outlet, fighting over phone charging. Dilbert asks whether violence is allowed, and Dogbert says it is not, but his producers are rewarded if it breaks out.
punchline: Dogbert officially bans violence while admitting the producers are financially incentivized to provoke it, mocking how reality TV manufactures conflict for ratings.
summary: Dogbert describes a manipulative reality show premise where contestants squabble over one outlet, with producers secretly rewarded for any brawls.

title: Van Gogh PR Strategy for Exploding Phones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We hired the Dogbert Public Relations firm to help us with our exploding phone problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We have two choices. We can either recall all of the phones, or we can convince people that having one ear is cool.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Recalls are expensive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, the Van Gogh strategy it is.

situation: The Boss explains that the company hired Dogbert's PR firm to deal with its phones that explode. Dogbert offers two options: recall every phone or persuade the public that having only one ear is fashionable. Because recalls cost too much, the Boss picks the second option.
punchline: The company would rather make customers who lose an ear to exploding phones believe it is trendy, like Van Gogh, than pay for a recall.
summary: A PR consultant gives a company the choice between a pricey product recall and a campaign to make losing an ear fashionable, and management happily takes the cheaper, absurd route.

title: Boss Refuses Escalated Hard Issues

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to escalate an issue to you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. Get it away from me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like issues. Especially the hard ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for all the nothing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shoo! Go!

setting: Boss's office, with an exterior building shot in the final panel
situation: Dilbert comes to his boss to escalate an issue, but the boss immediately refuses to deal with it. The boss says he dislikes issues, particularly hard ones. Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for doing nothing, and the boss shoos him away.
punchline: The manager's whole function is supposed to be handling escalations, yet he rejects any problem that is difficult, so Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for his complete lack of help.
summary: A manager waves off an employee's escalation because he would rather not deal with difficult problems, earning a sarcastic thank-you.

title: Bulking Up Before Weigh-In

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next month is Employee Health Awareness Month, so we decided to have a weight-loss competition.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll start on the first of the month, and the winner gets a week of paid vacation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When he thinks back on this, he'll realize he shouldn't have given us three weeks to bulk up before the first weigh-in.

situation: The Boss announces a weight-loss competition for Employee Health Awareness Month, with a week of paid vacation for the winner. Since the contest doesn't start for three weeks, two heavyset coworkers (one is Dilbert, the other Wally) quietly note that this gives everyone time to gain weight first.
punchline: The boss's poorly designed contest gives employees weeks of advance notice, so they can deliberately gain weight beforehand to make their later weight loss look more impressive.
summary: A manager's slimming contest has a built-in loophole that his staff plan to exploit by eating their way up to a higher starting weight.

title: Sinking Out of the Wrong Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just realized I'm in the wrong meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My best bet is to slowly sink below the table and slip away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someday, when my grandkids ask what I did for a living, I'm going to say I was unemployed.

situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table and realizes he is in the wrong meeting. He decides to quietly sink below the table to sneak out unnoticed, and by the last panel only the top of his head is visible. His coworkers sit stoically as he disappears.
punchline: Dilbert's thoughts reveal that his job is so meaningless that he'd rather tell his grandkids he was unemployed than admit what he actually did.
summary: Realizing he has wandered into the wrong meeting, an engineer plots a stealthy escape beneath the table while privately reflecting on how pointless his career is.

title: Hitler's Unwashed Socks Acquisition

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I accidentally talked the board into buying a company that has a tainted reputation.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How bad is the taint?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Imagine Hitler's unwashed socks.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That isn't so bad.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I'm just getting started. Now imagine I make you eat those socks. . .

situation: The Boss admits he accidentally convinced the board to acquire a company with a bad reputation. Catbert asks how bad it is, and the Boss compares it to Hitler's unwashed socks. When Catbert shrugs it off, the Boss escalates by threatening to make him eat the socks.
punchline: The Boss's comparison to a notorious dictator's dirty socks is outrageous, and he then makes it worse by threatening to force his subordinate to eat them, showing he'll dump the consequences of his blunder on others.
summary: After blundering into buying a disreputable company, a manager describes the damage with a grotesque analogy and then threatens to make his underling suffer for it.

title: Pretending Your Way Through Engagement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your employee engagement coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll make you a deal. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll pretend I'm happy to be here if you pretend you believe it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need more than that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also want you to pretend you're loyal to the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can do that, if you pretend you're interested in my career development.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can we do all of that without talking?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the best way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My job was a lot harder before I figured out all the shortcuts.

setting: Office meeting room, ending in the Boss's office
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how his employee engagement is going. Dilbert proposes a mutual deal where each pretends to be happy, loyal and caring, and the Boss happily piles on more pretend obligations. They agree to do it all without talking, and the Boss later muses that his job got easier once he found shortcuts.
punchline: Employee engagement is reduced to a mutual charade in which both sides fake enthusiasm and concern, and the Boss calls this a management shortcut.
summary: A manager and his employee strike a bargain to feign happiness, loyalty and career interest so neither has to do real engagement work.

title: Wally's Jargon-Filled Training Session

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to train our new hire.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The first thing you need to know is that we never use the DPX system when the MGB is down.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: The... what and the what?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hold your questions till the end.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You can use our PX4 to tunnel into the B9 data and produce a TMNP report.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But you'll need authorization from the LDG and the MICOO.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: I don't understand any of that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I told you to hold your questions until the end.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Always remember to jost the prim-pram whenever the GIP is fleeming toward kilp.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: Maybe I should ask someone else to train me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now we're making progress.

situation: The Boss assigns Wally to train a new hire. Wally sits with his coffee and rattles off meaningless acronyms and eventually pure gibberish, refusing to take questions until the end. When the confused trainee finally suggests asking someone else for training, Wally is pleased.
punchline: Wally deliberately trains the new hire with incomprehensible jargon so the trainee will give up and go away, sparing Wally the work.
summary: A lazy employee confuses his trainee so thoroughly with acronyms and nonsense words that the newcomer asks for a different teacher, which is exactly what he wanted.

title: Crashing Over Urgent-Looking Texts

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wrecked my car because I was responding to your urgent-looking text.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For the third time in a row.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What are you implying?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you trying to kill me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I blame your bad judgment.

situation: Alice, her arm in a sling, tells a seated coworker that she crashed her car while answering his urgent-looking text, and that this is the third time in a row. The coworker asks if she is accusing him of trying to kill her. She replies that she blames his bad judgment.
punchline: Alice bluntly accuses the coworker of getting her hurt, then slyly shifts the blame by calling it his bad judgment rather than her own for texting while driving.
summary: A bandaged employee tells a coworker his supposedly urgent messages keep making her crash her car, yet she pins the fault on his judgment rather than her own.

title: Strategy Email Sounds Like Sabotage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw your email about destroying the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only email I sent you was my strategy for the coming year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, maybe I read it too fast.

situation: Dilbert walks in and tells the Boss he saw the Boss's email about destroying the company. The Boss, confused, explains that the only email he sent was his strategy for the coming year. Dilbert backpedals, saying he may have read it too quickly.
punchline: Dilbert's mistake is no mistake at all, since he implies the Boss's strategy for the year is indistinguishable from a plan to destroy the company.
summary: An employee confuses his manager's business plan with a scheme to wreck the firm, then pretends it was just careless reading.

title: Coming In Early To Avoid Boss

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I come in an hour early tomorrow and leave early?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, okay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How about five hours early?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... Sure.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's say eight hours early and you won't even see me.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee asks the boss for permission to arrive an hour early and leave early. The boss agrees, and the coworker keeps escalating the request to five hours and then eight hours early. The boss keeps saying yes without noticing what is being asked.
punchline: By stretching the 'early' arrival until it covers the whole workday, the coworker is really arranging never to be seen working while the oblivious boss approves it.
summary: An employee gradually inflates a flexible-hours request until it amounts to skipping the day entirely, and his inattentive manager approves each step.

title: Drone Holds Boss's Artificial Soul

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pay no attention to the drone. That's where I keep my artificial soul.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's still in beta, so please don't say anything that might harm it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's go around the room and give our project updates.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pow!

situation: The Boss tells his meeting attendees that a hovering drone contains his artificial soul, which is still in beta, and asks them not to say anything that could harm it. He then asks everyone to give project updates, and Dilbert, looking nervous, ends up speaking in front of the drone. The drone is destroyed with a pow as the update is given.
punchline: Asking employees to give honest project updates is exactly what would harm the Boss's soul, so the drone is immediately destroyed by the bad news.
summary: A manager parks his soul in a drone, begs the team not to upset it, then invites the very project updates that kill it.

title: Honor Killing Over Social Media Gaffe

transcript.speaker: The Boss
