transcript.text: Our company spokesperson embarrassed us on social media.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Does this qualify him for an "honor killing"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, and you're a racist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's what he said on social media.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Okay, I'm in.

situation: The Boss tells Asok that the company spokesperson embarrassed them on social media. Asok asks whether this justifies an "honor killing," and the Boss rebukes him as a racist for even suggesting it. Once the Boss shows him what the spokesperson posted, Asok immediately agrees to join in.
punchline: Asok is condemned for casually suggesting an honor killing, but after reading the offending post he happily signs on, implying the spokesperson's gaffe was bad enough to make even the Boss's disapproval irrelevant.
summary: A manager scolds a colleague for proposing an extreme punishment over a PR blunder, then wins him over simply by showing the offending post.

title: Car Rental Software Explodes Engineer's Head

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Car rental

transcript.speaker: Car Rental Clerk
transcript.text: I hope you don't have some sort of technology job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Car Rental Clerk
transcript.text: Because the user experience you are about to endure might make your head explode.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Twenty minutes later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Why do you need to type so much? !!!

transcript.speaker: Car Rental Clerk
transcript.text: We got an engineer!

situation: Dilbert arrives at a car rental counter, where the clerk warns him that anyone with a technology job may not survive the rental software's user experience. Twenty minutes later Dilbert is clutching his head in frustration over how much data he has to type, and the clerk observes that they have another engineer on their hands.
punchline: The rental company's software is so badly designed that it reliably drives technically minded customers, who can see exactly how inefficient it is, into a breakdown.
summary: A rental clerk's prediction comes true when the clunky booking system sends a tech worker into a screaming fit.

title: Exploding Phones and Too Many Laws

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're getting bad press because the batteries in our new line of mobile phones keep exploding.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Load them into a big truck and park it in front of our competitor's building.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, that would be domestic terrorism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are way too many laws.

setting: Office, with a view of a building exterior in the middle panel
situation: The Boss complains that the company's new mobile phones keep exploding because of faulty batteries and is generating bad press. His proposed fix is to load the defective phones into a truck and park it outside a competitor's building. Dilbert points out this would be domestic terrorism, and the Boss simply complains that there are too many laws.
punchline: The Boss's solution to his company's dangerous product is to commit a crime against a competitor, and he reacts to being told it is illegal by blaming the laws rather than his own idea.
summary: Faced with a fiasco of combustible gadgets, a manager suggests sabotaging a rival and then grumbles when told it is a crime.

title: Arrested Body Double Covers Everything

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I thought you got arrested for killing the creator of Garfield's body double.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Almost. They arrested my body double.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do you have a body double?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's for situations like this.

situation: Alice confronts a coworker who is calmly playing on a handheld device, saying she heard he was arrested for murdering the body double of Garfield's creator. He casually corrects her: it was his own body double who was arrested. When she asks why he has one, he explains it exists precisely for situations like this.
punchline: The coworker treats having a stand-in to take the fall for a murder as a perfectly ordinary, practical precaution, deadpanning the absurdity.
summary: A man shrugs off a murder arrest because the person taken into custody was merely his designated stand-in.

title: Doing It Fast or Doing It Well

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you get that analysis to me by Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Yes, if I do it poorly.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Alternately, I can do it well and miss your deadline by a week.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That gives me no path to success.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Welcome to the world's saddest club.

situation: A coworker asks a colleague with big curly hair to deliver an analysis by Tuesday. She explains he can have it on time only if the quality is poor, or good work a week late. When he complains that neither option leads to success, she says he has joined a club of people stuck in lose-lose situations.
punchline: Unrealistic deadlines force a choice between bad work and late work, and her sarcastic 'saddest club' remark says everyone in the office is already trapped in the same lose-lose bind.
summary: A colleague lays out the only two outcomes of a tight deadline, both unsatisfying, and welcomes her frustrated requester to the club of people with no good options.

title: Survival of the Fattest Acquisition

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not how we did it at my prior company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We bought your old company, fired all of the employees, and discontinued all of its products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How is that possible?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called "survival of the fattest." It's just science.

situation: Dilbert tells his colleagues that his previous employer handled things differently. The Boss reveals that his current company acquired that old company, laid off everyone, and killed off its products. When Dilbert asks how that could happen, the Boss justifies it as natural science.
punchline: The Boss twists Darwin's 'survival of the fittest' into 'survival of the fattest' to excuse a big, wealthy company swallowing a smaller rival, treating ruthless corporate predation as a law of nature.
summary: A boss casually admits his firm devoured Dilbert's former employer and then waves away the carnage with a mangled evolutionary slogan.

title: Dilbert Prefers Old-Job Stories

transcript.speaker: New Coworker
transcript.text: Do you want to know how we would have handled this situation at my old job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing would interest me less.

transcript.speaker: New Coworker
transcript.text: My only other topics of conversation are my health problems and TV shows you haven't seen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I stand corrected.

situation: A new coworker offers to explain how things were done at his previous employer, and Dilbert bluntly refuses, saying nothing could interest him less. The coworker responds that his only other conversation topics are his health problems and TV shows Dilbert hasn't seen, which makes Dilbert reconsider.
punchline: The coworker's alternative topics are so dull that Dilbert admits his own claim was wrong, since stories about the old job now sound like the lesser evil.
summary: A chatty newcomer's list of remaining conversation topics proves even more tedious than the one Dilbert just rejected.

title: Karma Sorts Out Mars Volunteer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need volunteers to go to Mars in the spaceship we're building.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask Ted. He's dispensable because he's a terrible engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted designed the spaceship.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Karma will sort that all out.

situation: The Boss asks for volunteers to fly to Mars in the spaceship the company is building. Dilbert suggests Ted, calling him expendable because he is a terrible engineer. The Boss points out that Ted designed the spaceship, and Dilbert shrugs that karma will handle it.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to send the incompetent engineer on a deadly mission backfires because Ted designed the flawed spaceship himself, so Dilbert cheerfully accepts that Ted's own bad work will be his punishment.
summary: A manager seeks astronauts for a Mars flight and a coworker nominates the worst engineer, who turns out to be the one who built the rocket.

title: Overhearing Terrible Investment Advice

transcript.speaker: Coworker 1
transcript.text: What's the best way to invest these days?

transcript.speaker: Coworker 2
transcript.text: Penny stocks are the best value because they only cost a penny.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I hate overhearing bad advice!

transcript.speaker: Coworker 1
transcript.text: If I were you, I'd take out a second mortgage and load up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to get involved, but I'll feel bad if I don't!

transcript.speaker: Coworker 2
transcript.text: You'll get reliable stock-picking advice from strangers on television.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Run! Cover your ears and run!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it makes you feel any less awkward, I don't know what to do now, either.

setting: Conference room table at the office
situation: Two coworkers discuss investing while Dilbert sits nearby and overhears them. Their advice gets steadily worse, from penny stocks to taking a second mortgage to trusting strangers on TV. Dilbert can't stand it, covers his ears and flees, then returns admitting he has no idea how to handle the situation either.
punchline: Dilbert is so distressed by the awful financial advice that he flees, but he can't actually do anything about it and sheepishly admits he is just as awkward and clueless about how to intervene.
summary: A man agonizes over eavesdropping on dreadful money tips, bolts from the room, and then returns to confess he has no better plan.

title: Bribing Coworker To Do Job

transcript.speaker: Seated Coworker
transcript.text: I don't have time to help.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I bribe you to do your job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am literally offering to give you my personal money to do the job your employer pays you to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you willing to turn a blind eye to my total lack of effort, or should I find a better briber?

situation: A lazy coworker sitting with a coffee cup refuses to help, saying he has no time. Dilbert offers to bribe him with his own money to do the job he is already paid to do, then asks if the coworker will also ignore Dilbert's lack of effort or if he should find a better briber.
punchline: Dilbert treats bribery as a routine service, offering to pay a coworker to do his own job and overlook Dilbert's laziness, which satirizes how entrenched corruption and apathy are in the workplace.
summary: A man tries to pay off an unhelpful colleague to do the work he is already employed for, and even expects him to tolerate his own idleness.

title: Dilbert Pads Developer's Time Estimate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm having trouble managing our web developer because I don't know how long things are supposed to take.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it really take nine months to change the font on the home page?

transcript.speaker: Web Developer
transcript.text: How much do I owe you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell him MY project normally takes two years.

setting: Office break area and a developer's cubicle
situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that he can't manage the web developer because he doesn't know how long tasks should take. Dilbert asks if nine months to change a font is reasonable, and then the developer, apparently having been tipped off, offers to pay Dilbert. Dilbert tells the Boss to say his own project normally takes two years, implying he is in on the scheme.
punchline: Dilbert is secretly taking payoffs from the web developer to give the clueless Boss inflated time estimates that make the developer's absurdly slow work look normal.
summary: A boss who can't judge how long tasks should take is fed bogus benchmarks by a coworker who is quietly being bribed by the developer.

title: Brain-Trapping the Bored Coworker

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't get too close. He's brain-trapping.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He's doing a task so boring that he has to cover his ear holes so his brain won't try to escape.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's no way for it to get out now.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did he just get taller?

situation: Wally warns a young coworker not to approach Dilbert, who is hunched over his laptop with his hands pressed over his ears. Wally explains that the task is so dull Dilbert must trap his brain inside his head to stop it escaping. Once Dilbert drops his hands, his hair spikes up and he seems taller, as if the brain is straining to get out.
punchline: The work is so mind-numbingly dull that Dilbert's own brain wants to flee, so he has to physically clamp it in, and the bulging, taller-looking head suggests it is barely holding.
summary: Dilbert has to plug his ears so his brain can't flee a deadly dull assignment, while his coworkers watch and comment from a safe distance.

title: Work-Wife Gets Insulted Instead

transcript.speaker: Boss-like coworker (man with pointy hair)
transcript.text: Alice doesn't want to be my work-wife. How about you?

transcript.speaker: Man with pointy hair
transcript.text: As your work-wife, would I be able to jokingly insult you in front of others?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sure, ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Man with pointy hair
transcript.text: Okay, I'm in. Now run along, you ignorant sack of wet fertilizer.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This is fun!

situation: A coworker with pointy hair, holding a coffee cup, asks Asok to be his 'work-wife' after Alice refused. Asok, seated at his desk, naively agrees when the coworker asks if he can jokingly insult him in front of others. The coworker immediately insults him, and Asok walks away cheerfully saying it is fun.
punchline: The work-wife arrangement is really just a one-sided excuse to insult someone, and the oblivious Asok fails to realize he's being abused and thinks it's fun.
summary: A coworker recruits a naive colleague as his work-spouse so he can heap jokey abuse on him, and the victim cheerfully enjoys it.

title: Alice Trapped in Phone Zombie Trance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Alice. Alice... Alice... Alice... Alice...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't penetrate your phone-induced zombie trance, so I'll just text you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop doing that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't hear you because I'm looking at my phone.

situation: Dilbert repeatedly calls out to Alice, who is absorbed in her smartphone and doesn't respond. He gives up and texts her instead. When Alice tells him to stop, Dilbert, now staring at his own phone, says he can't hear her.
punchline: Dilbert mocks Alice's phone obsession by texting her, then immediately falls into the same phone-absorbed behavior, ignoring her reply.
summary: A man who complains about a coworker ignoring him for her phone ends up ignoring her in exactly the same way.

title: Dilbert Insults Your Rambling Email

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see my email?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mean your two-page document that has about twelve questions for me sprinkled throughout?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, that's the one. Why haven't you responded?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's hard to answer that question while being polite.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can be honest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your email was such a disorganized mess that I assumed everything you do is doomed to fail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't want to waste half a day deciphering it just so I could be on the losing side.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Next time, just say you were busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I was busy.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert whether he saw his email. Dilbert describes it as a two-page document with a dozen scattered questions, and when invited to be honest, he explains he didn't reply because the email was so disorganized he assumed the coworker's work was doomed to fail. The coworker suggests he should have just said he was busy, and Dilbert replies that he was indeed busy.
punchline: Dilbert's brutally honest explanation for ignoring the email insults the sender, and when told to use the polite excuse of being busy, he reveals that excuse was true as well.
summary: After ignoring a sprawling, confusing message, Dilbert bluntly tells its sender why he never answered and then notes that the polite excuse would have been accurate too.

title: Blame Rolls Downhill to Engineering

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO blamed the sales department for our low revenue.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sales blamed marketing and marketing blamed engineering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Guess why I'm here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To shield me from unfair accusa-tions?

situation: The Boss stands by Dilbert's desk and recounts how the CEO blamed sales for low revenue, then sales blamed marketing, and marketing blamed engineering. Dilbert, an engineer, hopefully guesses that the Boss has come to protect him from unfair accusations.
punchline: Dilbert naively assumes his boss is there to defend him, when the boss is clearly there because the blame has now landed on engineering, meaning Dilbert.
summary: After responsibility for poor revenue gets passed from department to department, the boss arrives to hand the blame to the engineer at the end of the chain.

title: Trading Support Without Reading Proposal

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss asked me to get everyone's buy-in on this.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll agree to your stupid idea if you support my great idea later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Deal.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Should I read it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see why.

situation: Dilbert hands Alice a document and says the boss wants everyone's buy-in. Alice offers to approve his idea in exchange for his future support of hers, and Dilbert agrees. She then asks whether she should read the document, and he says there's no reason to.
punchline: The two trade approval of each other's ideas without reading them, so the buy-in is a pure political deal and the proposal's merit is irrelevant.
summary: Two coworkers swap guaranteed endorsements of their pet projects, making the actual proposal's content beside the point.

title: Followship Class for Leaderless Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm too busy to take a leadership class, so I'm sending all of you to a followship class.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that so we can learn how to follow someone who never learned how to lead?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like a good question for your follow-ship teacher.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces he is too busy to attend a leadership class himself, so he is sending his whole team to a 'followship' class instead. Dilbert points out that this means learning to follow a boss who never learned to lead. The Boss dodges the criticism by telling Dilbert to take the question to the followship teacher.
punchline: The Boss avoids any responsibility for his own lack of leadership by deflecting Dilbert's accurate criticism to a teacher of a class he just invented for his subordinates.
summary: A manager skips training he needs and ships his staff off to learn how to cope with his shortcomings instead.

title: Safety Class Versus Impossible Deadline

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to go to a mandatory safety training class right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it safe for me to miss the deadline you gave me for this assignment?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, you lose either way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmm, maybe I could work all night from home then drive to work exhausted.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to attend a mandatory safety training class immediately. Dilbert asks whether it is safe to miss the deadline for his assignment, and the Boss says he loses either way. Dilbert then considers working all night and driving to work exhausted.
punchline: Management forces employees into a no-win choice between safety training and a deadline, so Dilbert's only workaround is to do something genuinely unsafe, which defeats the purpose of the safety class.
summary: A manager's contradictory demands leave an employee so cornered that he plans to endanger himself in the name of safety compliance.

title: Buy-In Without Reading Anything

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need everyone's buy-in on this.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do I have to read it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's the sort of idea I can get behind.

situation: Dilbert holds up a document and says he needs everyone's buy-in on it. A seated coworker asks whether he has to read it first. Dilbert says no, and the coworker happily says that is an idea he can get behind.
punchline: The coworker will support any proposal that doesn't require him to read it, which shows how thoughtless and lazy workplace approval can be.
summary: A colleague agrees to support a proposal only because approving it requires no actual reading.

title: Experience Is Worse Than Pessimism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting wildly different estimates for how long it will take to write the software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Based on my experience, I say take the longest estimate and multiply it by three.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is experience exactly the same as pessimism?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Experience is much worse.

situation: The Boss holds a sheet of paper and complains that the engineers have given wildly different estimates for how long the software will take to write. Dilbert advises taking the longest estimate and multiplying it by three. The Boss asks if that is just pessimism, and Dilbert replies that experience is much worse.
punchline: Dilbert implies that his long experience with software projects shows that even pessimistic estimates are usually too optimistic, so realism looks worse than pessimism.
summary: Asked how to reconcile conflicting project timelines, Dilbert offers a gloomy rule of thumb drawn from hard-won experience.

title: Form Required To Request Forms

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a capital allocation form.

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: Do you have a form to request that form?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a form to get a form?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: That's how we keep track of the forms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, give me a form to request a form.

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: Those are online.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where online?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: I don't know. I only do paper forms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who can I ask?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: Don't drag me into this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I demand to talk to your boss.

transcript.speaker: Clerk's Boss
transcript.text: I hope you brought a boss request form.

setting: Office administration desk and corporate building exterior
situation: Dilbert asks a clerk for a capital allocation form and is told he first needs a form to request that form. The request form is only available online, but the clerk only handles paper forms and refuses to help him find it. When Dilbert demands to speak to the clerk's boss, he is told he needs yet another form to do that.
punchline: Bureaucracy is so layered that even asking to escalate a complaint requires a form, making it impossible to ever get anything done.
summary: A man trying to obtain one simple form gets trapped in an endless chain of paperwork requirements, right up to the point of asking for a manager.

title: Wally Wins By Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ranked all of you based on your performance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally came out on top because he didn't make any mistakes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He also didn't do any work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why does everyone hate winners?

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss announces to his team that he has ranked everyone on performance. Wally ranked highest simply because he made no mistakes. Dilbert points out that Wally also did no work, and Wally responds by asking why everyone hates winners.
punchline: Performance rankings that reward only the absence of mistakes end up crowning the person who does nothing, and Wally smugly plays the victim of resentment.
summary: A manager's ranking system rewards the employee who avoided errors by avoiding all effort, and that employee acts wounded when his coworkers object.

title: Fitness Band Reveals Terrible Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hacked into your fitness band and analyzed your decision-making under different conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you are hungry, tired, or stressed, you make terrible decisions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How often is that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only when you're awake.

situation: Dilbert holds a tablet and tells the Boss that he hacked into the Boss's fitness band to study how he makes decisions. He reports that the Boss decides badly when hungry, tired, or stressed. When the Boss asks how often that is, Dilbert says it is only when he's awake.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss makes terrible decisions all the time, since being awake is the only condition needed.
summary: After snooping on his manager's wearable data, an engineer concludes that the boss's judgment is bad whenever he is conscious.

title: Topping a Signature Boast

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I once signed my entire first name to a document.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing! Watch me sign my entire FULL name to that document!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes you can be predictable.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing! I don't even have free will!

situation: Dilbert brags about once signing his entire first name on a document, and a coworker immediately tries to top him by announcing he will sign his entire full name. Dilbert observes that the coworker can be predictable, and the coworker tops that too by claiming he doesn't even have free will.
punchline: The compulsive one-upper can't resist topping even an insult about being predictable, and in doing so proves Dilbert's point by boasting that he lacks free will.
summary: A man who can't stop outdoing his colleague even turns a remark about his predictability into a contest he wins by claiming to be an automaton.

title: Happy Winner Versus Freeloader

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do I keep taking on more work while you do nothing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because you optimize for productivity, while I optimize for my happiness.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That makes you a freeloader.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I prefer the label "happy winner."

situation: Alice, holding papers, asks Wally why she keeps absorbing extra work while he does nothing. Wally, sitting with his coffee, explains that she aims for productivity while he aims for his own happiness. When Alice calls him a freeloader, he calmly proposes a nicer label for himself.
punchline: Wally reframes his chronic laziness as a winning life strategy, rebranding 'freeloader' as 'happy winner' because he gets paid while others do his work.
summary: A overworked colleague confronts the office slacker, who cheerfully recasts his idleness as a smarter choice than her diligence.

title: Work-Wife Declaration Creeps Out Alice

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I decided to call you my work-wife!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gurk

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm creeped out! I'm creeped out! I'm creeped out!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just like at home.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need a shower.

situation: A male coworker holding a coffee cup announces he has decided to call Alice his 'work-wife.' Alice is horrified and repeatedly shouts that she is creeped out. He responds that this is how his real wife reacts at home, and Alice walks away saying she needs a shower.
punchline: The coworker's deadpan reply reveals that his actual wife is also repulsed by him, which makes Alice's disgust even more justified and the 'work-wife' label even more unwelcome.
summary: A colleague's awkward attempt at office intimacy backfires when his own marriage turns out to inspire the same revulsion.

title: Tiny Website Change, Huge Delay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will our new website be live this week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That depends.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you request even the slightest change, it could set things back for months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I only want to change the home page title font.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, great. I should be done by next summer.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether the new website will launch this week. Dilbert warns that even the slightest change request could set the project back for months. The Boss immediately asks for a change to the home page title font, and Dilbert sarcastically says he'll be done by next summer.
punchline: The Boss ignores the warning about changes and instantly requests one, and Dilbert sarcastically replies that the trivial font tweak will now delay the site by about a year.
summary: A manager is cautioned that any tweak will derail the website launch, then promptly asks for a tweak anyway.

title: Worst-Case Scenario Spirals Into Squirrel Coat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the worst-case scenario?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A rogue nation could insert a cyberweapon in our software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The virus could destroy all technology on Earth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lacking the means to communicate over great distances, single people would only be able to marry people who lived nearby.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could end up marrying your daughter. That would make you my father-in-law and my boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That nightmare would cause me to denounce humankind and go live in the park, naked, with a family of squirrels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When winter came, I would be forced to strangle the squirrels, one by one, to make myself a coat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tan leather, so that would be a senseless tragedy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's try to avoid that.

setting: Office, with a final exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for the worst-case scenario of a project risk. Dilbert escalates through a chain of increasingly absurd consequences: a cyberweapon destroys all technology, which leads to him marrying the Boss's daughter, then fleeing to live with squirrels and killing them for a coat. The Boss responds with mild understatement.
punchline: Dilbert's worst-case reasoning snowballs into an absurd, grisly fantasy, and the Boss calmly says 'let's try to avoid that' as if it were a reasonable risk-management conclusion.
summary: Asked to name the worst thing that could happen, Dilbert chains together a cyberattack, an arranged marriage to his boss's daughter, and a naked life among squirrels that ends in a botched fur coat.

title: Boss Demands Buy-In, Dilbert Questions Value

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll approve this if you get buy-in from the rest of the department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What value are you adding in that scenario?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not firing you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, keep up the good work.

situation: The Boss holds a document and says he will approve it only if Dilbert first gets buy-in from the rest of the department. Dilbert asks what value the Boss is adding if Dilbert has to do all the persuading. The Boss responds by saying he is not firing Dilbert, and Dilbert sarcastically tells him to keep up the good work.
punchline: The Boss's only contribution is not firing Dilbert, and Dilbert sarcastically praises him for that as though it were a real accomplishment.
summary: A manager who pushes all the approval legwork onto his employee is asked what he actually contributes, and his answer is that he hasn't sacked the person.

title: Celebrity Endorsement After Exploding Phones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to regain customer trust after our exploding phone fiasco.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need a celebrity endorsement. People trust celebrities with their life-and-death decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe a famous cartoonist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see how that could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: The Boss tells Dogbert, who is acting as a consultant, that the company must regain customer trust after its phones exploded. Dogbert recommends a celebrity endorsement and suggests a famous cartoonist. The Boss cheerfully agrees, seeing no possible downside.
punchline: Dogbert's suggestion of a famous cartoonist is a self-referential jab at the strip's creator, and the Boss's naive 'I don't see how that could go wrong' sets up an obvious disaster.
summary: After a product safety debacle, a consultant dog proposes that a well-known cartoonist vouch for the company, and the oblivious boss thinks it's a fine plan.

title: Ignored Oxygen Repair Email Kills Crew

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The crew of our first spaceship suffocated on the launchpad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently, I got an email last week asking for approval to repair the oxygen generator.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You killed them with your incompetence?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't take all the credit. It was a team effort.

setting: Office, at a desk with a computer
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells an employee that the crew of the company's first spaceship suffocated on the launchpad. He explains that he received an email asking for approval to repair the oxygen generator. When the employee accuses him of killing them through incompetence, he modestly says it was a team effort.
punchline: The boss treats a fatal failure caused by his own neglected approval as an achievement he generously shares credit for, dodging blame while sounding humble.
summary: A manager casually admits that an unread repair request led to astronauts dying, then graciously refuses to claim sole credit for the disaster.

title: Dilbert Agrees Before Being Pressured

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you finish this by Friday?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't take no for an answer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, my answer is yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I knew you wouldn't disappoint me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we just planned that for Friday.

setting: Office desk in the Boss's office
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document and asks whether he can finish it by Friday, adding that he won't accept a no. Dilbert answers yes, and the Boss is pleased. Dilbert then points out that the 'yes' only means they have just scheduled the work for Friday, with no real commitment to the Boss's expectation.
punchline: Dilbert technically agrees to the Boss's demand but turns it into a vague statement that sets the deadline as Friday without promising the work will actually be done by then.
summary: A manager insists he won't hear a refusal, and his employee cleverly says yes while committing to nothing concrete.
keywords: won't take no for an answer

title: Sending Reporters the Exploding Phones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The press says I need to resign because of our exploding phones fiasco.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you can change their minds by sending the press our new model that doesn't explode.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I already sent them the exploding phones and said it was our new model.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your way left too much to chance.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the press wants him to resign over his company's exploding phones scandal. Dilbert suggests sending reporters the new, non-exploding model to repair the company's image. The Boss reveals he already sent the press the exploding phones, passing them off as the new model.
punchline: The Boss's plan to save his job is to deliberately deceive reporters with the dangerous phones, dismissing Dilbert's honest approach as too risky and showing his willingness to harm others to protect himself.
summary: Facing calls to quit over defective handsets, a manager secretly mails the faulty devices to journalists disguised as the improved version.

title: Drone Conscience Fails To Remind

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented an artificial soul to help non-believers act morally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a small drone that follows you around and reminds you not to be a jerk.

transcript.speaker: Coworker 1
transcript.text: Did it forget to remind you today?

transcript.speaker: Coworker 2
transcript.text: My drone says I shouldn't slap you.

setting: Office, with a final shot of the office building exterior
situation: Dilbert shows coworkers his invention, a small drone that acts as an artificial soul by following a person around and reminding them not to be a jerk. In the last panel, an exterior view of the building has two voices: one asks if the drone forgot to remind someone today, and the other says his drone is the only thing stopping him from slapping the first.
punchline: The drone conscience is so necessary that its owner is only being restrained from violence by its reminder, implying Dilbert is being a jerk to the very people he is lecturing.
summary: A tiny hovering gadget meant to keep people from being unpleasant turns out to be the only thing standing between an irritated colleague and a smack.
themes: technology as a fix for character

title: Exploding Phone as Performance Reward

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations, Ted. Your job performance has earned you a new mobile phone.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Isn't this the model that has the exploding battery problem?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job performance wasn't good either.

situation: The Boss hands Ted a new mobile phone, calling it a reward for his good job performance. Ted looks at the phone and realizes it is the model known for exploding batteries. The Boss reveals that the gift is not a reward at all, because Ted's performance was poor.
punchline: The supposed reward is actually a punishment, since the phone is a dangerous exploding model and the boss admits Ted's performance was bad.
summary: A manager disguises a hazardous, fire-prone phone as a prize for an employee he secretly considers underperforming.

title: Cartoonist Spokesperson Embarrasses For Cheap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're looking for a celebrity spokesperson, but we don't have much budget for it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All we can afford is a cartoonist. Can you do the job for $75?

transcript.speaker: Scott Adams
transcript.text: Deal!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you ever done anything on social media that would embarrass us?

transcript.speaker: Scott Adams
transcript.text: I thought that's what it's for.

setting: Office meeting table, with a brief exterior shot of a company building
situation: The Boss tells a bald, bespectacled man that the company wants a celebrity spokesperson but has little budget, so he offers the job to a cartoonist for $75. The cartoonist happily accepts. When the Boss asks whether he has posted anything embarrassing on social media, the cartoonist replies that he thought embarrassment was the whole point of social media.
punchline: The cartoonist, who is a cheap stand-in for a celebrity, says he assumed social media exists to embarrass yourself, which pokes fun at both social media behavior and the company's bargain-basement hiring.
summary: A company that cannot afford a famous face hires a bargain-priced cartoonist as its mascot, and he treats public embarrassment as the purpose of online posting.

title: Elbonia Trip Versus Office Misery

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How'd your business trip to Elbonia go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not so good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got food poisoning and spent two days in a fetal position praying for death.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It must feel good to be back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's closer to a tie than you'd think.

situation: A coworker with spiky hair asks Dilbert how his business trip to Elbonia went. Dilbert explains he had severe food poisoning and spent two days curled up wishing he would die. When the coworker says it must be nice to be back, Dilbert replies that being back is almost as bad.
punchline: Dilbert implies that being back at his office job is nearly as miserable as suffering through life-threatening food poisoning in Elbonia.
summary: After a miserable business trip abroad, Dilbert admits his return to the office is almost as unpleasant as the illness he suffered.

title: Boss Ignores Dilbert's 6 AM Objections

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you take a call with our Elbonian customers at 6 a.m. tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. All I need to do is put my health at risk by not getting enough sleep tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course, I'll hate your guts for making me come to work so early.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I would expect my bad attitude to infect my co-workers and make them less productive, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My lack of sleep will affect my decision-making, obviously.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I'm working on important projects, so the ripple effect could be catastrophic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, do you still want me to be here at 6 a.m. tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't have to be a sociopath to be a manager, but it helps.

setting: Office cubicle area, with an exterior office building shot in one panel
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to take a 6 a.m. call with the Elbonian customers. Dilbert lists every harm the early start will cause: damaged health, resentment toward the boss, lowered morale among co-workers, impaired decisions and catastrophic knock-on effects. After the full list, he asks if the boss still wants him there, and the boss simply says yes.
punchline: The boss is completely unmoved by the cost to Dilbert and everyone else, which shows that a lack of empathy is practically a management qualification.
summary: A worker spells out all the damage an unreasonably early meeting will do, and his manager shrugs it off without a second thought.

title: New Developer Must Rewrite Everything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our website developer quit one week before the site was scheduled to be finished.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I hired a new one so we can finish on time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently, you have never met a website developer before.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you will be done in about a week, right?

transcript.speaker: Website Developer
transcript.text: It will take me a month just to throw away the last guy's code.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the website developer quit a week before the deadline but says he hired a replacement so the project can still finish on time. Dilbert remarks that the Boss has clearly never met a website developer. The new developer then tells the Boss it will take a month just to discard the previous developer's code.
punchline: Developers distrust each other's code so deeply that the replacement will need far longer than the remaining week, just to throw away what already exists and start over.
summary: A manager assumes a freshly hired programmer can rescue a late website, but the newcomer insists on scrapping the predecessor's work first.

title: Lost URL Across Many Channels

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the URL for that site?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I sent that to you last week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To which of my seven email addresses did you send it?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe I texted it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a bad feeling about this.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe I used Slack. Or WhatsApp. Or I sent it to someone else.

setting: Office cubicle, with an establishing shot of an office building in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker for the URL of a website, and the coworker says he already sent it last week. Dilbert points out that he has seven email addresses, and the coworker keeps listing other ways he might have sent it: text, Slack, WhatsApp, or even to the wrong person.
punchline: The coworker has no idea how or to whom he sent the information, showing how a flood of communication channels makes even a simple link impossible to find.
summary: A worker can't remember which of countless messaging tools he used to share a simple web link, leaving his colleague with no way to find it.

title: Injured Employee Misses Pointless Safety Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I fell asleep at the wheel because I stayed up all night to meet your deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had to work all night because you made me attend a mandatory safety meeting yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But at least I got my work done on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forgot to tell you the meeting got moved to next week.

setting: Office, with an exterior view of a building in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert, bandaged and bruised from a car accident, tells his boss he fell asleep at the wheel after working all night to meet a deadline. He explains that he lost the evening to a mandatory safety meeting the day before. The boss then reveals the meeting was actually postponed, so Dilbert attended it for nothing.
punchline: Dilbert's sleep-deprivation crash was caused by a mandatory safety meeting that ironically never even took place, making his suffering completely pointless.
summary: A bandaged employee blames his car crash on an all-night work session forced by a safety meeting, only to learn his manager had rescheduled it without telling him.

title: Badmouthing Ted While He's Late

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems that everyone but Ted made it to this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we proceed without Ted, our decisions will be underinformed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we try to reschedule a meeting with all of us, we will miss the critical deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks to Ted, we have two ways to lose and no way to win.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I say we use this time to say bad things about Ted to make ourselves feel better.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll start.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ted is a lazy, selfish loser.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I could travel through time, I would prevent Ted's parents from meeting.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Don't look at me like I'm the one who came late.

situation: Dilbert and his coworkers are waiting in a meeting for Ted, who hasn't arrived. Dilbert explains that starting without him or rescheduling would both cause problems, then suggests they vent by insulting Ted. Alice and Dilbert trash-talk Ted, only for him to walk in and defend himself by claiming he isn't the late one.
punchline: Ted walks in mid-insult and, rather than being embarrassed, indignantly implies the coworkers are the ones at fault for staring at him as though he were tardy.
summary: A team stuck waiting for a missing colleague passes the time by roasting him, then he turns up and acts offended.

title: Dilbert Counters Office Travel Demand

transcript.speaker: Caller (phone)
transcript.text: Let's meet at my office on Friday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or... you could waste your day traveling to my office instead.

transcript.speaker: Caller (phone)
transcript.text: You're being a jerk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You started it.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, on a phone call
situation: On the phone, someone tells Dilbert to come to their office on Friday for a meeting. Dilbert agrees, then flips the proposal by suggesting the caller waste their own day traveling to his office instead. The caller calls him a jerk, and Dilbert points out that the caller started it.
punchline: Dilbert shows the caller how selfish the demand is by turning it around, and the caller's offense at the mirrored request exposes their own hypocrisy.
summary: A phone caller expects Dilbert to travel to them, so he cheerfully proposes the reverse and then rebuts the accusation of rudeness by noting who began it.

title: Bribing Coworkers to Do Their Jobs

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I started accepting bribes from co-workers to incent me to do my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it didn't work for your employer, why do they think it will work for them?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Something about optimism.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They didn't say why?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All I know is that no one paid me to listen to them.

situation: A coworker in a green sweater tells Dilbert that he now accepts bribes from colleagues in exchange for doing his job. Dilbert points out that the incentive didn't work for the coworker's employer, so why would it work for them. The coworker says he didn't get their reasoning because nobody paid him to listen.
punchline: The coworker is so thoroughly motivated by payment that he won't even listen to explanations unless he's paid, proving how little he does without a bribe.
summary: A worker who only performs when paid off by colleagues admits he can't even be bothered to hear their rationale without compensation.

title: Fast-Acting Poison for Internet Outrage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company we acquired is making us look bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How bad?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Internet is demanding that I drink poison and apologize to the world while I die.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I'm no doctor, but I'd go with something fast-acting.

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that a company they acquired is damaging their reputation. When Dilbert asks how bad it is, the Boss says the Internet is demanding he drink poison and apologize to the world as he dies. Asked for advice, Dilbert deadpans that he'd pick a fast-acting poison.
punchline: Dilbert treats the online mob's absurd, lethal demand as a real option and offers dry, darkly sarcastic advice about which poison to choose.
summary: After an acquisition drags the company's image into the mud, the boss reports that online critics want him to poison himself, and Dilbert coolly suggests a speedy method.

title: Boredom Injury Medical Leave Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to take an extended medical leave to recover from a boredom-related injury at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You gave me a task so boring that my brain tried to escape through my lower gastrointestinal tract.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sure it wasn't that bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found brain fragments in my pants.

situation: Dilbert tells his seated boss he needs extended medical leave for a boredom-related injury. He explains that a task he was assigned was so dull his brain tried to escape through his lower digestive tract. The boss dismisses it as exaggeration, and Dilbert replies that he found brain fragments in his pants.
punchline: Dilbert's absurdly graphic claim that boring work made his brain physically leave his body underscores how mind-numbing the assignment was, and the boss's dismissal is met with gross 'evidence'.
summary: An employee requests sick leave after a tedious assignment supposedly caused his brain to flee his body in a gruesome way.

title: Naked on Elbonian Airport Television

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard you appeared naked on Elbonian television.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The only television show in Elbonia is a live feed from their airport full-body scanners.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That can't be true.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: One of our subsidiaries built the system. Here's you.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he has appeared naked on Elbonian television. He explains that Elbonia's only TV programming is a live feed from airport full-body scanners, a system built by the company's own subsidiary. When Dilbert doubts it, the coworker shows him the footage on a handheld device.
punchline: The company's subsidiary built an airport scanner system whose images are broadcast as entertainment, so Dilbert's privacy was violated by his own employer's product, and the coworker has the footage on hand.
summary: A colleague informs Dilbert that his body-scanner image is the hottest programming in Elbonia, thanks to a system his own company's subsidiary built.

title: Fired for Offending the Janitor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I have to fire you because you said something that offended the janitor.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: What did I say?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know. The janitor has a thick accent and he's terrible at charades.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Did you take care of the guy who keeps putting banana peels in the recycling?

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: He won't do it again.

setting: Office, then a hallway with two janitors
situation: The Boss tells Ted he must be fired because he offended the janitor, but cannot say what Ted said because the janitor has a thick accent and is bad at charades. In the last panel, two janitors in tall blue hats discuss whether the banana peel offender has been dealt with, and one says he won't do it again.
punchline: Ted was fired over a vague, unverifiable complaint that was probably about banana peels in the recycling, and the janitors treat his firing as a satisfying punishment for a trivial annoyance.
summary: A manager sacks an employee over a complaint he can't even understand, which turns out to be janitorial revenge for a recycling mistake.

title: Castles in the Sky, Air Force One

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that is my idea for our new product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are there any ignorant objections?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea is totally ridiculous!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's like you're trying to build castles in the sky!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you heard of Air Force One, the plane used by the President of the United States?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's basically a castle in the sky. And someone did build it.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Well, if your idea is so good, why hasn't someone already done it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm guessing that everyone else had co-workers like you.

situation: Dilbert pitches an idea for a new product at a meeting and invites 'ignorant objections.' A coworker calls the idea ridiculous and says it's like building castles in the sky, so Dilbert points to Air Force One as a castle in the sky that was actually built. The coworker then asks why no one has done it already.
punchline: Dilbert implies that great ideas never get built because people like this coworker shoot them down before they start.
summary: After a colleague dismisses his product pitch with a cliche, Dilbert counters with a flying-fortress example and then explains why good ideas go unrealized.

title: Intern Begs to Approve Project

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I hear you need everyone's buy-in to proceed with your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone except you. No one cares what interns think.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: May I please approve it so I feel alive?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... Okay. But you owe me one.

situation: An intern holding a coffee cup approaches Dilbert, who is absorbed in his phone, and mentions that Dilbert needs everyone's buy-in for his project. Dilbert bluntly says the intern's opinion doesn't count. The intern then pleads to be allowed to approve it just to feel important, and Dilbert grudgingly agrees in exchange for a favor.
punchline: The intern is so starved for any sense of significance that he begs to give meaningless approval, and Dilbert turns even that pity into a favor owed to him.
summary: A powerless intern pleads for the chance to rubber-stamp a project so he can feel relevant, and gets treated as if he's doing the favor in reverse.

title: Hit Man Complains About Worst Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought I accidentally killed the creator of Garfield, but it turns out I killed his body double.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Our boss ordered me to do the hit. I have the worst job in the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I think that body double has the worst job.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm only talking about the living.

setting: Office break area, with both characters holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he thought he had accidentally killed the creator of Garfield but actually killed the man's body double. The coworker responds that his boss ordered him to carry out the hit, so he has the worst job in the world. Dilbert counters that the body double had it worse, and the coworker clarifies he means only among the living.
punchline: The coworker dismisses the dead body double's claim to the worst job by restricting the contest to living people, a dark twist on workplace one-upmanship about whose job is worst.
summary: Two coworkers swap dark tales of a botched assassination and argue over who is stuck with the most miserable job, until a morbid technicality settles it.

title: Texting Boss While He Drives

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hold on, I have to text my boss while he's driving.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll say it's a crisis so he has to text back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it legal to kill him that way?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, I checked with a lawyer first.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert she must text her boss while he is driving. She explains she will claim a crisis so he is forced to text back. Dilbert realizes she is trying to cause a fatal accident and asks if that is legal, and she calmly says she checked with a lawyer.
punchline: Alice is deliberately trying to get her boss killed by luring him into distracted driving, and she has already confirmed with a lawyer that it is not illegal.
summary: A coworker coolly plans to bait her driving manager into a deadly text exchange, having first confirmed the legal loophole.

title: Idea Person Delegates Entire App

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I have a great idea for an app.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: And I choose you to be on my start-up team.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'll be the idea person and you do all of the technology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So ... I would be doing 100% of the work?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I already did the hard part of coming up with an idea.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Your part is just typing.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So stop complaining and type me an app.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't that easy.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Can you recommend someone less lazy?

situation: A woman with an app idea recruits Dilbert for her start-up team, declaring herself the 'idea person' while he does all the technology. When Dilbert points out he'd be doing all the work, she insists the idea was the hard part and that he just has to type. When he says it isn't that easy, she asks him to recommend someone less lazy.
punchline: The founder treats her idea as the only valuable contribution and software development as mere typing, so she labels the engineer lazy for pointing out the real effort involved.
summary: A would-be entrepreneur claims the idea is the hard part and expects an engineer to simply type up her app, calling him lazy when he objects.

title: Viral Pants-Dropping Airport Video

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My business trip didn't go well.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I took off my belt for airport security and my pants fell off. Someone took a video and everyone is sharing it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is literally the first time I wish I had friends.

setting: Office break area, coffee in hand
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that his business trip went badly: his pants fell down at airport security when he removed his belt. Someone filmed it and the video is spreading widely online. Wally looks at the video on his phone and laments that he has no friends to commiserate with.
punchline: Wally's social isolation means he has nobody to console him about his embarrassment, which is the first time he has ever regretted being friendless.
summary: A wardrobe malfunction at airport screening goes viral, leaving a loner coworker wishing someone cared enough to sympathize.

title: Boss Denies Business Class for Bonus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The flight to Elbonia is seventeen hours. Can I fly business class?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because your pain will be temporary, but I won't get my bonus if I go over budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try being a team player for once.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know Satan had a team.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a business class ticket because his flight to Elbonia takes seventeen hours. The boss refuses outright, admitting he cares more about protecting his own bonus than about Dilbert's discomfort. When the boss tells Dilbert to be a team player, Dilbert retorts that he didn't realize Satan had a team.
punchline: Dilbert insults his boss by implying he is the devil, since the boss cheerfully sacrifices an employee's comfort to protect his own bonus.
summary: A traveling employee pleads for a comfortable seat on a marathon flight, only to learn his manager would happily let him suffer to pad his own pay.

title: Ted Fired for Second Suggestion

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We need to cut our expenses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend eliminating Ted's job.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: What??? I recommend eliminating Dilbert's job!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Just because he said it first???

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's not over-analyze it.

setting: Conference room during a cost-cutting meeting, then a hallway
situation: At a meeting about cutting expenses, Dilbert recommends eliminating Ted's job. Ted angrily retaliates by recommending Dilbert's job be eliminated instead. Ted ends up carrying a box of his belongings out, indignant that he was chosen simply because Dilbert spoke first, while a coworker brushes off his complaint.
punchline: Layoff decisions are made arbitrarily, simply favoring whoever spoke up first, and management dismisses any scrutiny of the flawed logic.
summary: A budget meeting turns into a game of who points the finger first, and the person who spoke second ends up packing his desk.

title: Foreign Accent School for the Lazy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting a foreign accent school for the lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People assume you're smarter when you know more than one language.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But learning a new language takes too much work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So I'll teach you how to speak your own language with a foreign accent.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People will assume you are bilingual at the very least.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And when you use bad grammar with a foreign accent, it makes you look adorable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll never need to do another courtesy laugh, either. People will just assume you didn't get the joke.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is one of your better ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should hear it with an accent!

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a green couch
situation: Dogbert pitches Dilbert on his new business: a school that teaches lazy people to speak their native language with a fake foreign accent. He lists the benefits, such as seeming bilingual, looking adorable with bad grammar, and never needing to fake-laugh at jokes. Dilbert, holding a drink, admits it's one of Dogbert's better ideas.
punchline: Dilbert compliments the idea, and Dogbert replies that he should hear it with an accent, implying that anything sounds more impressive or charming when delivered with a fake foreign accent.
summary: Dogbert sells a shortcut to seeming worldly and charming by faking an accent instead of learning another language.

title: Wally Denies Helping Co-Workers, Not Bribes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People are telling me you are accepting bribes to help co-workers on projects.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You think I'm helping my co-workers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point. That part didn't sound right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Trust your first instinct.

situation: The Boss confronts Wally with a rumor that he accepts bribes in exchange for helping co-workers on their projects. Wally responds only by questioning whether anyone could think he helps his co-workers. The Boss accepts this as a good point and drops the matter.
punchline: Wally's defense ignores the bribery accusation entirely and relies on his reputation for laziness, which is so strong that the boss finds the idea of him helping anyone more implausible than taking bribes.
summary: Accused of taking payments for assisting colleagues, a notoriously idle employee clears himself simply by implying that he never helps anyone.

title: Killed the Wrong Cartoonist

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I killed our spokesperson, Jim Davis, yesterday, as you ordered.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You killed the wrong cartoonist!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Now I hate Mondays even more.

situation: An employee tells his boss he carried out an order to kill the company spokesperson, cartoonist Jim Davis. The boss is horrified and says he killed the wrong cartoonist. The employee then sits at his desk and reflects glumly on his mistake.
punchline: The employee mixes up Dilbert's creator with Garfield's creator, Jim Davis, and the 'I hate Mondays' line is a Garfield trait, so he has become a bit like the cat he killed the wrong man for.
summary: A worker follows a murderous order from his boss but targets the creator of a fat lazy cat instead of the intended cartoonist.

title: Dilbert Uploads His Soul Via Drone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I couldn't find any evidence that I have a soul, so I built an artificial one and put it in a drone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When my physical body dies, the drone will upload my memories and personality to the cloud to live forever.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Your soul will be trapped in a server?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I wrapped it in a virus so I can travel.

setting: A cocktail party, with Dilbert and a woman holding drinks
situation: Dilbert explains to a woman at a party that, finding no evidence of a natural soul, he built an artificial one and installed it in a small drone. The drone will upload his memories and personality to the cloud after he dies. When she asks if his soul will be stuck in a server, he says he packaged it inside a virus so it can spread and travel.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of digital immortality is to turn his soul into a computer virus that infects other systems, treating malware as the afterlife's way of getting around.
summary: A man who couldn't locate his soul builds a replacement drone and plans to spread his digital afterlife around the internet as malware.

title: Work-Life Balance Through Circular Excuses

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't do your urgent task because I'm on deadline for my boss.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't meet your deadline because I have an urgent task from a co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I finally figured out the whole "work-life balance" thing.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, turns down a coworker's urgent request by claiming he is busy with a deadline for his boss. He then tells another person that he can't meet their deadline because of an urgent task from a coworker. Finally he tells Dilbert that he has figured out work-life balance.
punchline: Wally's work-life balance is simply using every task as an excuse to avoid other tasks, so he never has to do real work.
summary: Wally dodges every request by citing a different obligation, then proudly calls his avoidance strategy a balanced life.

title: Boss Fakes Interest In Wellbeing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm supposed to act interested in your well-being to boost your job performance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No thanks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... how's your wife, or girlfriend, or same-sex partner, or loneliness?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I think that covers it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look! My productivity is soaring!

situation: The Boss visits Dilbert's cubicle and announces he is supposed to feign interest in Dilbert's wellbeing to improve his performance. Dilbert declines, but the Boss rattles off a clinical list of personal-life questions anyway. Once the Boss walks away, Dilbert sarcastically declares his productivity is soaring.
punchline: The Boss's insincere, box-ticking show of concern obviously does nothing for morale, and Dilbert's claim that his productivity is soaring is pure sarcasm.
summary: A manager robotically recites a checklist of caring questions to a bored employee, then expects an instant boost in output.

title: Vague Deadline Dodged With Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When will you finish the technical review?

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: That will depend on a variety of unknowns.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: A lot can happen between now and whenever you imagine I might be done with it.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: No one knows the future.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: I'd be a liar if I said I did, and you don't want a co-worker who is a liar, do you?

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: Or do you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Lying would be better than whatever this is.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: In that case, I'll have it tomorrow.

situation: A coworker asks a bald, bespectacled engineer when he will finish a technical review. The engineer stalls with increasingly pompous claims about unknowns and the unknowable future, framing any firm date as dishonest. The exasperated coworker says a lie would be preferable, so the engineer finally promises it for tomorrow.
punchline: Only when told he is allowed to lie does the engineer give a straight answer, showing his philosophical evasion was just stalling.
summary: A worker hides behind talk of an unknowable future to avoid giving a due date, until his colleague begs him to simply fib.

title: Board Needs a Sociopath Hitman

transcript.speaker: Man in tie
transcript.text: The famous cartoonist we hired to be our spokesperson said something bad on social media.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh no. How bad is it?

transcript.speaker: Man in tie
transcript.text: Our board voted to kill him. Do you know any sociopaths?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm the head of engineering.

transcript.speaker: Man in tie
transcript.text: Good point. Pick any one of them.

setting: Office, with a final shot of the company's office building exterior
situation: An executive tells the boss that their company's celebrity cartoonist spokesperson posted something bad on social media, and the board has voted to have him killed. He asks if the boss knows any sociopaths who could do it. The boss replies that he heads engineering, and the executive agrees that any engineer will do.
punchline: Engineers are stereotyped as sociopaths, so the head of engineering is the obvious place to find someone willing to commit murder.
summary: A company wants its controversial spokesperson eliminated and decides its engineering department is the natural recruiting pool for a killer.

title: Coworker Constantly Praises His Old Job

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I will now compare my last job to this one because it is all I ever talk about.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everyone was so much smarter at my old job. Fuh-fuh-fuh-fuh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume that's why they fired you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Lucky guess.

situation: A coworker announces that he is about to compare his previous employer to the current one, then declares that everyone at his old job was smarter, making a nervous stuttering laugh. Dilbert dryly guesses that this is why the man was fired, and the coworker admits it was a lucky guess.
punchline: The coworker's own insult about smarter colleagues is turned back on him, and his reply 'Lucky guess' sarcastically implies that Dilbert's deduction was obvious, or that he was in fact fired for being dim.
summary: A man who can't stop bragging about his former workplace gets a blunt reality check from a colleague who suspects why he left.

title: Guessing Yes Without the Pre-Meeting

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Is the software finished as your boss promised me it would be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forgot to go to the pre-meeting for this meeting, so I'll guess the answer is . . . yes?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Okay, keep up the good work!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank goodness he doesn't know what the truth even looks like.

situation: A visiting executive asks The Boss whether the software is finished as promised. The Boss admits he skipped the pre-meeting where he would have learned the real status, so he simply guesses that it is done. The executive accepts the answer and praises the team, while Dilbert quietly remarks on the executive's inability to recognize the truth.
punchline: The executive happily accepts a blind guess as a status report, showing that he can't tell truth from fiction and that no one is really checking project status.
summary: A manager who missed his briefing guesses that a project is complete, and the gullible executive he is talking to simply believes him.

title: Better Than Uber, If Silent

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I like a man who always offers to do the driving on dates.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like Uber?
