transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: But less expensive, and no waiting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you're saying I'm better than Uber?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You would be if you didn't talk.

setting: Outdoor grassy hillside path, walking together
situation: Dilbert and a black-haired woman (Tina) walk along a grassy path while she says she likes a man who offers to drive on dates. Dilbert compares this to Uber, and she agrees it would be cheaper and faster. When he asks if that makes him better than Uber, she says he would be, but only if he stopped talking.
punchline: Tina's compliment is a backhanded insult: Dilbert only beats a ride-sharing driver if he keeps quiet, since his conversation is the unwelcome part.
summary: A woman's praise of a man who drives on dates turns into a put-down when she says Dilbert would top a ride-hailing service if he just stayed silent.

title: Firing the Bottom Ten Percent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to fire the employees you ranked in the bottom 10%.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that just put someone else in the bottom 10%?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything made sense until you started talking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry.

setting: Office, standing in a corridor or workspace
situation: The Boss instructs Dilbert to fire the employees he ranked in the bottom 10%. Dilbert points out that removing them would simply push a new group of people into the bottom 10%. The Boss complains that the plan made sense until Dilbert pointed out the flaw, and Dilbert apologizes.
punchline: The Boss prefers his flawed ranking-and-firing policy to remain unexamined, so Dilbert is blamed and made to apologize for pointing out the obvious logical flaw.
summary: A manager's plan to cull the lowest-ranked workers falls apart under a simple observation, and the manager resents the observation rather than the plan.

title: Board Acquires Despicable Company Without Googling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The board is proud to announce that we will be acquiring the Gawful Media Company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that Gawful is so despicable that a crime bill has their name on it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, don't blame me. I told the board that someone should Google them.

situation: The Boss announces at a board meeting that the company will acquire the Gawful Media Company. Dilbert points out that Gawful is so despicable that a crime bill carries its name. The Boss deflects responsibility, saying he had advised the board to Google the company first.
punchline: The board committed to a major acquisition without even a basic web search, and the Boss dodges blame by noting he merely suggested that someone else should have done the research.
summary: A company buys a notoriously disreputable media firm because nobody bothered to do a simple online search beforehand.

title: Arrested for Murdering a Body Double

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: Asok, you are under arrest for murdering the creator of Garfield's body double.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's not fair! It wasn't even a real person! It was a body double!

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: Actually, body doubles are human beings too.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're going to arrest me on a technicality?

setting: Asok's office cubicle, with a police officer standing over him
situation: A police officer arrests Asok for murdering the body double of the creator of Garfield. Asok protests that it wasn't a real person, only a body double. The officer points out that body doubles are human beings too, and Asok complains about being arrested on a technicality.
punchline: Asok absurdly claims a body double isn't a real person, and then calls the officer's correct point that body doubles are human beings a mere technicality.
summary: An intern is hauled in for killing a stand-in for a famous cartoonist and tries to argue that stand-ins don't count as people.

title: Brain Escaping Through Ear Holes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to research this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This task is so boring that I'm worried my brain will try to escape out of my ear holes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not a real thing, is it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow! It's starting!

setting: Office desk in the Boss's office
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document and asks him to research it. Dilbert warns that the task is so boring his brain may try to escape through his ears. The Boss doubts this is real, but Dilbert clutches his ear in pain, claiming it has started.
punchline: Dilbert dramatizes how mind-numbing the assignment is by pretending the boredom is physically forcing his brain out of his head, a claim the gullible Boss half-believes.
summary: A worker claims a dull assignment is so tedious his brain is trying to flee through his ears, and he pretends it is already happening.

title: Declining the Hotel Turn-Down Service

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to decline your turn-down service tonight so I can have some privacy.

transcript.speaker: Hotel Staff (phone)
transcript.text: We're going to do it anyway. Good luck finding your stuff after we randomly move it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't do that! I hereby turn down your turn down of your turn-down service!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Say goodbye to your phone charger!

setting: Dilbert's hotel room, with an open suitcase, a bed and a nightstand
situation: Dilbert phones the hotel front desk to decline the evening turn-down service because he wants privacy. The hotel replies that they will do it anyway and will randomly move his belongings. Dilbert retaliates by declaring he is turning down their refusal and threatens to take the hotel's phone charger.
punchline: Dilbert escalates a petty hotel dispute into a nonsensical recursive 'turn-down of the turn-down' and retaliates with a trivial threat to steal a phone charger, mirroring the hotel's own petty harassment.
summary: A traveler's attempt to opt out of nightly bed-turning is overruled by the hotel, so he responds with an absurd counter-refusal and a petty act of revenge.

title: Spreading Ted's Ashes Around Office

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ted's widow asked us to spread his ashes around the office because he loved his job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You didn't like Ted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Was that a requirement?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Don't let anyone see you flush it.

situation: Alice carries an urn into Wally's cubicle and explains that Ted's widow wants his ashes spread around the office since he loved his job. Wally volunteers eagerly, and Alice points out he didn't even like Ted. Wally shrugs that liking Ted wasn't a requirement, and Alice, understanding his true plan, tells him to flush the ashes without being seen.
punchline: Alice assumes Wally will simply dump Ted's ashes down the toilet, mocking both Wally's indifference to a dead coworker and the idea of honoring someone's dedication to a job that doesn't care about him.
summary: A colleague's final wish gets handed to the laziest person in the office, who treats it as a chore to be disposed of quietly.

title: Firing the Bottom Ten Percent

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Company policy says I have to fire the bottom 10% of performers, so... you're fired.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I thought I was near the top.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was before I fired everyone below you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you see any problem with your system?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes, it's exhausting.

setting: Office meeting room and building exterior
situation: Dilbert, acting as a manager, tells an employee he is fired under a policy requiring the bottom 10% of performers to be cut. The employee protests that he is near the top, and Dilbert explains he already fired everyone ranked below him, so the employee is now at the bottom. Asked whether his system has any problem, Dilbert only complains that it is tiring.
punchline: Dilbert keeps firing the 'bottom 10%' until the person left at the bottom is a good performer, and the only flaw he sees in this absurd system is that it is exhausting for him.
summary: A manager applying a rank-and-yank policy repeatedly dismisses the lowest performers until a strong employee ends up at the bottom, and he regards the effort as the only downside.

title: Boss Admits Mentoring Would Backfire

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need some mentoring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is awkward.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On one hand, helping you would make me appear wise and generous.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On the other hand, it would make you a more credible threat to take my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see you as more of an adversary than a subordinate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I withhold vital information that you need to do your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've already said too much.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you learn anything?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, unfortunately.

setting: Office, at the boss's desk and in a hallway
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for mentoring. The boss lays out his reasoning, admitting that helping Dilbert would make Dilbert a threat to his own job, so he deliberately withholds information Dilbert needs. Afterward a coworker asks if Dilbert learned anything, and Dilbert says yes, unfortunately.
punchline: The boss's candid explanation of why he sabotages his subordinate is the only thing Dilbert learns, and it's a depressing lesson about office politics.
summary: A manager openly confesses that he refuses to guide his employee because he fears being replaced by him.

title: Ranked Last, Fired Regardless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company makes me rank all of my employees. I put you last because you're not an engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to fire whoever is ranked lowest, and I can't afford to lose any engineers.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What if I work harder, and do a great job?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'd fire you for not being a team player.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss tells a non-engineer employee that forced ranking put them last purely because they aren't an engineer, and the lowest-ranked person must be fired. The employee asks if working harder and doing a great job could change things, and the Boss says they'd be fired anyway for not being a team player.
punchline: The firing is predetermined, so no amount of effort can save the employee, and the Boss will invent any excuse to justify it.
summary: A manager explains that a mandatory ranking system dooms a non-engineer to dismissal no matter how well they perform.

title: Alice's Humidity-Ravaged Hair Problem

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The humidity is wrecking my hair.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please don't stare.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't promise that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're staring!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid to turn my back on it.

situation: Alice walks up to Dilbert, who is seated at a table looking at his phone, and complains that humidity has made her hair huge and wild. She asks him not to stare, but he says he can't promise that. When she catches him staring, he explains he's afraid to turn his back on her hair.
punchline: Dilbert treats Alice's frizzy, spiky hair as a menacing creature that might attack if he looks away.
summary: A coworker's wildly frizzed hair becomes so alarming that her colleague can't stop watching it, convinced it might pounce.

title: Positive Names for Doomed Spaceship

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'm looking for a name for the spaceship that I designed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about "Death Tube"?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "Space Debris"?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: "Final Resting Place."

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I was hoping for something more positive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're positive it will explode.

situation: An engineer asks a group of coworkers to help name the spaceship he designed. They suggest grim names like "Death Tube", "Space Debris" and "Final Resting Place". When he asks for something more positive, they reply that they are positive it will explode.
punchline: The engineer wants positive names, but his coworkers' only certainty is that his design will explode, which they twist into a 'positive' answer and which reveals their low opinion of his engineering.
summary: Colleagues asked to christen a spaceship keep offering morbid names, then mock the designer's request for positivity by predicting the vessel's fiery doom.
